Chrome as a library — light, fast, everywhere, and easy.
One API on Linux, macOS and Windows. Add it in a few lines.
zebkit is Chromium's engine as one library you link into your own
application: Blink, V8 with every JIT tier, PDFium, FFmpeg and the rest of
what Chrome is made of, with nothing of Chrome's browser and nothing of
Electron's runtime. Your application stays yours, in C, C++, Rust, Python,
Go or JavaScript, with its own windows and toolkit. Where it needs the web,
it adds a zebkit view; where it needs a PDF, media, compression or crypto,
it calls zebkit's API: in C, or through the bindings for Rust, Python, Go
and JavaScript (zebkit-js, and zebkit.* in the application's own pages).
- Integrate it, don't build on it. Electron is a base: an application
is built inside it, on its runtime, its windows and its packaging.
zebkit is a part: an application adds it, as it adds SQLite, and keeps
its process, its toolkit and its way of shipping. It runs inside the
application's own event loop (zebkit_init(), zebkit_pump()), and draws
in the application's windows, as frames you draw or in a child of a window
you give it, an X11 window, an NSView or an HWND (examples/native-host),
and gives back the window a page is in for the system's dialogs.
- Take what you need. Web views, in a window or off-screen with their frames handed to you; a full PDF API; saving what a page plays; your own URL schemes; native UI from JavaScript; Playwright's API and CDP for agents. Use one, or all.
- The real Chrome engine. Pages see Chromium 157: its user agent and
client hints, window.chrome, popups blocked without a click, and
nothing of a debugger attached (docs/API.md has what still differs,
Google's sign-in among it).
- Lighter than Electron. Against the latest Electron, 45.2.1: 34% smaller, a cold start in 2.3 s against 6.6, a page in 29% less memory, and the DOM, text layout and JavaScript level (Benchmark).
- No Node. No second JavaScript runtime and no IPC through one. The
application is native code, or JavaScript run by zebkit-js on the
engine's V8.
- Chromium's libraries are yours. 17 C libraries inside the engine, about
7,490 functions on each of Linux, macOS and Windows (7,487 on all three, the
rest each system's own), exported under zebkit_vendor_*: SQLite, LevelDB, BoringSSL,
zlib, Zstandard, Brotli, ICU, HarfBuzz, libxml2, libwebp, libjpeg-turbo,
FFmpeg, dav1d, Opus, libvpx, FreeType and PDFium. You do not ship them twice.
- PDF built in. A full API on Chromium's PDFium: rendering and tiles, text with layout, search, outline, links, annotations as an editor has them (line endings, cloudy borders, free text with callouts and rich text, stamps, replies and states, measurement, XFDF and FDF), forms, redaction, page editing, merging, attachments, metadata, and signatures checked for integrity; hooks for an application's own annotation kinds, appearances, events with undo, render layers, OCR, fonts, trust and actions. In C, Rust, Python and JavaScript.
- 2D drawing and shaping. <zebkit/canvas.h> on the engine's Skia and <zebkit/text.h> on its HarfBuzz, without shipping either again.
- Media, saved as it plays. Whatever a page plays, a file, MSE/DASH or
HLS, written to MP4 or WebM as it was sent, without re-encoding and
without a second download (<zebkit/media.h>).
- Bytes as they are. A page's calls to the application go over its frame's own Mojo channel, large ones through shared memory: no base64, the page's JSON handed on as it was written, as fast as Electron's IPC for small calls and faster for large ones.
- The window around a page, from JavaScript. zebkit.ui draws
windows, prompts and dialogs with Chromium's views toolkit: signals,
JSX, Tailwind classes, and automation for tests and agents. Rich UI is
a page; zebkit.ui is the chrome around it (docs/UI.md).
- Playwright's API, natively. The whole of Playwright (locators,
actions that wait until they can be done, keyboard, mouse and touch,
routes, dialogs, downloads, contexts, workers, traces, HAR, video) runs
inside the engine, without CDP or a Node.js driver: 3 to 10 times faster
than Playwright over CDP, and a click in 3 to 5 ms instead of 33
(<zebkit/automation.h>, docs/AUTOMATION.md). Playwright's own
clients, in any of its languages, connect to it unchanged with chromium.connect().
- Made for agents. tools/zebkit-mcp gives them pages, PDFs, files, media
and native windows as MCP tools, over standard input and HTTP, within bounds
its operator sets (docs/MCP.md). They can also drive zebkit through
Playwright's API or over CDP, Chromium's own DevTools server, headless or
windowed.
- Customise it from your code, down to the desktop. Native hooks decide
what the engine does, in C, Rust, Python and JavaScript: permissions,
navigation, popups, dialogs, downloads, certificates and client
certificates, sign-in, network requests and responses at every stage,
settings at run time, your own URL schemes, what a page may call, scripts
before the page's own (docs/ROADMAP_HOOKS.md). And everything a page or
the engine would show the person or ask of the system goes through the
application: the window's frame (system, overlay or none, with the page as
the title bar), menus and the context menu, JavaScript dialogs and sign-in,
file and device choosers, screen capture, notifications, the tray, the
Dock and taskbar, sharing, the system's theme, power and displays
(Fit it into the desktop, docs/SYSTEM_INTEGRATION.md).
- Safe by default. A page has no zebkit object unless the
application grants it, per view, per origin and per capability; the
origin is the browser's, never the page's word; the renderer stays
sandboxed; permissions a browser would ask about are not granted.
A package is a directory with the library, the helper, the engine's data
and include/. Either unpack a release's archive
(zebkit-<version>-<target>.tar.xz from GitHub's releases), or build one:
mise run r      # dist/release (Linux), dist/release-macos (macOS), dist/release-windows; hours the first time
Each archive also holds the tools, built for its system beside the library
and ready to run from where it is unpacked: zebkit-run, zebkit-js and
zebkit-mcp (.exe on Windows, sandboxed there too).
On an Apple silicon Mac with full Xcode installed, scripts/dist.sh release
builds the engine locally into dist/release. Then run
scripts/example.sh macos-basic to build and launch the C embedding demo
in dist/example/Zebkit Embedded Browser.app.
Building needs about 30 GB for Chromium's tree (docs/BUILD.md). Below,
$PKG is the package directory.
zebkit is a library: your program keeps its main() and calls it. This
one renders a PDF's first page to a PNG and reads its text, with PDFium
and the image encoders inside zebkit, and nothing else to install:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <zebkit/pdf.h>
#include <zebkit/services.h>
/* Your program, your main(): zebkit is just a library it calls. */
int main(int argc, char **argv) {
    char *error = NULL;
    zebkit_pdf *pdf = zebkit_pdf_open_file(argv[1], NULL, &error);
    if (!pdf) {
        fprintf(stderr, "%s\n", error);
        return 1;
    }
    /* The first page as a PNG, at twice its size. */
    zebkit_pdf_render_options options = {.scale = 2, .background = 0xffffffff};
    int width, height;
    uint8_t *rgba = zebkit_pdf_render(pdf, 0, &options, &width, &height, &error);
    size_t size;
    uint8_t *png = zebkit_image_encode(ZEBKIT_IMAGE_PNG, rgba, width, height, 0, &size, &error);
    fwrite(png, 1, size, fopen("page1.png", "wb"));
    /* And its text. */
    char *text = zebkit_pdf_text(pdf, 0, &error);
    printf("%d pages; page 1 says: %.80s\n", zebkit_pdf_page_count(pdf), text);
    zebkit_free(text), zebkit_free(png), zebkit_free(rgba);
    zebkit_pdf_close(pdf);
    return 0;
}cc thumb.c -I$PKG/include -L$PKG -l:libzebkit.so.1 -Wl,-rpath,$PKG -o thumb   # Linux
cc thumb.c -I$PKG/include -F$PKG -framework Zebkit -Wl,-rpath,$PKG -o thumb   # macOS
./thumb report.pdf     # 2 pages; page 1 says: Quarterly report ...
The PDF API, compression, crypto, URLs, image codecs, ICU and the
libraries inside the engine (zebkit_vendor_*, FFmpeg's among them) need
no engine loop (docs/API.md); only HTTP through the engine's network
stack and web pages do.
Web pages need the engine running. Here the engine runs the loop: the
program starts it with zebkit_main() and works in its callbacks. A program
with its own loop (GTK, Qt, AppKit, winit) starts it with zebkit_init() and
calls zebkit_pump() (examples/native-host).
#include <stdio.h>
#include <zebkit/zebkit.h>
static void printed(zebkit_view *view, const char *json, const char *error, void *data) {
    printf("%s\n", json ? json : error);
    zebkit_quit();
}
static void loaded(zebkit_view *view, zebkit_load_event event, const char *url, void *data) {
    if (event == ZEBKIT_LOAD_FINISHED)
        zebkit_view_evaluate(view, "document.title", printed, NULL);
}
static void ready(void *data) {
    zebkit_view *view = zebkit_view_new("https://example.com/", 1024, 768);
    zebkit_view_on_load(view, loaded, NULL);
}
int main(int argc, char **argv) {
    return zebkit_main(argc, argv, ready, NULL);
}cc app.c -I$PKG/include -L$PKG -l:libzebkit.so.1 -Wl,-rpath,$PKG -o app   # Linux
cc app.c -I$PKG/include -F$PKG -framework Zebkit -Wl,-rpath,$PKG -o app   # macOS
clang-cl /MT app.c /I%PKG%\include %PKG%\zebkit.dll.lib %PKG%\zebkit_sandbox.lib   # Windows
./app --remote-debugging-port=9222     # with CDP for Puppeteer and Playwright
On Windows the executable takes part in Chromium's sandbox: it links
zebkit_sandbox.lib and calls zebkit_win_startup() first in main()
(docs/WINDOWS.md).
Without unprivileged user namespaces the engine refuses to start and says why: install its
helper, or in a container of its own add --no-sandbox (docs/SANDBOX.md).
The application serves its own pages from a scheme and gives them
functions to call; a page has nothing of zebkit unless it is granted.
/* The page calls zebkit.app.greet("Ada"). */
static void greet(zebkit_view *view, const char *origin, const char *args_json,
                  zebkit_call *call, void *data) {
    char answer[256];
    snprintf(answer, sizeof answer, "{\"hello\": %s}", args_json);
    zebkit_call_resolve(call, answer);
}
/* app://main/... from ./ui, in ranges for media. A real handler refuses "..". */
static void serve(zebkit_request *request, void *data) {
    char path[1024];
    snprintf(path, sizeof path, "ui%s", zebkit_request_url(request) + sizeof "app://main" - 1);
    zebkit_request_respond_file(request, path, NULL);
}
static void closed(zebkit_view *view, void *data) { zebkit_quit(); }
static void ready(void *data) {
    zebkit_view *view = zebkit_view_new("app://main/index.html", 1024, 768);
    zebkit_view_grant(view, "app://main", ZEBKIT_ALLOW_APP | ZEBKIT_ALLOW_PDF, NULL);
    zebkit_view_bind(view, "greet", greet, NULL);
    zebkit_view_on_close(view, closed, NULL);
}
int main(int argc, char **argv) {
    zebkit_scheme_register("app", ZEBKIT_SCHEME_STANDARD | ZEBKIT_SCHEME_SECURE | ZEBKIT_SCHEME_FETCH);
    zebkit_scheme_handle("app", serve, NULL);
    return zebkit_main(argc, argv, ready, NULL);
}
In the page, every call is a promise and bytes are Uint8Arrays:
const reply = await zebkit.app.greet('Ada');            // the application's function
const pdf = await zebkit.pdf.open(await (await fetch('report.pdf')).bytes());
const rgba = await pdf.render(0, {scale: 2});           // a page as pixels
const hits = await pdf.search('revenue');
const packed = await zebkit.compress('zstd', bytes, 19);
const hash = await zebkit.crypto.digest('SHA-256', 'abc');
Each thing the engine would show the person, or ask of the system, has a default that works and a function of the application's that replaces it. Nothing reaches the system without a decision the application can take; without a function, a page gets what a careful browser gives it, and nothing at all where a browser would ask.
import zebkit
zebkit.scheme_register("app")   # served by a scheme_handle(), as in the C example above
zebkit.init(["app"])
# The page is the title bar: the window's buttons over it, dragged by its CSS.
view = zebkit.View("app://main/index.html", 1000, 700, options={
    "frame": "overlay", "controls": {"height": 40, "color": "#1b1d2a", "symbolColor": "#ffffff"},
    "dragRegions": {"source": "css", "origins": ["app://main"]}})
# The application's menu bar (macOS) and keys, with state that changes in place.
zebkit.app_set_menu([{"title": "File", "items": [{"title": "Autosave", "id": "autosave", "checked": True}]}],
                    lambda item: zebkit.app_update_menu_item(item, checked=False))
# A tray icon, the Dock's or the taskbar's badge, and the page's notifications as the application's.
tray = zebkit.Tray(open("icon.png", "rb").read(), "My application")
zebkit.app_set_badge("3")
zebkit.on_notification(lambda event: print("show in my own UI:", event))
# What a page asks for: a USB device, a screen to capture, a colour, a share.
view.on_device_chooser(lambda request: request.respond(request.metadata["devices"][0]["id"]))
view.on_media_access(lambda request: request.respond(True, None, "view"))
view.on_share(lambda request: request.respond(True))
# The system: its theme and its changes, the session's lock, the screens.
zebkit.on_environment_changed(lambda env: print("dark" if env["colorScheme"] == "dark" else "light"))
zebkit.on_power_event(lambda event: print(event["event"]))   # suspend, resume, lock, unlock
print(zebkit.displays())
docs/SYSTEM_INTEGRATION.md has each surface, its default, its status on
each system and why; docs/API.md has the calls in the four languages;
examples/custom-titlebar is a window whose title bar is the page.
zebkit on crates.io, with
zebkit-build to put the engine
beside your program; the build downloads the engine for your system once and
checks its SHA-256.
[dependencies]
zebkit = "0.4.0"
[build-dependencies]
zebkit-build = "0.4.0"// build.rs: puts the engine beside the executable
fn main() { zebkit_build::bundle(); }
// main.rs
fn main() {
    std::process::exit(zebkit::run(|| {
        let view = zebkit::View::new(Some("https://example.com/"), 1024, 768);
        view.grant("https://example.com", zebkit::Allow::APP, None);
        view.bind("greet", |call| {
            let answer = format!("\"hello, {}\"", call.args_json());
            call.resolve(&answer)
        });
        view.on_close(zebkit::quit);
    }));
}
ZEBKIT_DIR points the build at a package (bindings/rust/README.md).
zebkit on PyPI is the binding; the
engine is the archive for your system from the
releases of the same version,
with ZEBKIT_DIR pointing at it:
pip install zebkit
export ZEBKIT_DIR=/path/to/zebkit-0.4.0-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnuimport zebkit                      # pure Python on ctypes: nothing to compile
def ready():
    view = zebkit.View("https://example.com/")
    view.grant("https://example.com", zebkit.ALLOW_APP)
    view.bind("greet", lambda name, origin: f"hello, {name}")
zebkit.main(ready)                 # the engine is found in $ZEBKIT_DIR
bindings/golang, on cgo: views, pages calling Go
functions, the application's schemes, the page hooks and the system's
services, on Linux and macOS. Build with the engine's headers and library:
go get github.com/ikey4u/zebkit/bindings/golang@main
export CGO_CFLAGS="-I$ZEBKIT_DIR/include" CGO_LDFLAGS="-L$ZEBKIT_DIR -Wl,-rpath,$ZEBKIT_DIR"os.Exit(zebkit.Main(func() {
    view := zebkit.NewView("", 1024, 768)
    view.Grant("https://example.com", zebkit.AllowApp, "")
    view.Bind("greet", func(call *zebkit.Call) {
        call.Resolve(fmt.Sprintf("\"hello, %s\"", call.Args))
    })
    view.OnClose(zebkit.Quit)
    view.Load("https://example.com/")
}))
zebkit-js runs an ES module on the engine's V8, for applications
written in JavaScript, with views, the same APIs, and native windows:
// zebkit-js main.mjs
const view = new zebkit.View('app://main/index.html', {width: 1024, height: 768});
view.grant('app://main', ['app', 'pdf']);
view.bind('save', async (name, text) => {
  await zebkit.fs.writeFile(`${zebkit.args[0]}/${name}`, text);
  return {saved: true};
});
view.on('close', () => zebkit.quit());// zebkit-js examples/ui/todo.mjs: a window of native widgets, styled with
// Tailwind's classes and kept up to date by signals (an excerpt)
const {h, signal, computed, For, window} = zebkit.ui;
const [tasks, setTasks] = signal([]);
const done = computed(() => tasks().filter((t) => t.done).length);
const Task = (task) =>
  h('view', {class: 'flex-row items-center gap-3 p-3 rounded-xl bg-[#141a2e]'},
    h('button', {class: 'w-8 h-8 p-0 rounded-full bg-[#7c5cff] text-white',
                 onClick: () => toggle(task)}, task.done ? '✓' : ''),
    h('text', {class: 'grow text-[#e6e8f2]'}, task.text));
window({title: 'Today', width: 460, height: 680}, () =>
  h('view', {class: 'flex-col gap-4 p-6 bg-[#0b1020]'},
    h('text', {class: 'text-3xl font-bold text-white'}, 'Ship something great'),
    h('text', {class: 'text-sm text-[#8a91aa]'}, () => `${done()} of ${tasks().length} done`),
    h(For, {each: tasks}, Task)));
Playwright's API runs inside the engine (docs/AUTOMATION.md): every
command of Playwright's protocol, in the application's process, with no
CDP and no Node.js. From C it is one call, zebkit_automation_call(view, "Frame.click", "{\"selector\": \"#go\"}", done, data); Python has it with
Playwright's names:
import zebkit
from zebkit.automation import Page, expect, run
async def test():
    page = Page()
    await page.goto("https://example.com/")
    await expect(page).to_have_title("Example Domain")
    await expect(page.get_by_text("documentation examples")).to_be_visible()
    await page.screenshot(path="example.png")
    zebkit.quit()
zebkit.main(lambda: run(test()), ["python", "--headless"])
Playwright's own clients, its test runner and its other languages included, connect to the engine's Playwright endpoint unchanged:
tools/zebkit-run --headless --playwright-port=0   # prints "Playwright listening on ws://127.0.0.1:<port>/<token>"const browser = await chromium.connect('ws://127.0.0.1:<port>/<token>');
const page = await (await browser.newContext()).newPage();
Agents and tools that speak CDP drive zebkit as they would drive Chrome:
tools/zebkit-run --headless --remote-debugging-port=9222 https://example.com/
Any CDP client connects to http://127.0.0.1:9222.
An MCP client gets the engine's capabilities as tools from tools/zebkit-mcp, a
separate program, with file access and origins denied until its operator grants
them (docs/MCP.md):
ZEBKIT_DIR=<package> cargo build --release --manifest-path tools/zebkit-mcp/Cargo.toml   # or the archive's
zebkit-mcp --allow-origin https://example.com --allow-write ~/agent-files   # on standard input and output
zebkit-mcp --http 8931 --allow-origin '*'                                   # on 127.0.0.1, with a tokenmise example:linux:basic    # examples/window.c: a browser window
mise example:rust:window    # the same in Rust
mise example:ffmpeg         # examples/ffmpeg.cpp: a library inside the engine
(cd examples/gpui-browser && cargo run --release)   # a tabbed browser in GPUI-KIT
Against the latest stable Electron, 45.2.1 (Chromium 156), measured the same way:
one harness, the same pages, two thin hosts that do the same thing, every process
counted, medians of 5 to 11 runs taking turns, Linux x86-64, 2026-11-06 and 07
(scripts/electron-compare.sh, docs/reports/electron-compare.md).
- Size. zebkit keeps the whole web platform applications use: HTML, CSS, JavaScript with every JIT tier, WebAssembly, WebGL, media with H.264 and AAC, HTTP/3, PDF.
- Speed. Chrome's own profile-guided optimization reaches Blink because
zebkit is built with CFI as Chrome is; every speed change is kept only when it
gains more than it costs in size (docs/SIZE_AND_SPEED.md).
- Where Electron is ahead: one process fewer a page, and memory on two of the ten sites, YouTube and The Verge, where advertising and video decide.
- How each number is made: docs/SIZE_AND_SPEED.md.
The same Playwright commands three ways, headless, medians
(docs/reports/automation-bench.md, scripts/automation-bench.sh):
- zebkit's API, in-process: your program calls the command through
<zebkit/automation.h>, Python's zebkit.automation or Rust's zebkit::automation; it runs inside the engine, with no Node.js and no protocol.
- Your Playwright scripts, connected to zebkit: Playwright's own Node.js
client, unchanged, with chromium.connect() to zebkit's endpoint; its test
suite (v1.64.1) passes 4,046 of its tests there, Chrome 4,196
(docs/AUTOMATION.md, section 7).
- Playwright with Chrome: Playwright as usual, over CDP.
- Why it is faster: one call in the renderer where Playwright's server makes several round trips over CDP, no JSON between processes, no Node.js process (Playwright's alone reached 175 MiB); and the frames a click's checks wait for are made at once instead of at 60 Hz on a page without a display.
- A screenshot is 2.7 times faster: the fresh frame it takes is made at
once instead of at the next 60 Hz tick, the PNG is deflated at level 1 with
the Up filter (2 ms where Chrome's default level takes 13, for 59 KB
instead of 40 KB on this page), and the picture's shared memory is made in
one call instead of a page fault at a time. What is left of the 12 ms is the
page's frame (4 ms), copying the picture out of the compositor (4 ms) and
encoding it (4 ms). The pixels themselves, with no encoding
(zebkit_automation_screenshot_pixels(), zebkit's own), take 9 ms. Over CDP
zebkit does what Chrome does: frames at 60 Hz, Chrome's PNG.
upstream/ (Chromium's tree, about 30 GB), out/, dist/ and .cache/
are generated and not tracked.
zebkit is Chromium plus a small patch set (patches/), built from source.
Where Chromium lacks something an application needs, zebkit patches
Chromium rather than working around it (docs/BUILD.md).
zebkit is free software under the GNU Lesser General Public License, version 2.1 or (at your option) any later version: LICENSE. Applications of any license, open or closed, can use it as a library.
The engine contains Chromium and the libraries it uses (Blink, V8, Skia,
PDFium, FFmpeg in its LGPL configuration, ICU, SQLite, BoringSSL and others),
each under its own license. Every release archive carries LICENSE, a
NOTICE that says where its source is, and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt with
every third-party license text. docs/LICENSING.md says
what an application that ships zebkit has to do.
Contributions are accepted under the same license: by sending a pull request you agree that your contribution is licensed under the LGPL 2.1 or later, as the rest of zebkit.

Magenta solar panels may be agrivoltaics' cleverest trick yet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
14:31:39 UTC
23:31:39 KST

Vegetable farms and solar farms both need lots of sunlight and open space. But how do we divide our limited lands between these two priorities? One elegant solution is to put crops and solar panels on the same land—and share the broad spectrum of incoming sunlight between them.
A new study in Cell Reports Physical Science does this with photovoltaic cells that are semi-transparent: They capture some wavelengths of sunlight to make electricity, while letting the wavelengths most critical to photosynthesis pass through and reach the plants below. The new study suggests that broccoli can be grown in the magenta shade of these solar panels—without sacrificing the harvest.
Agrivoltaic schemes—putting plants and solar on the same land – could help us avoid clearing more land for human use. Climate studies suggest that this might work especially well across a wide sunbathed swath of the United States, from Texas up to Nebraska and west to California. Devoting just one percent of U.S. farmland to agrivoltaics could cover up to 20 percent of the nation’s electricity needs.
But traditional photovoltaic panels are opaque—and by shading plants, they can reduce crop yields. So engineers are trying to create new photovoltaic cells that divide the spectrum of sunlight between plants and electricity generation—similar to how governments segment different frequency bands for television, radio, cell phones, and other uses.
A 2020 study looked at panels that allow red wavelengths, critical for photosynthesis, to pass through—while harvesting green and blue wavelengths to make electricity. Basil grown under these panels produced similar yields, while spinach yields decreased. But the researchers estimated that by selling both electricity and crops, farmers growing spinach could generate 35 percent more income from the same land.
In the newest study, scientists evaluated a different kind of semi-transparent panel that lets most red and some blue wavelengths pass through—casting a magenta light on the plants—while converting much of the rest to electricity.
Broccoli cultivated under them grew more slowly, requiring an additional 25 days for harvest, but produced roughly the same yield. Meanwhile, these magenta sunscreens improved the microclimate below, reducing the “vapor pressure deficit”—a measure of when plants need to halt photosynthesis to avoid excessive water loss. This may have improved the plants’ efficiency in converting sunlight into plant biomass, which increased by 2.8- to 4.5-fold compared to unshaded plants.
The shaded plants’ levels of macronutrients such as calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus were either higher than or similar to unshaded plants, while levels of some micronutrients such as iron, copper, and zinc were slightly lower.
This was only a preliminary study. Future studies should look at larger plots, farmed across multiple seasons, and in different locations with varying climate and sunlight. It suggests that for now, the future of agrivoltaics might be best seen through rose-colored glasses.
Lu et al. “Evaluating land productivity with semi-transparent colored CdTe thin-film PV and broccoli cultivation in agrivoltaic systems.” Cell Reports Physical Science, 2026.
Image: Broccoli growing beneath semi-transparent, colored solar panels at the experimental site at Kärrbo Prästgård farm in Sweden. ©Silvia Ma Lu

14:31:39 UTC
23:31:39 KST

Vegetable farms and solar farms both need lots of sunlight and open space. But how do we divide our limited lands between these two priorities? One elegant solution is to put crops and solar panels on the same land—and share the broad spectrum of incoming sunlight between them.
A new study in Cell Reports Physical Science does this with photovoltaic cells that are semi-transparent: They capture some wavelengths of sunlight to make electricity, while letting the wavelengths most critical to photosynthesis pass through and reach the plants below. The new study suggests that broccoli can be grown in the magenta shade of these solar panels—without sacrificing the harvest.
Agrivoltaic schemes—putting plants and solar on the same land – could help us avoid clearing more land for human use. Climate studies suggest that this might work especially well across a wide sunbathed swath of the United States, from Texas up to Nebraska and west to California. Devoting just one percent of U.S. farmland to agrivoltaics could cover up to 20 percent of the nation’s electricity needs.
But traditional photovoltaic panels are opaque—and by shading plants, they can reduce crop yields. So engineers are trying to create new photovoltaic cells that divide the spectrum of sunlight between plants and electricity generation—similar to how governments segment different frequency bands for television, radio, cell phones, and other uses.
A 2020 study looked at panels that allow red wavelengths, critical for photosynthesis, to pass through—while harvesting green and blue wavelengths to make electricity. Basil grown under these panels produced similar yields, while spinach yields decreased. But the researchers estimated that by selling both electricity and crops, farmers growing spinach could generate 35 percent more income from the same land.
In the newest study, scientists evaluated a different kind of semi-transparent panel that lets most red and some blue wavelengths pass through—casting a magenta light on the plants—while converting much of the rest to electricity.
Broccoli cultivated under them grew more slowly, requiring an additional 25 days for harvest, but produced roughly the same yield. Meanwhile, these magenta sunscreens improved the microclimate below, reducing the “vapor pressure deficit”—a measure of when plants need to halt photosynthesis to avoid excessive water loss. This may have improved the plants’ efficiency in converting sunlight into plant biomass, which increased by 2.8- to 4.5-fold compared to unshaded plants.
The shaded plants’ levels of macronutrients such as calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus were either higher than or similar to unshaded plants, while levels of some micronutrients such as iron, copper, and zinc were slightly lower.
This was only a preliminary study. Future studies should look at larger plots, farmed across multiple seasons, and in different locations with varying climate and sunlight. It suggests that for now, the future of agrivoltaics might be best seen through rose-colored glasses.
Lu et al. “Evaluating land productivity with semi-transparent colored CdTe thin-film PV and broccoli cultivation in agrivoltaic systems.” Cell Reports Physical Science, 2026.
Image: Broccoli growing beneath semi-transparent, colored solar panels at the experimental site at Kärrbo Prästgård farm in Sweden. ©Silvia Ma Lu

French Onion Chicken
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
14:30:00 UTC
23:30:00 KST

I worked in a French restaurant for ten years, and nothing takes me back quite like a warm bowl of French onion soup. This French Onion Chicken trades the spoon for a fork, with juicy, golden-seared chicken smothered in sweet caramelized onions, savory gravy, and plenty of gooey melted Swiss cheese. Everything comes together in one skillet, right on the stovetop, bringing all that deep, restaurant-style flavor into your own kitchen. Not bad for just $1.75 per serving!
All recipes are rigorously tested in our Nashville Test Kitchen to ensure they are easy, affordable, and delicious.
French Onion Soup, Meet Chicken Dinner
One thing I love about classic French onion soup is how just a handful of inexpensive ingredients can develop so much flavor. It’s a classic for a reason, and those caramelized onions are a huge part of it! I wanted that same deep onion flavor in this chicken version, so giving them enough time to turn deeply golden, sweet, and almost jammy makes all the difference. It takes a little patience, but the process is simple, and I’ll walk you through it step by step. Then I use flour, butter, beef broth, dried thyme, and a splash of balsamic vinegar to create a rich gravy with just enough acidity to balance the sweetness of the onions.
To make the most of the chicken, I slice two large breasts in half horizontally to make four hearty portions. (The ones I used were huge anyway, so each serving is still plenty generous!) The thinner pieces also cook more quickly and evenly, which is a nice bonus. I also swap the traditional Gruyère for budget-friendly Swiss, then pop a lid on the skillet until the cheese is nice and melty. You still get that deliciously cheesy French onion finish without needing to turn on the oven (and the simple cheese swap helps you save a little money in the process!).
Recipe Success Tips
- Remove the chicken as soon as it reaches 165°F to keep it juicy. Thin chicken cutlets can dry out quickly if overcooked, so I always recommend checking the thickest part with a meat thermometer. Once they reach 165°F, transfer them to a plate and loosely tent with foil. This gets them off the direct heat while the onions cook and helps retain some warmth without continuing to fry the chicken.
- Slice the onions thinly so they caramelize more evenly. Thinner slices soften and release moisture faster, helping them caramelize in less time than thick chunks. I follow our caramelized onions recipe for this dish, but use vegetable oil along with the butter to help keep costs down.
- Give the onions about 40 minutes (and don’t rush them with high heat!) I start them over medium-high heat for 5 minutes, then reduce to medium for about 35 minutes, stirring occasionally. You’re looking for onions that are deeply golden-brown and very soft. If they’re browning too quickly or starting to burn, lower the heat. You want to develop their natural sweetness, not scorch them!
- Cook the flour in the butter before adding the broth. I push the caramelized onions to one side of the skillet, then stir the flour into the melted butter to create a roux. This thickens the broth into a rich, creamy gravy. Stir well as you add the broth to prevent lumps, and add an extra splash if the gravy gets too thick.
What to Serve with French Onion Chicken
The only thing missing from the classic French onion soup experience is the crostini! Try toasting thin slices of our no-knead bread until crisp and serving them alongside the chicken to scoop up the extra sauce. A store-bought baguette works just as well if you’re not much of a baker. As for sides, I served my French onion chicken with creamy mashed potatoes and sautéed green beans, just like you see in the photo here. The potatoes are perfect for soaking up the rich gravy, while the garlicky green beans add a little freshness and crunch. You could also spoon the chicken and onions over creamy polenta for something different.
how to make French Onion Chicken step-by-step photos
Gather and prepare your ingredients: Grate 1 cup (100g) of Swiss cheese from a block. I recommend freshly grated cheese because it melts more smoothly than pre-shredded cheese, which often contains anti-caking ingredients. Thinly slice 2 onions (about 3 cups) and set them aside with your cheese. If you’re using Better Than Bouillon like I am, prepare 1½ cups of beef broth according to the package directions.
Slice the chicken breasts: Using a sharp knife, carefully slice 2 boneless, skinless chicken breasts (about 1½ lbs. total) in half horizontally to make 4 thinner cutlets. Try to keep them as even in thickness as possible so they cook at the same rate.
Season the chicken: Pat the chicken dry with paper towels, then season both sides evenly with ½ tsp salt and ½ tsp black pepper. Removing excess surface moisture helps the chicken develop a golden-brown crust instead of steaming in the skillet.
Sear until golden brown: Heat 1 Tbsp vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Once the oil is hot and shimmering, add the chicken in a single layer, working in batches if needed. Cook undisturbed for 4-5 minutes per side, until the outside is beautifully golden brown and the thickest part reaches an internal temperature of 165°F. Cooking time will vary depending on the thickness of your chicken.
Keep the chicken warm: Transfer the cooked chicken to a plate and loosely tent it with aluminum foil while you prepare the onions. This keeps the chicken off the direct heat so it doesn’t become dry or tough.
Add the butter and oil: In the same skillet you used to sear the chicken, add the remaining 1 Tbsp vegetable oil and 1 Tbsp butter. Leave those flavorful stuck-on bits from the chicken in the pan, as they’ll add extra savory depth to the onions and gravy.
Add the onions: Add the 2 thinly sliced onions (about 3 cups) and remaining ¾ tsp salt to the skillet. Stir to coat them evenly in the oil and melted butter.
Start softening the onions: Cook over medium-high heat for about 5 minutes, stirring often. The onions will begin to soften, release moisture, and shrink in volume, but they won’t be deeply browned just yet.
Caramelize the onions: Reduce the heat to medium and continue cooking for about 35 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the onions are very soft and deep brown in color. Keep an eye on them and lower the heat if they’re browning too quickly.
Once caramelized, push the onions to one side of the skillet, add the remaining 2 Tbsp butter and 2 minced garlic cloves (about 1 Tbsp), and cook for 1 minute, until the garlic is fragrant.
Add the flour: Sprinkle in 2 Tbsp all-purpose flour (20g) and stir to combine with the butter and onions. Cook for 1 minute to remove the raw flour taste.
Make the French onion gravy: Pour in 1½ cups beef broth, 1 Tbsp balsamic vinegar, and ½ tsp dried thyme. Stir well, scraping the bottom of the skillet to incorporate all those flavorful browned bits. Cook for about 2 minutes, stirring, until the sauce thickens into a spoonable gravy.
Return the chicken to the skillet: Add the 4 cooked chicken cutlets and any accumulated juices back to the skillet to warm through. Spoon some of the caramelized onions over each piece of chicken so they’re coated in the delicious gravy.
Add the cheese: Evenly divide 1 cup (100g) of grated Swiss cheese over the 4 chicken cutlets, piling it on top of the caramelized onions.
Melt the cheese and serve! Place a lid on the skillet for about 3 minutes, or until the Swiss cheese is completely melted and gooey. Serve hot with plenty of rich onion gravy spooned over the top. Enjoy!
Storage & Reheating
Store leftover chicken with the French onion sauce in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3-4 days. The gravy will thicken as it cools, but it does loosen up again when reheated.
Reheating
I recommend reheating the chicken gently in a covered skillet over medium-low heat to help keep it from drying out. Add a splash of beef broth or water to loosen the gravy if needed, and heat until the chicken reaches 165°F. You can also reheat individual portions in the microwave, covered, in short intervals.
Freezing
You can freeze this French onion chicken in an airtight, freezer-safe container for up to 3-4 months for best quality. Just keep in mind that the melted Swiss cheese may change texture slightly after freezing. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator before reheating as directed above.

- The buttery lemon sauce with briny capers makes our Chicken Piccata a delicious alternative when you’re craving something lighter but still full of flavor.
- If garlic is more your thing, try our Creamy Garlic Chicken for golden-seared chicken breasts smothered in a rich sauce made with a whole head of garlic.

Jonathan Kanter is using AI to take on Big Tech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
14:10:44 UTC
23:10:44 KST

When Jonathan Kanter stepped down as head of the Justice Department’s Antitrust Division in 2024, he set out to keep fighting to dismantle illegal monopolies. But this time, he’s continuing the fight in the private sector, and with a perhaps unexpected tool: AI.
Jonathan Kanter is using AI to take on Big Tech
The former DOJ watchdog wants to fuel antitrust cases against all kinds of monopolists.
Alongside former acting Antitrust Division chief Doha Mekki, Kanter recently launched a new tech startup, FluxCap. The team is stacked with former DOJ staffers and former Palantir engineers, and it’s selling an AI-based legal research and analysis tool that helps plaintiffs build and strengthen cases against the kinds of well-heeled companies Kanter and Mekki took on at the Antitrust Division. FluxCap is launching with a focus on antitrust cases, but it plans to expand into other practice areas as well.
Kanter imagines FluxCap as a “force multiplier” for antitrust watchdogs taking on powerful opponents in Big Tech and elsewhere.
“This, to me, it’s existential”
“This, to me, it’s existential,” he tells The Verge in an interview. “Because it’s the only way that enforcement is going to work in the long term, is if technology and other tools are able to help scarce resources go significantly further than they can today.”
FluxCap’s platform, built off proprietary technology and existing large language models, is primarily intended for research and analysis. It’s trained to pick up the facts and legal framework that will determine whether a case succeeds, then find potential holes in attorneys’ logic. To help attorneys prepare for trial, FluxCap can also help sift through vast piles of discovery materials, searching for signals that a company acted in anticompetitive ways. It’s part of a wave of legal tech tools that are using AI to try to help lawyers do more with less and make the legal process more efficient.
Getting the tool to find relevant evidence was one of the hardest parts, Kanter says. Executives are unlikely to come out and say they’re monopolists, but surrounding context can give a very specific meaning to certain messages. In the antitrust trial against Live Nation-Ticketmaster, for example, the government played a recorded phone call between the Live Nation CEO and a customer who decided to switch to a different ticketing platform. In response, the CEO reminded the customer that a new arena in town could make it harder to deliver as many concerts to his venue. The customer testified he took it as a “not-so-veiled” threat that Live Nation could cut off events programming if he didn’t also accept its ticketing service.
FluxCap’s team of former government lawyers spent months testing the system with existing and hypothetical test cases to see if it could really help build a solid argument. Getting “basic legal tools” (which Kanter calls “BLTs”) to understand that kind of nuance is difficult because “lawyering isn’t about right or wrong answers,” he says. “Both sides can be right and both sides can be wrong. And what you’re essentially trying to do is you’re trying to persuade a court, a jury, a regulator to reach a certain outcome.”
The team counts antitrust boutique firm Kressin Powers as one of its first customers, and Kanter says it’s in talks with both public and private enforcers. “It gives them that virtual capacity so that a small team can take on a large team,” Kanter says, adding that it provides the manpower of roughly “20-plus people working around the clock.”
The seeds of FluxCap began inside the Antitrust Division, where Kanter and his team were already trying to stretch their limited resources with technology. During the Biden administration, the DOJ went to trial against Google twice and brought monopolization suits against Apple and Live Nation, among other actions. But the Division’s resources and staff pale in comparison to companies with multibillion- to trillion-dollar market caps and large legal teams to review documents and mount defenses. The entire Antitrust Division was appropriated $245 million by Congress for fiscal year 2026, with more than 400 attorneys on staff across several issue areas.
“It’s just not realistic to have the resources necessary to take on these big companies”
The imbalance is even greater for state attorneys general, who have pushed forward with antitrust action as the Trump administration has hung back. Earlier this year, state AGs won a case against Live Nation that the DOJ under the Trump administration settled, and states also sued to block the Paramount-Warner Media merger before ultimately settling, when the DOJ declined. “A large state AG might have 10 people working on a case,” Kanter says. “It’s just not realistic to have the resources necessary to take on these big companies.”
During Kanter’s time as antitrust head, he and others tried AI-based BLTs but found them lacking for complex legal research. “Every antitrust lawyer has tried asking questions to ChatGPT or [AI legal research software] Harvey or one of those tools, and they do okay,” Kanter says. “But they miss the nuance.” While Kanter was at the DOJ, the Antitrust Division secured a $45.5 million grant from the government’s Tech Modernization Fund to implement better tools for managing cases and reviewing evidence. Kanter says his team “never had the opportunity to put that to work” before leaving office, but what they’re building now is “even more ambitious and better than I could have imagined when I was at DOJ.”
Tech alone can’t fully even the playing field, Kanter says. “Government is always going to be outmatched, and they desperately need more funding, and desperately need more budget, and more headcount.” Even if that happens, however, private defendants are likely to “far outweigh anything that the government could ever produce, whether it’s federal government or states or private plaintiffs,” he says. “We believe this will be the great equalizer that will allow those teams to go toe to toe with anyone regardless of their size and regardless how deep their pockets are.”

Meet Drops, the new music app bringing back the fun of sharing songs with friends
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

There’s a new music discovery app borrowing the endless vertical-scrolling format of TikTok. But instead of watching videos, users swipe through short clips of songs, hoping to stumble upon their next favorite artist.
Launched Monday by Harman, a Samsung subsidiary, Drops aims to make discovering new music feel social again.
Available on iOS and Android in the U.S., the app lets users scroll through 10- to 30-second snippets of songs, accompanied by lyrics, album artwork, artist photos, and captions. The idea is to give listeners just enough of a track to grab their attention, whether it’s a particularly good lyric, a catchy hook, or a beat that makes them want to hear more.
The company says Drops is meant to feel like a return to how people used to discover music in the first place. Before every platform’s algorithm recommendations, people often heard about new songs through friends, music blogs, or online communities. Drops is trying to recreate that experience.
“You send a friend a song and say, ‘You have to hear this.’ Then you end up texting, ‘Skip to 1:47, that’s the best part.’ The part that hits usually isn’t the first few seconds, and there wasn’t a good way to share just that moment,” Clare Hunter, general manager of Drops, told us.
Hunter explained that the idea for Drops began taking shape after Harman acquired music management software company Roon in 2023.
“I used to spend hours making mixtapes for my friends, picking the songs, the order, and decorating the cover. Drops is the version of that I always wanted,” Hunter added.
The app is easy to navigate, with tabs including “For You,” “New,” “Showcase,” and “Following,” along with relevant and trending hashtags.
Users can like, comment, repost, share, and save tracks to collections called Droplists. They can also send songs directly to other users, follow other profiles, and exchange direct messages.
To listen to the entire track, Drops offers integrations with major streaming services, including Apple Music, Qobuz, and TIDAL. Users can jump directly into the full version of the song through their connected streaming platform.
Notably, the company says it doesn’t use generative AI for audio or visuals. Songs appear as they were originally released, using official album artwork and licensed artist photography. At a time when AI-generated music and slop are becoming harder to avoid, this will likely appeal to many users.
Another part worth noting is that Drops pays rights holders and reports plays back to its partners. Those partners include Universal Music Group, Beggars Group, Empire, Symphonic Distribution, and UnitedMasters.
Plays also count toward streams on those services, meaning Drops isn’t trying to replace existing music subscriptions.
Drops is currently invite-only, with U.S. users able to join the waitlist.

Automattic debuts a platform to deploy vibe-coding apps amid a changing internet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

WordPress has been a crucial technology and content management system for websites like TechCrunch. Now, WordPress.com owner Automattic is responding to the changing state of the web by debuting a new service called Spacefast, which will allow users to deploy vibe-coded websites and apps.
Spacefast is designed to provide infrastructure for the vibe-coded apps, including databases, authentication, file uploads, emails, and analytics, to make them functional websites, apps, or services. The product competes with the likes of Lovable and Emergent, which offer both interface and rails for vibe-coded apps, but in a more open way.
Users can connect Spacefast with other agents and chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, Hermes, OpenClaw, Grok Bot, Muse, Pi, Cursor, OpenCode, and Amp. Alternatively, they can connect a Git repository to Spacefast to get started.
The product is headed by Batuhan İçöz, who worked on it during one of the company’s hackathon sprints earlier in the year. At that time, he worked on the company’s cross-platform messaging app Beeper and said that he often got Vercel links from his non-technical friends while exploring vibe coding.
“I thought there had to be a better way for everyone to set up and deploy their projects. Automattic already has good infrastructure, but we have been traditionally associated with just WordPress. I thought, why do I have to use Cloudflare when we have a CDN (content delivery network) just as good? So I started working on what was called Stattic and now Spacefast,” he told TechCrunch over a call.
İçöz eventually disseminated the solution to his friends and added more features to make the product more dynamic. Automattic soft-launched the product in September to get feedback before today’s launch. 
The company has seen varied use cases of their product, with people and organizations using it for internal mockups, slideshows, and offer-related websites. However, that’s not the only competition Spacefast has. Productivity and design software like Figma, Canva, and Notion have launched products that sit at the intersection of vibe coding, mockups, and presentations.
İçöz thinks that, compared to something like Lovable, Spacefast has the advantage of giving users a choice of their agent and using the solution their way. The counter-argument might be that a certain kind of user wouldn’t want to choose and just have everything figured out for them.
Spacefast said that it also has the advantage of being within Automattic to launch solutions like web analytics, WordPress integration, and e-commerce features (through WooCommerce) easily to compete better with the whole lot.
“For enterprises, the problem right now is IT sprawl, as their marketing teams are churning out landing pages on services like Lovable, and they want to consolidate and work with a company that understands the enterprise needs. With our existing products, we have experience serving enterprise customers,” İçöz noted.
A challenge for newly minted products in the AI world is to retain people post-launch. Users might get excited to try out a new product, and then move on to the new shiny thing within days or weeks. İçöz is cognizant of the fact and said that he expects people to churn, as they might not be interested in making apps at all.
“I think what we need to do as a product is make sure that when you build something with SpaceFast, it is so easy, and the results are so much better than without Spacefast,” İçöz emphasized.
Many websites and publishers are struggling with dwindling traffic due to AI chatbots and summaries, right now, to the point that Google itself saw its ad revenue growth drop. İçöz acknowledged that people are making websites with ChatGPT or Claude now as compared to deploying something on WordPress, and he said some sites won’t need a content management system at all as the web expands.
Spacefast comes amid turbulent months at Automattic. In an OpenAI/Sam Altman-style saga, the company’s board forced CEO Matt Mullenweg out, but he was back in control within days. The rebel board was eventually replaced, and the interim CFO left within weeks of appointment. In October, TechCrunch reported that the company had begun layoffs across several properties and more cuts were expected.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk is defending the Cybertruck and the company’s decision to stop producing the polarizing steel-clad truck, claiming that the order rate far exceeds its production.
Tesla will shut down production of the Cybertruck in about eight months Musk said in an X post on Monday. He also said the company will try to make as many of the vehicles as possible before then, though Tesla will “have to return deposits for a lot of people.”
Musk argued the Cybertruck was not unprofitable, and that Tesla was ending production because the “opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production.”
In other words, Musk is arguing that Tesla can make more money by using the factory space and resources dedicated to the Cybertruck for building Cybercab robotaxis. Musk said last week that Tesla plans to use the factory space to build more two-seater Cybercabs.
The first Cybertrucks were delivered to customers in late 2023, when it seemed like it could be a breakthrough hit for the company. Reservations for the vehicle had ballooned to 1 million, according to Musk, who also predicted that the company would sell around 250,000 of the trucks annually.
But those reservations never translated into actual sales. Tesla doesn’t break out sales of the Cybertrucks, but industry experts estimate a total of about 71,000 Cybertrucks have been sold since the first deliveries began in November 2023.
Many of those sales came from inside Musk’s ecosystem of other businesses. For instance, SpaceX (now known as SpaceXSI), which he also leads and is the largest shareholder of, purchased $131 million worth of Cybertrucks from Tesla in 2025, according to the company’s S-1 registration statement ahead of its IPO. Another Musk company, xAI, also bought $430 million worth of Tesla Megapacks for its data centers, before it merged with SpaceX.
But sales of the Cybertruck, which lagged for months, could see a final bump now that it’s going out of production. Still, even a scarcity boost is unlikely to push the truck’s demand to the lofty projections from several years ago.

Children of Men: The Future Is a Mirror for the Present
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
13:27:01 UTC
22:27:01 KST

Children of Men (2006) Directed by Alfonso Cuarón. Written by Alfonso Cuarón, Timothy J. Sexton, David Arata, Mark Fergus, and Hawk Ostby, based on the novel by P.D. James. Starring Clive Owen, Clare-Hope Ashitey, Julianne Moore, and Michael Caine.
I’m going to start with a pair of definitive statements that I know are annoying but very much believe to be true: All science fiction is political, and all stories about the future are actually about the present.
Science fiction, in its broadest definition, is about imagining and extrapolating stories from significant changes to ourselves, our societies, and our worlds. Sure, there are varying degrees of intentionality, and there are certainly people who genuinely think (erroneously) that they are telling a story unaffected by all the pesky problems and prejudices of the world around them.
At the other extreme we have Children of Men, a film that is crafted to say several pointed and complicated things about the world, and does it so exquisitely it has only grown more important and powerful in the twenty years since it was released.
Children of Men is loosely based on the 1992 novel The Children of Men by British author P.D. James (also known as Phyllis Dorothy James White, Baroness James of Holland Park). The film is more of a creative variation on a theme than a direct adaptation, a fact that Alfonso Cuarón was clear about from the start and James herself was happy with in the end. I did read the book around the time it was released, as I was a young fan of James’ mystery novels, but I was much too young to appreciate its themes and don’t remember what I thought about it.
The Children of Men is about a near future in which humans can no longer produce children, and it explores the resulting social, political, and philosophical tensions in the United Kingdom. The main character is an Oxford historian, the plot moves through both halls of government power and dissident groups, and the story explores tyrants rising to power amidst society’s despair, the exploitation of immigrant populations, and the role of faith and religion in both personal and political lives. Because the book is heady, intellectual, and came out in 1992, there are a lot of example of people insisting it cannot possibly be science fiction, such as this New York Times comparison of book and movie from 2006: “The Children of Men is not another of Ms. James’s famed detective novels, and it is not, as it has sometimes sloppily been described, science fiction. It is a trenchant analysis of politics and power that speaks urgently to this social moment, a 14-year-old work that remains surprisingly pertinent.”
It’s silly to frame “science fiction” and “a trenchant analysis of politics and power that speaks urgently to this social moment” as separate categories, but it’s a divide people apply to the movie as well, including the people who actually made the movie. I guess the book can’t be sci fi because it’s too serious about explaining its world, and the movie can’t be sci fi because it doesn’t explain its world, and I already find this “is it sci fi???” line of discussion tedious.
Yes, it is. Let’s move on.
The idea for turning James’ novel into a film came not long after the book was released, but it took several years and several screenwriters to get any traction. Paul Chart wrote the first version, then Mark Fergus and Hawk Otsby rewrote it. From early articles, it looks like their script was a lot closer to the book. Mexican filmmaker Alfonso Cuarón read their version of the screenplay but wasn’t much interested in it—at least, not at first. He has said in interviews that he initially dismissed it, but something about the story stuck in his mind. When he and screenwriter Timothy J. Sexton took their own crack at the screenplay, they approached it from a rather unexpected angle. As Cuarón described it, “We said: let’s do something like Y tu mamá también—but in the future.”
He was referring to his breakout film Y tu mamá también (2001), a sexy coming-of-age road movie set during Mexico at the end of the 1990s. It is not, on the surface, a film that bears any resemblance to Children of Men, but I think Cuarón’s reasoning makes sense. He had previously made two Americanized versions of British literary classics, The Little Princess (1995) and Great Expectations (1998), and he would spend two years in the UK making Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (2004). Y tu mamá también looks like the outlier in that filmography, but it’s a film Cuarón made to consciously reject the polished Hollywood style of filmmaking in order to better portray the people and places of his home country.
P.D. James’ The Children of Men is yet another very British book, but the parts of the story that fascinated Cuarón weren’t about the people who rise to power or gather to argue about the world’s problems, or even the details of how the near-future world functions. He was looking at it from post-9/11 perspective on world politics and thinking about how he could employ a more intimate scope to use the movie’s speculative world to illuminate our real one.
To do that, he narrowed the scope of the story compared to what’s in the novel, and shifted the sociopolitical commentary away from exploring how and why authoritarian regimes rise to power, moving instead toward looking at what the societies they build do to the least powerful among them. The speculative element underlying the near-future world is more or less the same: Nearly two decades ago, humanity suffered a mass infertility epidemic that science has not been able to cure, and no children have been born since. Cuarón has said repeatedly (probably because he was asked repeatedly) that he had absolutely no interest in trying to explain the infertility, because as soon as you start explaining it people start nitpicking the explanation. He’s completely right about that. He’s also right that it’s irrelevant.
The film follows Theo Faron (Clive Owen), a man living in London in the futuristic year of 2027. Very little about the world is exposited directly, but we learn enough to know that many terrible things have befallen cities and nations around the world. The United Kingdom has closed its borders to immigration and showers the population with propaganda about how Britain is the last civilized place in the world. Refugees are violently rounded up, locked into cages, and shipped to internment camps.
…I know. This won’t be the last time we all collectively pause to stare dully into the middle distance and think about how this movie came out in 2006 and has only become more resonant over the past twenty years.
Theo is an interesting character for a movie that ends up having quite a lot of action in it. While the film is tightly confined to his perspective, he’s not actually a very active protagonist, at least not at first. He’s deeply depressed but not numb, although it seems like he wishes he could be; the only warmth and connection in his life is the time he spends with his hippie friend Jasper (Michael Caine cosplaying as John Lennon). When a group of pro-immigration activists led by Theo’s ex, Julian (Julianne Moore), abduct him and demand that he help them, he at first refuses, then reluctantly agrees to do it for the money, not the ideology. Julian’s group wants papers to help transport an undocumented young woman, Kee (Clare-Hope Ashitey), safely to some unknown destination.
After Julian is killed in an ambush, Theo learns that Kee is pregnant—the world’s first known pregnancy in eighteen years. Julian had been helping her escape Britain to meet up with a group of people trying to solve humanity’s infertility. But Julian’s successor, Luke (Chiwetel Ejiofor), wants to use Kee and her child to persuade the British government to change its policies, so Theo, Kee, and another woman, Miriam (Pam Ferris) flee the group to make it to Kee’s rendezvous and get her out of the country.
From the ambush and Julian’s death all the way to the end, Children of Men is a chase movie. It is all about getting from one place to another while evading people who want to stop them. I don’t think this is a bad thing. In fact, I think it’s great. Many excellent movies are chase movies! The Terminator (1984) is a chase movie. Alfred Hitchcock’s North by Northwest (1959) is a chase movie. One of the greatest movies ever made (according to me), George Miller’s Mad Max: Fury Road (2015), is the purest distillation of a chase movie.
Of course, a chase isn’t engaging if we don’t care about who’s being chased and why, and we won’t care about those things if the concentrated action feels disconnected from larger stakes or consequences. An interesting thing about Children of Men is how the movie manages this by being very careful in what it doesn’t tell us. We know that Kee and her child are important, not just because protecting a mother and newborn is always important, but because the world will change with them in it. But we don’t know how. We don’t know what will become of Kee when she reaches the rendezvous. We can’t know, because Theo and Kee don’t know, and the film never strays from its tight focus on them. We don’t even really know who Kee is going to meet. Just like the characters, we’re asked to trust that she is running in the right direction, and that Theo is doing the right thing by helping her.
Without knowing what the endpoint is going to be, the film has to prove to us that it probably won’t be worse than where the characters start. And that’s not enough. The chase itself also has to be interesting.
It helps that the cast is fantastic—Owen and Ashitey are wonderful as two characters who would otherwise have absolutely no reason to interact—and the danger escalates relentlessly without ever feeling like we’re losing track of what’s going on.
Even beyond that, there are two specific achievements of the production that elevate Children of Men from ‘pretty good dystopian action movie’ to a truly great film. The first is the efficiency of the worldbuilding, and the second is the astonishing craftsmanship that went into the cinematography and visual effects.
In a 2006 article, Cuarón explained how he modeled his approach to Children of Men on the Italian-Algerian war film The Battle of Algiers (1966), directed by Gillo Pontecorvo. The Battle of Algiers is a movie about Algerian revolutionaries during the war for independence from France in the ’50s; it’s a fictionalized reconstruction based on the tactics and events of the campaign, but it’s filmed in the style of a newsreel or documentary, with a cast made up of non-professional actors, to mimic the feeling of watching real-world events play out on television news. Cuarón said of the film, “The amazing thing about The Battle of Algiers is the social reconstruction. It’s meticulous, and the sense of reality is so unique.”
The speculative premise behind Children of Men is introduced in the opening scene, where Theo and the world learn about the senseless death of the world’s youngest person. The nature of the world is revealed moments later, when the coffee shop Theo has just exited is destroyed by a bomb—and he still goes to work. When he decides to cut out early, it’s the death of an eighteen-year-old across the world that he uses as an excuse for his boss, not the fact that he was steps away from being blown to pieces in a senseless act of violence. Along the way we see news reports, propaganda, advertisements for gentle suicide drugs, and armed soldiers keeping people in cages at train stations, and it’s all vivid and visceral enough that was we can feel how miserable and unsafe it would be to walk those streets. We understand why Theo is depressed, why Jasper hides in the woods to grow and smoke weed, why the dissidents lash out with so much anger, why strangers weep over the death of a teenager they’ve never met.
The movie was filmed on location in London in 2005, which means they were creating a fake terrorist bombing mere weeks after real terrorist bombings in the city. But London of 2005 didn’t look like the dystopian London of 2027 the film needed, so Cuarón brought on visual effects supervisor Frazer Churchill to transport the extremely familiar sights—Fleet Street, Trafalgar Square, Battersea Power Station—into a grimier, grittier future, one where many people have given up on the hope of things ever getting better. It was an even bigger task to transform the real town of Bexhill-on-Sea into the crumbling, overcrowded refugee internment camp without any of it looking fake or computer-generated.
And amidst all that, there is, of course, a newborn baby, who is an on-set dummy covered by CGI, because a premature VFX newborn preserves our immersion in the story better than a real, clean, chubby baby of the wrong age would. The baby was created by Tim Webber and his team.
One visual model Cuarón had in mind for this violent, run-down vision of Britain’s future was Stanley Kubrick’s A Clockwork Orange (1971), but there are also points where he and cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki specifically use real-world imagery. He gave the art department images from “Sri Lanka, Iraq, Northern Ireland, Somalia, Chernobyl, the Balkans,” and he also pushed the largely English crew to “make it more Mexican.” That is, he wasn’t only relying on what people think a shabby futuristic England might look like, but using the film’s imagery to link a speculative near-future with the very real present.
A film’s story isn’t just told in what is shown on screen, but also in how it’s shown. That brings us to one of the most technically interesting aspects of Children of Men, which is its brilliant cinematography.
One thing worth mentioning is how much of the film uses natural lighting. Cuarón and Lubezki didn’t want the film to look stylized or futuristic; they wanted it to look like a documentary of the here and now. So Lubezki used as little artificial lighting as he could get away with, which meant altering some scenes from night to day to allow more light, or sometimes waiting for the fickle English weather to be more favorable. The film isn’t particularly dark or hard to see, because the lack of light is never used to obscure or muddle what’s on screen. It’s treated as part of the environment, so we see the characters as though they are moving through the world.
This is further emphasized by the film’s paucity of closeups. Most of it is filmed from something of a distance, with handheld cameras giving the sense of news or documentary footage. When there are closeups, it’s often because the characters are very close to each other, such as when five of them are jammed into that tiny Fiat.
And then there are those famously long shots, one of the things Children of Men is best known for.
A lot of people with a lot more patience than me have studied individual shot length in movies throughout history and around the world. There are some interesting broad trends: shots in the silent era were trending quite short (four to six seconds) before sound slowed things down, but in general shots have been getting faster and faster since then. The average length of shots depends very much on which countries you look at; Indian movies are infamously rapid-fire, some with shots every one to two seconds, adding up to thousands of shots. Action movies, no matter where they come from, also tend to have a very large number of very quick changes. We’ve watched some films from the other end of the spectrum; Stanley Kubrick loved to make movies with fewer long shots and it’s obvious in both A Clockwork Orange and 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968). But for the most part, especially in movies made more recently than the ’60s or ’70s, it’s pretty normal for a film to have 1000-2000 shots, with a common length of four to six seconds each.
Children of Men is 109 minutes long and contains just 460 shots. That gives the film an extremely long average shot length, especially for an action film that uses handheld cameras. It’s even more insane when you realize that the longest shots are among the most dynamic in the film, with the most action and violence.
Now, before anybody gets geared up to “well, actually” me, I will clarify that Children of Men has a number of extremely long apparent single shots that are made up of shorter—but still unusually long!—shots composited together using VFX. A relatively simple example of combining shots to create an apparent long shot is the coffee shop explosion at the very beginning of the film. The camera meets Theo as he enters the crowded coffee shop, then follows him out onto the street, then captures the explosion behind him. In reality, that shot was filmed on two separate days, with the explosion on the second day blowing up the same location on the same street, but now (obviously) empty.
That’s pretty straightforward compared to the wildly impressive scene later in which the characters are in a car that’s ambushed on a rural country road. It looks like a single shot. It really does. Go back and watch it. It looks like a single shot, even though we know it would be physically impossible to shoot that in a single take. It features five characters talking over each other in a small car interior, numerous attackers coming at the car from every direction, and camera motions that travel over and around and through the car. And it lasts for over six minutes. It was in fact filmed in six different chunks over the course of a week—including some parts where Cuarón, Lubezki, and a camera operator were actually strapped to a rig on top of the car. All of those pieces had to be matched, adjusted, and connected to achieve the seamless look that ends up on screen.
But the scene I find most incredible is the nine-minute shot near the end of the film, which starts when Theo and Kee are separated by the Fishers in the refugee camp, follows Theo through gunfire and explosions as he goes after Kee, through a crowded building until he finds her, then follows them again as he escorts her out of the building while both soldiers and refugees fall silent with awe at the sight of Kee’s newborn baby.
It’s an astonishing scene. Everything about it is breathtaking. The city is falling into chaos, gunfire and shouting and explosions fill the soundscape, the handheld camera first swings between characters like a witness trying to follow a conversation, then races and ducks and dodges along with Theo as he flinches, crawls, and stumbles his way through the warzone. Absolutely nothing about the scene is scripted or filmed to feel heroic. It’s desperate and terrifying, there are people injured and dying everywhere, and we can barely keep track of where we are. There’s no safety in moving from the open streets into the building, because the building is under attack and people are dying in the hallways. When Kee’s baby begins to cry, a stunned, breathless quiet spreads through the building and through the scene.
But the hushed awe doesn’t last. It’s broken by another explosion, and the fighting starts all over again.
It’s not clear from various sources exactly how much of that scene is a single continuous take, but Cuarón and Owen have both spoken about how it took weeks of preparation to get everything ready, and hours of setup for every time they wanted to record a take. If the camera operator tripped six minutes in, they would start over. The moment where blood splashes on the camera lens was unintentional; Cuarón said he tried to stop the take to start over, but because of the explosions nobody heard him and they kept recording. They left the blood on the lens for some of the final scene, but the take is not actually cut when the blood vanishes; they had a visual effects artist remove the droplets digitally for the second part of the scene.
Cuarón and Lubezki filmed as much of the movie in single takes as they could, and used digital effects to seamlessly combine what they could not, because the goal was never to show off their single-take virtuosity. The goal was something a lot more visceral.
Those long shots are the movie’s way of saying: Don’t look away. There’s so much pain and cruelty and suffering. Don’t look away. The world mourns the senseless death of a teenager while people die in the streets. Don’t look away. The rich surround themselves with treasures while there are people crammed into cages. Don’t look away. The violence might pause for a child but it certainly isn’t going to stop. The men with guns don’t care if you are a citizen with the right papers. This dystopia looks exactly like places you’ve seen on the news. These refugees look just like the ones your own governments treat so badly. Don’t look away.
I love this movie. It’s exquisitely crafted, and it provides a smart, incisive look at the world that manages to be contemporary and timeless, even twenty years later. I know I’m not the only one who feels this way; the movie received near-universal praise upon release and remains beloved. Children of Men is still one of the absolute best sci fi movies of the 21st century.
One particularly brilliant aspect I keep thinking about is how the movie ends. We don’t know what will become of Kee and her baby. We don’t know what will become of the world. We have absolutely no idea what, if anything, will change. Because the movie isn’t about that. Even though the film has the structure of an action film, with a recognizable male star at its center, it is not offering the comforting, simplistic fantasy that a white man’s heroic actions will immediately and noticeably save the world. We want to think Kee and her baby will change things, but we don’t know for sure because the future is—quite literally, in the final scene—shrouded in fog.
Children of Men is instead offering a more fragile, but ultimately more valuable, perspective: There is hope in trying to make the world better, even for one young woman and her child, even in the face of overwhelming obstacles, even if you won’t live to see the outcome.
So what do you think of Children of Men? Great movie, right? It’s such a great movie. Watching it again after some years was such a treat.
A Smorgasbord of Mindfuckery
For November and early December, we’ll be watching a handful of films that don’t fit together but also don’t quite fit anywhere else. What they have in common is that I’ve been shuffling them around my list for ages because I wasn’t sure when to watch them.
November 4 — Cube (1997), directed by Vincenzo Natali
This one was suggested way back when I first started this column and has been on the list ever since, but it turns out “Canadian horror movies about people trapped in giant homicidal mazes” is a rather limited niche.
November 11 — Brazil (1985), directed by Terry Gilliam
This could be a leftover from our October theme of movies about the near future, but it’s also very much its own thing that defies classification.
November 18 — Wax, or the Discovery of Television Among the Bees (1991), directed by David Blair
Another one that was suggested very early on. I can barely even figure out what it’s about from descriptions and articles, or even if it’s about anything at all. I’m happy to watch it anyway. It may or may not feature bees. Or television.
December 2 — Memories (1995), directed by Koji Morimoto, Katsuhiro Otomo, and Tensai Okamura
I don’t really know where to put an animated anthology collection of three short films, so we’ll just go ahead and watch it now.
December 9 — Donnie Darko (2001), directed by Richard Kelly
