The first five disks are the ones defined in USER DIRECT in the MDISK lines. The last 3 are the ones LINK’ed from MAIN.
To exit EDIT saving your changes, use the FILE command. To leave without saving changes, use QUIT. You’ll need to clear the terminal to continue (the “MORE…” message in the bottom right). On x3270 PA2, which clears the terminal, is Alt-2.
Another interesting file you might look into. It is a comprehensive list of all disk partitioins, the users those partitions are used by, the CUU they are attached to, and the start and end of the partition, in cylinders. All entries look like this one:
VOLUME   USERID      CUU   DEVTYPE   START      END     SIZE
GCCBRX   $ALLOC$     110      3350   00000    00000    00001
                                     00001    00050    00050    GAP
         MAINTC      293      3350   00051    00100    00050
         MAINTC      191      3350   00101    00150    00050
         MAINTC      394      3350   00151    00200    00050
         MAINTC      194      3350   00201    00250    00050
         MAINTC      395      3350   00251    00300    00050
         MAINTC      393      3350   00301    00350    00050
         MAINTC      193      3350   00351    00400    00050
         MAINTC      493      3350   00401    00450    00050
         MAINTC      19C      3350   00451    00500    00050
         MAINTC      195      3350   00501    00550    00050
         MAINTC      295      3350   00551    00551    00001
Creating a new user (or VM) would be more work than I’d like to cover here. It’d mean adding new disks, partitioning them, creating filesystems, and adding them to the configuration. Perhaps more importantly, it’d require me to learn a whole lot of things before I could confidently do it.
So, instead of creating a new user, we’ll change the CMSUSER user name and password (passwords can’t have more than 8 characters and are case insensitive). Keep in mind this is how it used to be in the 1970s - modern mainframes are much better protected.
My plan of having a user for me, one for my wife, and users for my kids will have to wait for another day.

Viewing files without using TYPE
TYPE is a fine command (those with CP/M and MS-DOS experience will remember it), but VM/370 CE bundles a full-screen file viewer.

Using other text editors
So far we have used EDIT. It’s an editor that comes with IBM’s VM/370 R6 and is the one you might see in period videos, but we have another one that’s much nicer: EE.
On your termminal, write:
EE PROFILE EXEC
Using EE
Typing EE PROFILE EXEC brings up the editor, in our case, with the PROFILE EXEC file loaded.
EE is a much modern editor, and behaves like current tools, such as ISPF. One nice thing it has is the command are on the left (that region filled with equals signs). Move the cursor up and enter “i3” on one.
When you hit enter, you’ll see EE inserted 3 lines (because that’s what i and 3 mean in this context).
To enter new text (or change what’s on the screen), just move the cursor there and start typing.
We really don’t want that sitting in our PROFILE EXEC file, so we’ll remove those 3 lines.
Now the file is the same as when we started. Pay attention to the purple line at the bottom, and press F3 to quit EE.
Tricked you! F3 will not work because we changed the file (EE doesn’t realize the contents are the same as they are on disk). We’ll use the QQuit command to quit. Think of it as “:q!” on Vim.

On the container images, these files are not exposed to the host directly, and you’ll have to map the container folder to the host yourself.

Fun things to do with your VM/370 CE machine
What can I do with a VM/370 CE mainframe?
This page assumes you have a machine (emulated or not) running the VM370 Community Edition OS available. There are a couple ways to get one, and you might want to choose the one that appeals to you the most (or the one that’s less work - it’s up to you).
What is the Community Edition?
The Community Edition is a huge set of improvements and fixes applied on top of the last VM/370 that was released by IBM without a license restricting its use. These improvements and fixes have been developed and published in a variety of ways since the release of the original OS. If we were to compare it with Linux, VM/370 R6 (the release CE is based on) would be Linux 1.0 as published by Linus from his bedroom and VM/370 CE would be latest Fedora (insert your favorite maximalist distro here). It has many features that didn’t exist in R6 and a couple things that would have been called science fiction back then. It’s quite capable, even if the machines it can run on are limited to a single CPU and 16M of memory (IBM calls it “storage”).
Running with Docker
The easiest way to run this is with Docker installed. How to install it depends on your platform, and we won’t cover it here. Besides, Docker is only one option - you can use Podman as well - it has some nice features, and can pretend it’s Docker, so you can use the same commands with both. When you are set up, you can just issue a shell command to have your own machine.
docker run -it --name vm370 -p 3270:3270 rbanffy/vm370ce
This will bring up the machine and display the machine’s console on your terminal.
The container image we are using is based on the excellent work of the VM/370 Community Edition team. You can see their releases on vm370.org. The Community Editions runs only software that’s either open source or public domain.
Other options for getting a mainframe
If you work in an organization that’s cool enough to have an actual IBM mainframe, you can check if your operations team will allow you to have a small VM running nested VM/370 Community Edition. IBM mainframes have legendary backwards compatibility and there should be no (technical) issue bringing up an environment for you. There might be a lot of process hurdles, however, so tread carefully and have a good excuse at hand. “Doing fun stuff” is not it. Trust me, I’ve tried this approach and it didn’t end well.
Another possible source of used mainframes is eBay or your local IT asset disposal company, but, seriously, you probably don’t want the hassle of a dedicated power line for the machine, or the basement space to have one. And, if you get a real machine, you might also get a valid license to run something more modern, like z/VM, z/OS, and a fairly modern Linux. They are also quite expensive and require expertise to set them up, and, many times, to fix them (people who decommission these machines often don’t bother disconnecting cables when just cutting is faster).
3270 terminals
IBM mainframes use screen-oriented terminals. They worked more or less like a web browser - the mainframe would send you a screen with a form, you’d write some information on the fields of the form, and the terminal would send the information back to the mainframe, restarting the cycle. If you think this looks like how HTML forms work, you are right, but this was in the late 1960s, not the mid 1990s.
Our examples use the x3270 emulator that’s available on any modern Unix-like environment (which includes Linux).
Start x3270 and connect it to your host. If you are running on your computer, it’ll be “localhost:3270”. Since I’m running mine on a small cluster, I’ll point the terminal to the entry address in the cluster.
With that taken out of our way, we can start to have fun.
Logging on
For normal things, we’ll log on to the CMSUSER VM, or, if you renamed it, to your own VM. The default password is “CMSUSER”:
On the banner screen, press ENTER.
The screen will clear. You can then enter logon cmsuser:
And enter the password, “cmsuser”:
As expected, the password isn’t shown. The red cursor means that.
You can also logon using LOGON CMSUSER CMSUSER, typing the password after the user name, but that horrifies me even more than having the username as the password. Back when VM/370 was invented, intrusions were a lot less of a problem than they are now. Please do not expose your VM/370 mainframe directly on the internet.
At this point, you are logged on. There is a lot going on under the hood - CP, or “control program” asked VM/370 to create a virtual machine for you, and this virtual machine was started with the CMS operating system. The commands we’ll see are CMS commands (unless noted). When you press ENTER again, a program, called “PROFILE EXEC” will run:
We can examine it. Note that “PROFILE EXEC” means the name is “PROFILE” and the type is “EXEC” (a script). To show the contents of the file, use:
TYPE PROFILE EXEC
Unlike Unix, commands and file names are case insensitive, so it’s fine to type them either way. Be careful, however, so you don’t overwrite your files accidentally.
Unlike most terminals, a 3270 doesn’t scroll. If you fill the screen, you’ll need to press the PA2 key (don’t look for one on your keyboard - there isn’t one). PA2 clears the terminal and receives the next page of text from the mainframe. On x3270, PA2 is Alt-2. On c3270, it’s Control-C.
Customising your PROFILE EXEC
Our current PROFILE EXEC prints a welcome message that’s informative, but that we can always read later. Let’s remove that message from our profile. For that, we’ll use a little bit of the EDIT editor.
EDIT PROFILE EXEC
Now we need to move down 12 lines. The command space is in the bottom of the screen, with the green cursor. Enter DOWN 12. This will move the highlight to the line we want to delete. Now use the DELETE command.
Now, to save the file and exit, enter FILE. You’ll see the MORE prompt in the bottom right - this indicates you need to press the PA2 key (Alt-2) to continue. 3270 terminals are screen oriented (think web browsers in the 1960s) and don’t scroll - you need to ask them for the next page. This has the advantage of allowing you to edit information on your screen and only causing the computer (the mainframe, in our case) to pay attention when you send it the information you edited. Most other computers that use terminals have to deal with each keystroke separately.
With this change done, the welcome message will not be displayed when you log in. If you want to see it again, you’ll need to type TYPE WELCOME MESSAGE U. Try it.
Running a BASIC program
What is a vintage computer without a BASIC interpreter, right?
Let’s start with the most basic BASIC program: a Hello World.
On your terminal, type:
EDIT HELLO BASIC
Note that “basic” is not a suffix, but a type - it’s a separate parameter. The type of the file is a property of the file and will remain with it unless forcibly changed.
When you press enter (or send) you’ll end up on the EDIT program. On the surface, it looks a lot like vi from the Unix side: it’s terse, hard to use, and sometimes counter-intuitive. It’s also hard to guess how to exit it. That’s about where the similarities end.
Let’s start typing our program:
10 print 'hello world'
When you press enter, you’ll see the line was entered. It was also changed to uppercase (see the “CASE=U” at the top line?). Let’s save the file and quit the editor. Type “file” and press Enter.
The line at the bottom shows a “MORE…” note. This means the terminal is waiting for you before it shows more output. Press PA2 (Alt-2 for x3270) and you’ll see you have exited EDIT.
Now we can run our program:
BASIC HELLO
You’ll see your command (“basic hello”) show up at the top of the screen (after the message indicating EDIT finished), then the message you ordered it to print “HELLO WORLD”, followed by another line telling how much CPU it used and how long did it take to run your program.
A bit of FORTRAN
VM/370 CE comes with a couple hello world programs. You can use the DIR command (which is also something added to vanilla VM) to list what files are in the disk you are seeing. We typed our own in BASIC, but there is one in C and one in FORTRAN. Let’s see the FORTRAN one:
TYPE HELLO FORTRAN
Let’s compile that FORTRAN program (so we can run it)
To compile it, run:
FORTRAN HELLO
The computer will output:
FORTRAN IV (G) COMPILATION COMPLETE.
Ready; T=0.84/2.59 23:39:34
It’s about time we mention the message. It’s telling me the program run using 0.84 seconds of CPU and took 2.59 seconds to complete. It also told me what time it is for the computer.
After compiling the program, you might have noticed two new files appeared:
HELLO    LISTING  A1  F   120     19      3  01/09/26   23:39  CMS191
HELLO    TEXT     A1  F    80     14      2  01/09/26   23:39  CMS191
The first one is a nicely formatted listing, and, in ancient times, you’d find it printed alongside the punched cards you submitted for compilation. It is formatted for 132 columns, as big printers of the time used to be.
   FORTRAN IV G LEVEL  21                 MAIN              DATE = 26009  TIME = 23.39.33             PAGE 0001
    0001              WRITE(6,1)                                                        HEL00010
    0002         1    FORMAT('HELLO WORLD FROM FORTRAN')                                HEL00020
    0003              STOP                                                              HEL00030
    0004              END                                                               HEL00040

  SYMBOL    LOCATION      SYMBOL    LOCATION      SYMBOL    LOCATION      SYMBOL    LOCATION      SYMBOL    LOCATION

The other is telling me it’s a text, but it appears it’s a lie:
In order to run the Fortran program we just compiled, we’ll do:
LOAD HELLO ( START
Let’s see what that means:
So… LOAD will load one or more relocatable object code, which is the TEXT file (we knew it was a lie!). So, we are asking LOAD to load the HELLO TEXT file, and we are passing the START option to it (so the code runs).
LOAD HELLO ( START
Execution begins...
Ready; T=1.23/3.90 00:09:54
Looks like nothing happened. But it actually did. There is a new file:
FILE     FT06F001 A1  V    24      1      1  01/10/26    0:09  CMS191
If we look into it, we’ll see:
So, the program ran, and the output went into this oddly named file. This is the first parameter of the WRITE statement. WRITE(6,1) means write to file 6 using the format defined on the line labeled 1. You can also see the “6” in the middle of the file type. We can redirect the output of file 6 to the terminal:
FILEDEF 6 TERMINAL
Now the program outputs to the terminal. Why the first character is missing is an interesting problem. I am not sure why this is happening, neither are my current mainframe gurus. Our current best guess is that this is because the first character of a line being interpreted by the line printer. This is arcane knowledge I don’t fully understand myself, The “right” way to output to a terminal is, and I’ve seen it done in period source code, have a space in the first column of the output string. When the system is outputting to a file, it deals with the output and the first character is suppressed, as it would be by the printer.
What was the magic we used to redirect? Let’s see what FILEDEF does. Do a HELP FILEDEF:
FILEDEF                                                   CMS Transient command
Use the FILEDEF command to establish data definitions for OS ddnames, to define
files to be copied with the MOVEFILE command, or to override default file
definitions made by the assembler and the OS language processors.  The format
of the FILEDEF command is:
+----------+------------------------------------------------------------------+
| FIledef  | ddname nn *  device                                              |
|          |                                                                  |
|          | device:                                                          |
|          |    Terminal [(optionA optionD[)]]                                |
|          |    PRinter  [(optionD[)]]                                        |
|          |    PUnch    [(optionD[)]]                                        |
|          |    Reader   [(optionD[)]]                                        |
|          |    DISK [FILE|fn ddname|ft [A1|fm]] [DSN ?|q1 q2 ...]            |
|          |             [(optionA optionB[)]]                                |
|          |    DUMMY    [(optionA[)]]                                        |
|          |    TAPn     [(optionA optionC[)]]                                |
|          |    CLEAR                                                         |
|          | optionA:                                                         |
|          |    BLOCK|BLKSIZE nnnnn  CHANGE|NOCHANGE     LRECL nnnnn          |
|          |    PERM                 RECFM a                                  |
|          | optionB:                                                         |
|          |    CONCAT               DISP MOD            DSORG PS|PO|DA|IS    |
|          |    KEYLEN nnn           LIMCT nnn           MEMBER name          |
|          |    OPTCD a              XTENT 50|nnnnn                           |
|          | optionC:                                                         |
|          |    7TRACK|9TRACK        TRTCH a             DEN den              |
|          | optionD:                                                         |
|          |    UPCASE|LOWCASE                                                |
+----------+------------------------------------------------------------------+
where:
ddname | nn | *
         is the name  by which the file is referred to in your program.  OS
         ddname syntax rules should be followed.  If a number nn is specified,
         it is translated to a FORTRAN data definition name of FTnnF001.  An
         asterisk (*) may be specified with the CLEAR operand to indicate that
         all file definitions not entered with the PERM option should be
         cleared.
Devices:
Terminal is your terminal (terminal I/O must not be blocked).  Terminal input
         will be truncated to the console input buffer length of 130
         characters.
… and so on. Fortran, by default, outputs to whatever is defined as file “6”, which ends up being “FILE FT06F001”. This is all related to the way batch processes were set up where things like input and outputs were specified by a configuration for when a program is run. This was done in a language called JCL (for Job Control Language). It was uncommon for programs to be run interactively at the terminal, and even having a terminal was considered a luxury most programmers didn’t have - they’d submit their code in special forms that someone else would type, convert to punch cards, and feed to the compiler.
Running our own programs
There is a lot of code you can use. For exaple, the IBM System/360 Operating System FORTRAN IV Programmer’s Guide has an example, primes.fortran I copied into this repo:
C PRIME NUMBER PROBLEM
C FROM IBM System/360 Operating System FORTRAN IV Programmers Guide
C https://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/360/fortran/
C GC28-6817-4_OS360_FORTRAN_IV_G_and_H_Programmers_Guide_197309.pdf
C page 108
C Modified for brevity from 1 to 1000 to 1 to 100
  100 WRITE (6,8)
    8 FORMAT (52H FOLLOWING IS A LIST OF PRIME NUMBERS FROM 1 TO 100 /
     X 119X,1H1/19X,1H2/19X,1H3)
  101 I=5
    3 A=I
  102 A=SQRT(A)
  103 J=A
  104 DO 1 K=3,J,2
  105 L=I/K
  106 IF(L*K-I)1,2,4
    1 CONTINUE
  107 WRITE (6,5)I
    5 FORMAT (I20)
    2 I=I+2
  108 IF(100-I)7,4,3
    4 WRITE (6,9)
    9 FORMAT (14H PROGRAM ERROR)
    7 WRITE (6,6)
    6 FORMAT (31H THIS IS THE END OF THE PROGRAM)
  109 STOP
      END

Other interesting languages available
PL/I
PL/I is another language popular in mainframes, and is used to this day. It’s much closer to more to what users of other recent languages would find familiar. It even includes a C-like preprocessor that allows including external files, conditional compilation and code-generating loops.
To invoke the compiler, use:
PLI FILENAME1 [FILENAME2 ... FILENAMEn]
This will compile all the files mentioned. The compiler has lots of options, so it’s a good idea to read the built-in for the compiler. For that, as usual, type:
HELP PLI
REXX
Rexx is the “glue language” of IBM mainframes. It’s simple, easy to use and interpreted. To write a REXX program you use the text editor. Using the file type EXEC will make it callable from the command line, but, in order for it to be recognized as a REXX program, the first line needs to be a comment delimited by /* and */. The language itself reminds me of later versions of BASIC after line numbers were no longer a thing:
/* REXX program to display the first 20 prime numbers */
count = 0
num = 2
DO WHILE count < 20
  IF is_prime(num) THEN DO
    SAY num
    count = count + 1
  END
  num = num + 1
END
EXIT
is_prime: PROCEDURE
  ARG n
  IF n < 2 THEN
    RETURN 0
  DO divisor = 2 TO TRUNC(SQRT(n))
    IF n // divisor = 0 THEN
      RETURN 0
  END
  RETURN 1
C
Pascal
ALGOL

Navigating the disks
The VM370CE distribution has a lot of disks. You can check which ones you have immediate access with. If you logged on as CMSUSER, you can use the LISTFILE (we abreviated it to “LIST”) command to see what files are on your default disk. In CMS, commands can be abbreviated - the actual command is LISTFILE but LIST is neat enough.
To check the disks you have, use QUERY DISK (query can also be abbreviated - Q will suffice for the computer to understand what you want):
To list what’s on a disk, you’ll use LISTFILE * * [disk]. The first “*” is a wildcard that will show all file names, the second is for all types. If you are familiar with windcards from CP/M, MS-DOS, or Unix, these don’t behave the same.
The third parameter is the disk:
So… Looking at the output of LISTFILE and LISTFILE * * A, we can conclude we were start from disk A. In this case, A is a shortcut to disk 191 (mainframes always were supposed to have lots of disks, and our emulated one - a maxed out 4381 - has more than most companies could afford, or that would fit in most period accurate computer rooms). In our case, 191 is the “address” of the disk, and tells where the disk is connected to the virtual machine. Disks also have 6-character labels (or “VOLSER” in mainframe slang). A is “CMS190”.
Let’s check the other disks:
Disks D, E, F, and G are empty. That wouldn’t be a surprise if we had paid attention to the output of QUERY DISK - it clearly says they have zero files, and use 5 blocks (rounded to 0% of the disk).
There is also disk S (or 190, or ). It has 172 files, so it’ll take a couple pages to list everything. In the list you’ll see a lot of interesting files - this disk contains system utilities - there’s ACCESS, EDIT, QUERY, SET, SORT, GLOBAL, and other things that we have seen before or that look like things an OS would provide (not a big surprise, as its label is “CMSDSK”). Binary programs seem to be of type “MODULE”. Let’s remember that. Try listing all files of type MODULE in S:
DIR * MODULE S
CMS offers a flat file system, so we can’t have subdirectories. This is a big difference for people who are used to Unix or Windows systems and to organize files using them. Another difference, that’ll feel more familiar to Windows users (and CP/M users before them) is that the system exposes multiple volumes instead of the single-root hierarchy of Unix systens.
Finally, a more subtle difference is that there is no such thing as the “current” disk. If you don’t specify a disk letter, the file is interpreted as A, which is your “home”. You don’t ever “change” to another disk, and you always mention them explicitly.
A plain VM/370 would map CMS system files to disk S. The Community Edition we are running has the OS on drive S, and OS extras on disk Y. Disk U contains utilities.
Uploading files to your machine (and playing games)
For this example, we’ll use the GAMES.VMARC file available at the h390-vm group at groups.io. The easiest way to upload a file to your mainframe is with the x3270 app - on the File menu select “File Transfer”:
Since we are uploading a VMARC file (think a .zip or .tar.bz2), we’ll chose a binary transfer. The file will be saved to our disk D.
It might be a while if you are running Hercules on an underpowered Raspberry Pi Zero W. I assume a local instance on a sensible computer will be a lot faster. When the transfer is finished, a new dialog will pop up telling you so.
Now we need to understand how to open a VMARC file. Luckily for us, VM370CE has a very comprehensive help system. On the terminal, issue a:
HELP VMARC
Listing the contents of the file seems like a good first step:
VMARC LIST GAMES VMARC D
Let’s get one of the games:
VMARC UNPACK GAMES VMARC D TICTOE MODULE D
It’s there!
Now we want to run it.
TICTOE
… and it works!
As most people know, the only winning move with Tic Tac Toe (and Global Thermonuclear War) is not to play. The other games are a lot more interesting.
Moar games

We are done with CMSUSER for now, so we’ll be good users and log off our machine:
Adding a user for you
It’s no fun to log in as CMSUSER every time you want to do something. You’ll want a user for yourself, with reasonable permissions to do things to the machine. In my case, I want to create an “RBANFFY” user for me.
Here’s the first surprise for those who come from other platforms - you wouldn’t create a user, you’d create a VM, and you log in to that VM. You can create a user without creating a VM for it, but that would not be what you actually want. Users and VMs are defined the same way, with the USER keyword.
Creating a VM is a bit involved - you’ll need to do a lot of things before - allocate and format storage, for instance. We’ll leave that for later.
In the meantime, if you want to rename the CMSUSER VM to your preferred name (and change the password), we can explain that. We’ll start logging on as MAINT (which means, logging on to the MAINT VM).
We’ll also learn a lot of interesting things about our system, and a couple new commands for the EDIT editor.
Editing USER DIRECT
The first thing we want to do is to check which disks are available to this VM.
Note that we share a couple disks with other VMs. This is counterintuitive to people used to do VMs the Windows or Linux way - under VM/370 (and its descendants) VMs can share filesystems, not disks. Think of it as mounting a remote filesystem, but there is no remote server - this is done within the hypervisor. We are sharing volumes CMSDSK, MNT29D and MNT19E with other users (we saw it logged in as CMSUSER).
The file we want to look into is USER DIRECT. Let’s first find where it is located. Use LISTFILE USER DIRECT * to list files named USER DIRECT in all volumes you can access. Your terminal will show something like:
LISTFILE USER DIRECT *
USER     DIRECT   A1
Ready; T=0.07/0.13 12:20:46
So, we see the file is in our default disk (A), which is volume MNT191. Let’s edit it - on your terminal, run EDIT USER DIRECT.
The top line tells you the file and the mode you are working in.
EDIT    USER     DIRECT   A1  F  80 ZONE=  1- 72 VERFY=  1- 72 CASE=U TRUNC= 72
This tells me we have the USER DIRECT file, located on A (ignore the 1 for now), that it is a fixed line length file of 80 columns (F  80), and that everything we type will be converted to uppercase (CASE=U). It also says TRUNC= 72 to tell us we can’t go past column 72. This was used for punchcards to identify the card (which is a line in the file).
To navigate, you can use EDIT’s commands up and down. When you follow them with a number, they repeat the operation that number of times. If you are lost, you can use top or bottom to get to the top of the end of the bottom of the file. Let’s do a DOWN 14.
This is how you define VMs. They are called users here, so you might be confused. Some VMs start automatically while others will only be started on LOGON (and will shut down on LOGOFF). This first definitions are, as the comment explains, created to make it easier to define your own users, and you can’t log-on to them yourself.
The file gets more interesting when you look at the ASSIST user. Do a LOCATE ASSIST:
  Note: The user ALGOL is also interesting, but we won’t talk about it right now.
Here you see a couple commands before the disk definitions. They tell the user will log-on to the CMS operating environment (IPL means “Initial Program Load” and is what other systems would call “boot”). It’ll then tell how the console is to be used (like an IBM 3215 console as device 009). It’ll also set up a card reader/puncher (one IBM 2540 connected on 00C and 00D) and a printer (an IBM 1403).
USER ASSIST ASSIST 15M 16M G
 IPL CMS
 CONSOLE 009 3215
 SPOOL 00C 2540 READ A
 SPOOL 00D 2540 PUNCH A
 SPOOL 00E 1403 A
  Note: The first line tells us the user name (ASSISS), the password (yes, in clear text), and how much memory the machine should have allocated.
Let’s now look into the user we might want to rename. In EDIT, do a LOCATE CMSUSER:
USER CMSUSER CMSUSER 15M 16M G
 IPL CMS
 CONSOLE 009 3215
 SPOOL 00E 1403 A
 SPOOL 00C 2540 READ *
 SPOOL 00D 2540 PUNCH A
 LINK MAINT 190 190 RR
 LINK MAINT 19D 19D RR
 LINK MAINT 19E 19E RR
*        cuu type adr num volser mode readpw   writepw  multpw
 MDISK   191 3350 001 115 VM50U0 MR   ALL      WRITE    MULT
 MDISK   192 3350 116 115 VM50U0 MR   ALL      WRITE    MULT
 MDISK   193 3350 231 115 VM50U0 MR   ALL      WRITE    MULT
 MDISK   194 3350 346 115 VM50U0 MR   ALL      WRITE    MULT
 MDISK   195 3350 461 094 VM50U0 MR   ALL      WRITE    MULT
Now you’ll want to open a second x3270 window and log on as CMSUSER.
LOGON CMSUSER CMSUSER
DASD 190 LINKED R/O; R/W BY MAINT; R/O BY 004 USERS
DASD 19D LINKED R/O; R/W BY MAINT; R/O BY 002 USERS
DASD 19E LINKED R/O; R/W BY MAINT; R/O BY 004 USERS
LOGON AT 13:10:22 GMT MONDAY 01/19/26
VM Community Edition V1 R1.2
Notice these are the 3 disks mentioned in the LINK commands after the card reader/puncher and the printer are added. They are being linked from the user MAINT

The first five disks are the ones defined in USER DIRECT in the MDISK lines. The last 3 are the ones LINK’ed from MAIN.
To exit EDIT saving your changes, use the FILE command. To leave without saving changes, use QUIT. You’ll need to clear the terminal to continue (the “MORE…” message in the bottom right). On x3270 PA2, which clears the terminal, is Alt-2.
Another interesting file you might look into. It is a comprehensive list of all disk partitioins, the users those partitions are used by, the CUU they are attached to, and the start and end of the partition, in cylinders. All entries look like this one:
VOLUME   USERID      CUU   DEVTYPE   START      END     SIZE
GCCBRX   $ALLOC$     110      3350   00000    00000    00001
                                     00001    00050    00050    GAP
         MAINTC      293      3350   00051    00100    00050
         MAINTC      191      3350   00101    00150    00050
         MAINTC      394      3350   00151    00200    00050
         MAINTC      194      3350   00201    00250    00050
         MAINTC      395      3350   00251    00300    00050
         MAINTC      393      3350   00301    00350    00050
         MAINTC      193      3350   00351    00400    00050
         MAINTC      493      3350   00401    00450    00050
         MAINTC      19C      3350   00451    00500    00050
         MAINTC      195      3350   00501    00550    00050
         MAINTC      295      3350   00551    00551    00001
Creating a new user (or VM) would be more work than I’d like to cover here. It’d mean adding new disks, partitioning them, creating filesystems, and adding them to the configuration. Perhaps more importantly, it’d require me to learn a whole lot of things before I could confidently do it.
So, instead of creating a new user, we’ll change the CMSUSER user name and password (passwords can’t have more than 8 characters and are case insensitive). Keep in mind this is how it used to be in the 1970s - modern mainframes are much better protected.
My plan of having a user for me, one for my wife, and users for my kids will have to wait for another day.
Updating the USER directory
[TBA]
Viewing files without using TYPE
TYPE is a fine command (those with CP/M and MS-DOS experience will remember it), but VM/370 CE bundles a full-screen file viewer.
[TBA]
Using other text editors
So far we have used EDIT. It’s an editor that comes with IBM’s VM/370 R6 and is the one you might see in period videos, but we have another one that’s much nicer: EE.
On your termminal, write:
EE PROFILE EXEC
Using EE
Typing EE PROFILE EXEC brings up the editor, in our case, with the PROFILE EXEC file loaded.
EE is a much modern editor, and behaves like current tools, such as ISPF. One nice thing it has is the command are on the left (that region filled with equals signs). Move the cursor up and enter “i3” on one.
When you hit enter, you’ll see EE inserted 3 lines (because that’s what i and 3 mean in this context).
To enter new text (or change what’s on the screen), just move the cursor there and start typing.
We really don’t want that sitting in our PROFILE EXEC file, so we’ll remove those 3 lines.
Now the file is the same as when we started. Pay attention to the purple line at the bottom, and press F3 to quit EE.
Tricked you! F3 will not work because we changed the file (EE doesn’t realize the contents are the same as they are on disk). We’ll use the QQuit command to quit. Think of it as “:q!” on Vim.
Talking to other mainframes
Mounting a disk on another running Hercules instance
Hercules can run without a UI in Shared Device Server mode. In this mode, it can start and no environment needs to be IPL’ed.

Printing
To a virtual printer
Hercules supports routing a printer to a local file. On the packaged version of MVT 3.8j a 1403 line printer is mapped to the prt/prt00f.txt file, and on VM/370 there are two 1403 printers, mapped to io/print1.listing and io/print2.listing. On the container images, these files are not exposed to the host directly, and you’ll have to map the container folder to the host yourself.

In the recent years C++ received a lot of backlash due to its complexity and (perceived) feature creep. However, since C++11 I really enjoyed writing C++ with its strict type system (including const), range-based for loops, smart pointers, and how much you can do with templates. On the other hand, I know that it can be very tricky to write, for instance, a correct iterator, to get handling of rvalue references right, or to read error messages that involve templates.

Borrowing a Microsoft-signed shim to abuse Secure Boot on corporate hardware
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
09:22:30 UTC
18:22:30 KST

Created on Sun. 08 Nov 2026
Halli hallo everyone, this blog post is a continuation of the p3ng0s series that has been going on on this blog for a few years. This is my latest research on how secure boot works that I did back in April of this year and this blog post is a tease for p3ng0s V2 release that will happen probably in 1 Year from now.
Before I start on this post I want to explain something really quick I will focus the rest of this year and early next year on finishing maldev academy writing a small research paper on PIC malware and doing CRTO 1 + 2. I really want to add a bunch of stuff to p3ng0s but first I need to finish the stuff I just mentioned so that I am not mentally distracted when doing p3ng0s V2. I really wan't to push the physical security side of the OS and I have a bunch of great ideas. This secure boot work that I'm gonna explain here is a direct parallel to this work. It was an idea I had in the middle of developing V1 but I pushed it back too V2 to avoid scope creep and then ended up implementing it anyway on a V2 branch. So if you like this post you can use this technique right now, a mini tutorial is mentioned at the end of the post here.
Before going to much into the weeds of secure boot let me just put this out here. Before doing this research I personally knew nothing exactly about secure boot. To me it actually just was this annoying BIOS option that blocked me from booting into linux when I bought a new laptop, I knew it was a Microsoft pushed thing and because of that I was never very happy of buying hardware and having to disable this feature to then use the computer how I wanted. You reading this post I would like you to take a minute to think about the following questions, obviously this works best if like me your knowledge of secure boot was limited: what you think secure boot actually is? What do you think this feature is actually for? Why does it exist?
Great so after some thinking my conclusion before reading up about secure boot in detail was to lock down what operating system is running on the machine. I thought well there's these keys that say okay this OS can boot this OS cannot more or less. And that you needed specific keys to boot and those where microsoft controlled. This answer is close but not exactly right. The actual reason secure boot exists is for the following: Ensuring the integrity of the booting OS. Now the wording here is very important isn't ensuring integrity the same as locking to one booting OS? (at least that is how I would interpret that statement back then). Well turn's out not at all ensuring integrity means: Yes yes the signature of this OS is in the database of accepted OS and that is it.
Now some companies do allow employees to run linux right? Does that mean the CISO of those is just nuts and disables secure boot on his fleet? Turn's out that is a flat NO. There is this thing called Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011 and is used to sign 3rd party operating systems that can work with Microsoft keys that are installed on 99% of BIOSes out there. Okay so turns out secure boot can just work with ANY keys you can just make your own enroll them in your BIOS and sign your linux build with them and that's it it will just work.
Here is a screenshot of the bazzite OS tutorial on enrolling their keys inside of your BIOS. Okay so now we understand 2 things: 1. Microsoft has 3rd party keys for some linux distributions, 2. If you can mess around in the BIOS you can just enroll your own keys. Now let's just sit with this and think what is secure about this? Like if I can just enroll my own keys how is this secure? Well turn's out secure boot was not to target consumers nor physical access to a machine, secure boot was only to stop one specific attack: EFI malware. Like if a malware is sitting on the EFI level and windows does not wipe EFI partitions on computer reset you have a "Immortal" malware excluding the fact that if you just wipe every partition this problem goes away but yeah that is besides the point.
Now so we know that Microsoft signs 3rd party OS for secure boot access but these OS are always changing and those keys don't change that often but the grub version the OS those things keep on moving so how come 1 key that never really changes unless expires changes but the software underneath changes all the time does that not break integrity of the boot chain? Well yes it does this is where something called a shim and MOK enrollement comes into play!
Okay here is a provided diagram of how MOK enrollment looks like. Do you see the issue that I have with this? To me it seems a bit trivial well if I can pick the keys during mok enrollment why not just pick my own keys? From there it's jackpot I booted my OS on hardware that has secure boot enabled! Okay so in the previous chain let me explain something clearly the BIOS has microsoft 3rd party keys installed, the shim is 3rd party microsoft signed if the grub image is signed with a unrecognized key the shim fails and boot's into this MOK software where you can PICK the key that matches the GRUB and linux signature.
Okay so like I mentioned a few times now this 3rd party program from Microsoft for those magic keys, who is in them? Turns out a few OS: ubuntu, debian, fedora and some others. These open source OS are well open source can't I find the shim and make my OS just stand as ubuntu? Like opsec wise this would be gold I make my "hacking" OS look like ubuntu on the secure boot chain and if the computer itself has those 3rd party certificates installed I win and can boot into a dropbox or whatever on the hardware of the place I am targeting.
Let me introduce you to my new favourite website pkgs.org a website where you can search for packages across multiple linux distributions! And when we search for a package named shim we can find something that I find hilarious! A package named shim-signed. Well well well what do you guys think I am going to do with those? Exactly we will borrow them ;)
          So what we need is the MOK software for enrolling our crap and we need well the actual
          shim signed by Microsoft. Really quick in this example I did skip something: how I know
          it's actually Microsoft signed here is the command to check: sbverify --list you_shim_file.efi
          and the output should have something similar:
        
Okay so since this is all BOOT adjacent things we need to actually mess around with EFI partitions and how things are actually booting. Quick note if you fuck up here well your drive / USB won't boot, hehehe happened to me a few times call it a right of passage! Right so to get the SHIM installed you will need to take your EFI partition and mount it! From there you should see the following files:
Start with generating your keys with the following command:
openssl req -newkey rsa:4096 -nodes -keyout "./MOK.key" -new -x509 -sha256 -days 3650 -subj "/CN=some name/" -out "./MOK.crt"
Once you have your keys make sure you sign your kernel with the keys
sbsign --key "./MOK.key" --cert "./MOK.crt" --output /boot/vmlinuz-linux /boot/vmlinuz-linux
          Side note to sign the kernel you cannot do that on a live USB unless you build it yourself.
          In the case of p3ng0s I specifically added a hook that does this during build time your can
          see it under the file airootfs/etc/pacman.d/hooks/zzzz98-mok-signing.hook of the V2 branch.
          But technically you can install for example kali linux directly to a USB drive: boot that drive and then sign that kernel
          then unboot the drive and do the EFI steps on that usb drive and you would have the same tech working on kali linux.
          Honestly to do this I recommend copy pasting this entire blog post into claude and asking him
          to generate you a tutorial and walk through that with him!
        
Okay next you need to rename the EFI file we found before to "grubx64.efi" and sign it:
mv ./BOOTx64.EFI ./grubx64.efi # rename
sbsign --key "/where_you_put_your_shim/MOK.key" --cert "/where_you_put_your_shim/MOK.crt" ./grubx64.efi --output ./grubx64.efi # sign grub
Okay after that you take your actual shim and name it "BOOTx64.EFI" and place the MOK software next to it:
cp -r "/path_to_your_shim/shimx64.efi" ./BOOTx64.EFI
cp -r "/path_to_your_shim/mmx64.efi" ./mmx64.efi
After that make sure you convert your certificates to a format secure boot will accept like so, and place the key inside of the EFI partition for quick access later:
openssl x509 -in "./MOK.crt" -outform DER -out ./borrowed-mok.der
This is what the EFI partition should finally look like inside of it's BOOT folder:
Okay now we have the drive primed and ready with our newly acquired Microsoft signed shim! The way this works is simple you have a laptop with well secure boot active and the Microsoft 3rd party certificates pre-installed (They are most of the time btw especially on corporate machines since well some software actually needs them on on windows. But also some don't have it installed HP wolf security for example was hit and miss some did some didn't, cutaway was maybe last year or 2 years where they stopped enabling it :P)
So in our case let's make it realistic we just plug in the drive and go inside of the BOOT from other device option usually F7 but it changes on some models of computers (NOTE: you don't need BIOS passwords for this option LOL). From here we select our newly created drive and we will boot the sim and fail the grub signing section and be present with the MOK enrollment software like so:
Here we select Enroll Key from disk and navigate to the BOOT/ folder where our key was put in the previous steps!
How we just say yes we want to enroll that key
Great and here we can just continue to boot and grub will just appear! Yeah so not so secure boot after all....
          Okay so if you want to use this on p3ng0s when you clone archlive make sure
          you do a git checkout on the V2 branch and before running
          the build command you need to place the shim and mok manager inside of the
          overlay/airootfs/etc/p3ng0s/shim folder!
          I did update the Live ISO.pdf file for p3ng0s that has the instructions
          on how to build the OS with the steps for secure boot it can be found
          here
          before I make V2 fully public and update the official documentation.
        
Well I hope you liked this little blog post on something I found kinda fun to poke at! Surprise for Cast of 'Return of the Living Dead' Sequel. They Were Replaced by AI (kotaku.com) 46
			
		 	
				A crowdfunded sequel to the movie Return of the Living Dead was uploaded last weekend  — but producer Richard Driscoll is drawing criticism for what he did to the 1985 punk/zombie classic. 
Kotaku reports:
[The release of the movie] came to the surprise to the original cast, who were attached to star in the follow-up.  Instead it seems Driscoll opted to use AI to generate the film... 
In 2024, Driscoll, who operates his own no-budget streaming service "DragonFLIX," launched an Indiegogo page for "TRASH's REVENGE Return of the Living Dead Universe." Unlike other fan projects, this one had a large portion of the original cast involved, with stars Randolph and Linnea Quigley acting as producers. It also threw in Quigley's fellow Sorority Babe in the Slimeball Bowl-O-Rama Michelle Bauer and the Oscar nominated Eric Roberts, who has seemingly been in everything except The Living Dead.... 
But after some confusion and radio silence between the cast and director, this incredible movie did not come to be.  Last Halloween night, Driscoll pushed out [the almost entirely AI-generated]  The Return of the Living Dead: Aftermath... The results won't surprise you. Robotic line delivery. Nonsensical sequence of events. Object impermanence. Everything's wet. Everyone looks shocked. At one point the video just flips around like you're watching on a phone someone dropped. And while the Return cast didn't film any of this footage, their likenesses are peppered throughout.
"It turned out to be a fiasco," says Quigley. "I warned him, "Whatever you do, don't do any AI, because people don't like it, the fans don't like it." Living Dead alumni, even those who weren't attached to this film, have spoken out against Aftermath. They seem most concerned about the existing and continued use of their likeness, given that Driscoll has seemingly pivoted 'Trash's Revenge' into an additional project. Randolph encourages those who provided any funding to ask for a refund through their credit card company. While Romero's original film was public domain, Return of the Living Dead was not. Randolph also encourages Amazon, who bought MGM in 2022, to take legal action. 
A review on Reddit calls it "the worst 'film' I've ever seen," a production that "manages to not only be the worst zombie film ever made but is also the nadir of exploitation filmmaking.
[T]hings quickly descend into madness and we get lots of bits of A.I. reporters out on the streets being attacked by A.I. zombies...  [T]here are some A.I. cops battling it out too...

370 Books in 20 months: South African author defends her use of AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
07:21:33 UTC
16:21:33 KST

CAPE TOWN - South African writer Coral Hart has published more than 370 books since February 2025 using artificial intelligence, a process she passionately defends despite criticism and threats.
"Grifter", "villain" -- insults abound on social media to describe the author who, in her forties, has become the symbol of AI's arrival in publishing.
Coral Hart -- a pseudonym she uses to protect her real name -- told AFP in an interview she had received "tens of thousands" of hate messages and several death threats.
In this hostile environment, few authors using AI agree to speak publicly and show their faces.
"I chose to be the one to step up and say, these are conversations we need to start having," Hart said.
"This is here... They're not going to switch it off or unplug it because a bunch of authors said so."
Before she started writing with AI around 20 months ago, Hart had been working in publishing for 14 years and written several dozen works without the technology.
It took her three months to familiarise herself with the various AI models and build a framework capable of producing a book.
Now she juggles between ChatGPT, which is "really good at dialogue, terrible at prose"; Claude, "really good story structure, terrible at sex drives"; and others like Grok, "completely unhinged" but good on "spicy scenes".
"If you say, ChatGPT, write me a book, or, Claude, write me a book, you're going to get a flaming dumpster fire of trash back because it doesn't have anything (to work with)," Hart said.
The author defines the story concept, a style, details of the characters, and chapter outlines. And only then will her system generate the books.
Hart said when she started, "we could write one paragraph at a time. I usually took two or three prompts to do that."
"I can now draft the whole book in one sequence."
Since last year, AI models have "improved vastly", Hart said. "The prose has improved. The syntax has improved. The sentence structure has improved."
The first draft of a book is generally not good, the writer said.
It is run through AI for "developmental edits" and then again "to fix any continuity issues, story issues, flat middles, character arcs that are incomplete, plot threads that have been dropped, people whose eye colour has changed."
At the end of this process, a human proofreader reads through the text to fix any "AI tells that have slipped through" and do some rewriting. "And it's usually ready to go."
Although one of her novels made it into Amazon's top 100 bestsellers, the vast majority of her 371 titles -- many of them romance -- are tailored to certain readers based on rigorous market research.
She has sold more than one million books, by her own estimate, in digital, print and audio formats, earning more than $1 million so far this year.
The South African now heads an operation that has trained several hundred people in her method and is preparing to launch software for AI authors called Authorythm.
As for her own production, she mentions her use of AI only when required by a sales platform.
"For the last 16 years, nobody's asked me what my creative process was," said Hart, who publishes under more than 10 other pen names.
Now, she was ready to make it public "for the right reasons".
Regularly accused of contributing to "AI slop" -- low‑quality AI-generated content in text, video, music, or images -- Hart points to the ultimate yardstick: "Books are selling."
"Readers don't read rubbish books; they return them," she said.
The writer has followed the debate around a novel by Haitian-Canadian Thelyson Orelien that was withdrawn from the shortlist for France's Goncourt prize after accusations that he used AI, which his publisher confirmed on Wednesday.
Critics had praised the book and sales were strong before the controversy, she said, asking: "If you need an AI label to hate something, do you hate it, or do you hate AI?"
- by Thomas Urbain (AFP)

Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
07:20:37 UTC
16:20:37 KST

Computer Science > Computation and Language
  [Submitted on 9 Oct 2026]
Title:Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallel sampling for faster generation than autoregressive models, an increasingly important advantage as inference becomes a dominant computational workload. However, DLMs degrade quickly with fewer sampling steps, process the full sequence at every step, and require many passes over the dataset to reach good quality. We introduce Next-Concept Modeling (NCM), a two-stage, coarse-to-fine framework: a multiscale residual VQ-VAE encodes text into a hierarchy of discrete codes, and a transformer generates one level at a time, predicting all codes within a level in parallel. At matched parameter scales, NCM achieves better generative perplexity than the strongest DLM baseline on LM1B while running $21\times$ faster. On OpenWebText, NCM is competitive with the strongest DLM while running $10\times$ faster; on XSum, it matches the strongest DLM's ROUGE-L while being $31\times$ faster. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations.

is Opus 5.5 nerfed?
I just had Gemini 4 Argon analyze 1,400 Claude Code sessions and it found that on November 3, something definitely happened.
the model name didn't change, but the way it does reasoning took a sharp turn.
quick test on a real bug showed Opus 5.5 high jumping into action too quickly, getting confused and being unable to find a fix after 3 full hours.
meanwhile Opus 5.5 xhigh takes a moment to think, finds a fix after a few minutes.
this blew up and I want to clarify: I'm not an AI tools reviewer, this isn't a scientifically bulletproof benchmark.
the starting point was my personal frustration, going from Opus 5.5 is amazing to I can't get work done with this thing anymore.
@bot kick off a job in the fleet repo on bb-1 using opus 5.5 xhigh to investigate this for me. Curious how accurate the claims are. Dig through my cliproxy logs in clickhouse to see if things changed

Being a meat proxy for AI should be grounds for getting people fired
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
06:55:38 UTC
15:55:38 KST

Being a meat proxy for AI should be grounds for getting people fired
I generally keep the content of this blog neutral, but the issue I'll cover today is genuinely pissing me off. I apologize in advance for the more aggressive tone that this post will have because I think it's necessary in this to get the point across.
When someone is assigned a task, be it to review a PR, work on a reasonably complex coding task, or even just asked a simple question, and all they do is prompt the agent "do X" and copy-paste the results back to you, with zero guidance or validation on behalf of the human (meaning it was 100% handled by the agent), and oftentimes failing to disclose or actively attempting to hide the fact that the work was fully AI generated, this should in my opinion be considered as an attempt from the dev to scam the company. It should result in the developer receiving a warning and even the threat of potential termination of employment in more serious cases and if the dev fails to comply.
I've seen many react to this topic by thinking "Isn't all work supposed to be AI generated nowadays? What's the problem with that?". But there's a huge difference here. I'm not talking about the usual AI-assisted workflow which is commonplace nowadays where the human guides the agent, corrects it, reviews what comes out of it and opens PRs based on something that has been properly validated and cleaned up for other humans to review.
I'm talking about a specific scenario that has become worryingly common over the last few months where the human was simply a meat proxy between you and whatever agent they used, making it so that the person added no value and you should've just launched an agent yourself and skipped them entirely. They might have even potentially made things worse for you by doing so, and in more egregious cases even intentionally attempted to hide this face and/or use this as a way to strip themselves of any responsibility regarding the code they write and merge (e.g. "This code broke master and took down production? It was opened and merged under my user? No, you see, it's not my problem because it was the AI who did this, not me!").
This behavior is becoming increasingly prevalent in the software engineering industry and it's damaging it. I think this behavior should be punished because devs who do this are:
- Wasting your time, because if all they do is proxy their work to an agent, you might as well skip the person and do that yourself
- Forcing you to do their work for them, because you now have to not only review and validate agentic output that they did not, but also potentially have to be one dealing with the consequences of any nonsense code that they may have managed to merge when you were not paying attention
- Wasting the company's time and resources, as this behavior is basically a convoluted way of stating that they are 1) getting paid a salary to do nothing essentially, 2) harming the company's products, and 3) wasting the time of anyone having to deal with them, particularly when the dev intentionally tries to hide their actions and pass AI generated output as their own words or code
It's essentially a novel way to silently scam the company and colleagues and is in my eyes no different than other known software engineering scams such as covertly having two jobs or hiring a third-party to do your work for you and act as if they were you while you do something else.
I always saw the software engineering field as being comprised of two groups of people: people who are devs because they are passionate about building software, and people who don't actually enjoy software but joined the field because it's a job that pays well. The latter being something that I find to be a perfectly fine thing to do as long as, you know, you actually do your job. Pre-AI, although sometimes I've found people in this group to not have been doing a particularly impressive job, they were still doing it nonetheless. So things were fine then.
But now that AI is widespread, I've been bumping into many folks who basically weaponized AI to make it seem like to their managers they are being extremely productive by opening hundreds of PRs with very complex descriptions and bold claims of having fixed major issues and/or greatly improved systems, when in reality a deeper look reveals that this "work" is actually just a bunch of unreviewed vibe-coded nonsense that not only doesn't fix or improves anything at all, but also actively harms whatever products they are "working" with and massively complicates the work of the devs who have to deal with the consequences of said garbage code and actually care about building good products and using AI responsibly.
This is getting so insane that I've even had cases where I would DM someone on Slack and notice right away that I'm talking to an AI. Not in the sense that they've set up an agent to handle their messages for them (wouldn't be surprised if people start doing this though), but that they are copying my question to an agent and pasting back the response (without disclosure, so making it seem that they wrote it themselves). WTF?
When chatting about this problem with colleagues, some of them suggested that the answer might be to throw AI back at the person (so if you get a barrage of unreviewed AI-generated review comments on your PR, throw another unreviewed AI-generated barrage of AI responses back at the person). But I feel that this just makes everything worse. It may get the PR itself out of your hands, but the code will suffer as a result and you'd still have to end up dealing with the consequences of that.
I don't understand why someone who doesn't like their job would try so hard to come up with ways to not do it that they would be fine with messing up their colleagues' work in order to achieve it. Nobody is forcing anyone to work in tech. If someone doesn't like it, they can just quit and do something they actually enjoy. It's what I would've done at least if I was in their situation.

Asahi Linux Drops MIT and Goes Full GPL After Spotting LLM-Assisted License Laundering
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
05:35:00 UTC
14:35:00 KST

Asahi Linux Drops MIT and Goes Full GPL After Spotting LLM-Assisted License Laundering (itsfoss.com) 138
			
		 	
				 It's FOSS reports:
Asahi Linux is the reason you can run Linux on an Apple Silicon Mac today. For years, the project put most of its own code under the MIT license so that anyone, including the BSDs, could reuse it as needed...   They have announced that Asahi is moving all of its repositories to the GNU General Public License version 2 or later.  Going forward, all Asahi Linux code will be under strong copyleft licenses only. 
Asahi Linux compares their dilemma to the 1990s, when "permissively licenced projects were viewed by tech companies as free real estate to pilfer and exploit," adding that "Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it...   The malicious practices of the 90s and 2000s have reared their ugly heads once again, this time driven in large part by both the insatiable appetite of frontier AI labs for high-quality training data, and militant animosity toward the Free Software community."  In short, they argue that for Asahi Linux, using the permissive MIT license "is no longer viable."
Some time ago, we were made aware of multiple attempts to exploit our permissive licensing to hijack our work, with a direct view to replacing the project and aggressively monetising Linux on Apple Silicon. In some extreme cases, in-development feature code was being lifted straight out of our personal forks and published without attribution or lazily rewritten with LLM assistance to obfuscate its origin. The MIT licence explicitly allows this, and has no carveouts to protect against bad faith actors. As such, we made the difficult decision to begin the process of transitioning all of our repositories to the GNU General Public License version 2 or later. Going forward all Asahi Linux code will be licenced under strong copyleft licences only.  
It's FOSS explains that "Under the GPL, anyone who distributes a modified version has to release the source under the same license. You can't legally build a closed, paid Apple Silicon distro on top of GPL code. And if a product's source has to be public, the copying is easier to spot."
And their article also points out that before AI, bad actors attempting code laundering "usually meant manually rewriting code line by line, renaming variables and stuff, and shuffling functions around until it no longer looked like the original. LLMs made it much more easy and cheaper of course."
 In case you did not know, Asahi Linux forbids AI generated code contribution...  As far as I can tell, this is the first time a major open source project has moved to copyleft specifically because of AI-assisted code laundering. Projects have relicensed before, but usually to stop cloud providers from reselling their work as a service. This one is specifically about AI...
The move has drawn criticism, particularly from the BSD side, which was one of the main reasons Asahi chose MIT in the first place. OpenBSD's Apple Silicon support relies on Asahi's m1n1 bootloader.

Apple capped engineers at a $200 daily AI budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
05:30:11 UTC
14:30:11 KST

Stork AI Daily/November 2026/Sunday, November 8, 2026
Apple capped engineers at a $200 daily AI budget.
By Wren Calloway·Reads 40 AI newsletters a day so you only read one.
TL;DR
- Apple has reportedly capped the daily AI spending budget for some of its engineers at $200.
- University of Michigan researchers found non-English prompts consume up to 179 times more energy.
- Palo Alto Networks is reportedly in talks to acquire AI security startup Clutch for $500 million.
- OpenAI launched GPT-6 Cyber to help approved security testers find vulnerabilities and build exploits.
- An obscure SSH edge case on Alpine Linux turned a standard account lock into a root-access trap.
- TokenEconomizer tracks coding-agent sessions to drastically cut wasted token spend on specific repos.
Apple has reportedly slashed the daily AI spending limit for some of its own engineers, dropping the cap from $300 down to $200. The internal reduction points to a stark reality that nobody in Cupertino wants to admit out loud: the company's AI expenditures are threatening to blow past their allocated budgets, and leadership is pulling the emergency brake.
When the world's most valuable tech giant starts treating compute like rationed office supplies, the rest of the industry needs to pay immediate attention. This is not about Apple lacking the liquid cash to fund its internal development. It is about the fundamental, inescapable economics of generative AI at enterprise scale. Uncapped access to advanced models creates an exponential cost curve that will ruin profit margins, even for a hardware empire that prints money.
For working builders, the takeaway is brutal but entirely necessary. The days of throwing unlimited tokens at a messy problem just to see what sticks are rapidly coming to an end. If your current product architecture relies on brute-force inference without strict, automated cost controls, you are not building a sustainable business—you are building a financial time bomb. The next massive competitive advantage in the AI space will not just be raw capability. It will be extreme efficiency. Startups that figure out how to cache intelligently, route to smaller models, and optimize their prompts will survive the coming squeeze. The ones who assume compute will just keep getting cheaper are going to run out of runway long before they run out of ideas. If Apple is sweating the daily API bill, you should be terrified of yours.
Today's Fight
Apple cuts engineer AI budgets to $200 a day.
By Wren Calloway·The Daily
The richest company on earth is rationing compute. If Apple is sweating the internal API bill, your startup's token bloat is a fatal disease.
Apple has reportedly slashed the daily AI spending limit for some of its own engineers, dropping the cap from $300 down to $200. The internal reduction points to a stark reality that nobody in Cupertino wants to admit out loud: the company's AI expenditures are threatening to blow past their allocated budgets, and leadership is pulling the emergency brake.
When the world's most valuable tech giant starts treating compute like rationed office supplies, the rest of the industry needs to pay immediate attention. This is not about Apple lacking the liquid cash to fund its internal development. It is about the fundamental, inescapable economics of generative AI at enterprise scale. Uncapped access to advanced models creates an exponential cost curve that will ruin profit margins, even for a hardware empire that prints money.
For working builders, the takeaway is brutal but entirely necessary. The days of throwing unlimited tokens at a messy problem just to see what sticks are rapidly coming to an end. If your current product architecture relies on brute-force inference without strict, automated cost controls, you are not building a sustainable business—you are building a financial time bomb. The next massive competitive advantage in the AI space will not just be raw capability. It will be extreme efficiency. Startups that figure out how to cache intelligently, route to smaller models, and optimize their prompts will survive the coming squeeze. The ones who assume compute will just keep getting cheaper are going to run out of runway long before they run out of ideas. If Apple is sweating the daily API bill, you should be terrified of yours.
Source: bloomberg.com
The Rest of the Field
Non-English prompts use up to 179 times more energy.
The globalization of AI comes with a massive environmental tax. Building for an international audience just became an infrastructure nightmare.
Researchers at the University of Michigan have uncovered a staggering disparity in AI resource consumption. According to their findings, processing AI prompts in non-English languages consumes up to 179 times more energy than running the exact same prompts in English. Worse, this massive spike in power draw often results in lower accuracy.
This completely shatters the illusion of effortless multilingual AI. If you are building a product intended for a global user base, your compute costs and latency just became wildly unpredictable based entirely on the user's native language. The tokenization systems underlying modern models are heavily optimized for English, punishing everyone else with bloated token counts and agonizingly slow inference.
This is a disaster for localized SaaS. If a French or Japanese user costs you exponentially more to serve while receiving a worse product, the unit economics of global expansion are broken. Until the foundational models overhaul their multilingual tokenization, builders will have to heavily restrict non-English features or eat the massive efficiency loss.
Palo Alto Networks in talks to buy Clutch for $500M.
Agentic AI is a security nightmare waiting to happen, and enterprise defense giants are writing massive checks to plug the holes.
Palo Alto Networks is reportedly in discussions to acquire the cybersecurity startup Clutch for approximately $500 million. The specific goal of this massive proposed buyout is to enhance control over AI agents and strictly manage their access to internal company systems.
We are finally seeing the enterprise reaction to autonomous agents. Everyone wants AI that can take actions on their behalf, but nobody wants a rogue script hallucinating its way into the payroll database. Clutch built the exact guardrails that massive corporations need before they let agentic workflows touch their proprietary data, and Palo Alto is paying a premium to own that chokepoint.
If you are building autonomous tools for B2B clients, access control is no longer a feature—it is the entire product. The enterprise market is terrified of agentic sprawl. The startups that win will be the ones that can show their AI won't accidentally delete the production database when given a vague prompt.
Source: techcrunch.com
OpenAI releases GPT-6 Cyber to approved security testers.
The offensive AI arms race is officially productized. Handing automated exploit generation to testers is a massive escalation in the security wars.
OpenAI has officially launched GPT-6 Cyber, a restricted AI model specifically designed to identify software vulnerabilities and construct functional exploits. Access is currently strictly limited to approved security testers, keeping the offensive capabilities out of the public API for now.
This is a massive shift in how we approach software defense. We have moved from AI that suggests better code to AI that actively hunts for zero-days and writes the payload to break them. By productizing exploit generation, OpenAI is acknowledging that the only way to secure the next generation of software is to attack it with the same automated ferocity that malicious actors are already developing.
For working developers, the margin for error just vanished. If a commercially available model can automatically find and exploit vulnerabilities in your codebase, security through obscurity is dead. You now have to assume that every endpoint you expose will be instantly probed by an agent smarter than the engineer who wrote it.
Source: openai.com
Proton cancels staff AI re-interviews after employee revolt.
Interrogating your entire workforce about their prompt history is a fast track to losing your best talent.
Proton has abruptly canceled its planned AI-use re-interviews following significant internal pushback. The privacy-focused company had intended to question nearly all of its staff regarding how they use AI in their daily workflows, but widespread employee resistance forced leadership to scrap the initiative entirely.
This is a spectacular misread of company culture. Trying to audit the daily AI habits of your entire engineering and product org feels less like policy enforcement and more like a witch hunt. Developers are already using AI to write code, draft emails, and debug systems; threatening them with re-interviews only guarantees they will start hiding their usage instead of optimizing it.
The lesson here is simple: you cannot mandate transparency through intimidation. If you want to know how your team is utilizing new models, give them enterprise accounts and track the telemetry. Treating AI adoption as a suspicious activity to be interrogated is a guaranteed way to drive your top performers to a competitor who actually trusts them.
Source: 404media.co
Google introduces new school AI controls.
Google is forcing schools to choose between modern search and keeping AI out of the classroom, and the bundle is breaking.
Google has rolled out new AI controls specifically tailored for educational institutions. However, the update has sparked immediate debate over whether schools can actually retain access to traditional Google Search while selectively opting out of its deeply integrated AI functionalities.
The tech giant is running into the hard limits of forced adoption. By baking generative summaries directly into the core search experience, Google has created a nightmare for school administrators who want to prevent automated plagiarism without blocking the internet's primary research tool. The friction here shows that treating AI as an un-toggleable default doesn't work in highly regulated environments.
For builders, this is a masterclass in the dangers of feature coupling. If your core product is indispensable but your new AI features are controversial, tying them together doesn't force adoption—it forces churn. Users need the ability to downgrade to the deterministic version of your software, or they will simply find a provider who lets them turn the magic off.
The NFL partners with Carnegie Mellon for AI football analysis.
Sports analytics just moved from spreadsheets to computer vision. The team that trains the best model will own the draft.
The NFL has formed a direct partnership with researchers at Carnegie Mellon University, handing over extensive game film and proprietary player-tracking data. The collaboration is aimed at advancing AI development to fully automate the analysis of football strategy and player performance.
This is what happens when massive proprietary datasets meet specialized models. The NFL is sitting on decades of high-framerate, multi-angle telemetry that no one else has access to. By opening that vault to CMU, they are building the foundation for AI that can read defensive coverages and predict route running faster than any human scout.
The moat here isn't the algorithm; it's the data. If you want to build a truly defensible AI product, you need to find an industry that has been hoarding unstructured data for years and figure out how to parse it. The organizations that own the raw footage will dictate the future of automated analysis.
Source: instagram.com

The NFL has formed a direct partnership with researchers at Carnegie Mellon University, handing over extensive game film and proprietary player-tracking data. The collaboration is aimed at advancing AI development to fully automate the analysis of football strategy and player performance.
This is what happens when massive proprietary datasets meet specialized models. The NFL is sitting on decades of high-framerate, multi-angle telemetry that no one else has access to. By opening that vault to CMU, they are building the foundation for AI that can read defensive coverages and predict route running faster than any human scout.
The moat here isn't the algorithm; it's the data. If you want to build a truly defensible AI product, you need to find an industry that has been hoarding unstructured data for years and figure out how to parse it. The organizations that own the raw footage will dictate the future of automated analysis.
