Is Jensen Huang’s job on the line? Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld estimates it’s “about a 50-50”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
05:26:29 UTC
14:26:29 KST

Nvidia’s board announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang told staff he was unfaithful to his wife. But this isn’t a case of just another CEO having an extramarital affair. The romantic interest is Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy who was feeding information back to Beijing. In short, the stakes reach well beyond Nvidia, given how many tech and financial partners depend on its place at the center of the AI economy. “I’m responsible for an entire industry,” Huang recently told Bloomberg in a sit-down.
A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington dismissed the allegations in late October as “groundless smears and slanders,” and no one has been charged. But U.S. intelligence officials reportedly briefed President Donald Trump about their concerns a year ago, and unnamed senior officials inside the Trump administration told the Times that they doubt Huang could have remained unaware all that time of Alice Huang’s intelligence-gathering role for China. When Trump was first briefed, the Times reported, officials didn’t believe Huang knew, and it isn’t clear whether their assessment has changed. The board, meanwhile, says it sees no sign that national security or company secrets were compromised.
The question is whether Huang can survive this. To think through what could come next, this editor spoke Sunday with famed professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and founder of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, which has hosted Huang at its CEO summits. Sonnenfeld likes Huang, he said, and he called Huang’s career salvageable but put the odds at “about a 50-50.” He also had a lot more food for thought.
First, the damage. Until now, Huang has been “revered and trusted by everybody in technology,” Sonnenfeld noted. But he called this episode “remarkably poor judgment.” Even if Huang was merely naive, he said, “any employee in Nvidia other than him would be fired over this,” and the recklessness alone would mean “an irretrievable loss of confidence.”
Sonnenfeld suggested that Huang’s saving grace could be what social psychologists call idiosyncrasy credits, if he can prove he was being duped. The term comes from Edwin Hollander, a social psychologist who proposed in a 1958 paper that people earn latitude in a group by showing competence and following its rules. Huang has been earning latitude since he co-founded Nvidia in 1993. But all that goodwill can run out when a screw-up looks self-serving or touches the group’s core norms. Here that group includes Nvidia’s board, its roughly 42,000 employees who are bound by security rules, and, in a looser sense, the U.S. government, given it restricts its exports.
We also talked about precedents, except, as it turns out, there really are none for what’s unfolding right now. Executives who survive personal scandals sometimes pick up where they left off at another company, Sonnenfeld observed. Former HP CEO Mark Hurd is one example. Between 2005 and 2010, he drove HP to the top of the tech industry by revenue, then was pressured to resign after he filed inaccurate expense reports that hid a personal relationship with a contractor. Oracle hired him about a month later. Huang has no equivalent because Nvidia is his company
As for the bench at Nvidia, that doesn’t really exist either. While there is typically a hierarchy inside companies of Nvidia’s scale and importance, Huang has kept things as flat as possible, with about 60 direct reports by his own account. That structure makes it hard to figure out who would succeed him (though his children, both of whom work at Nvidia, are sometimes the subject of succession speculation). That won’t stop the worldwide guessing game that’s sure to follow. And boards in crisis often reach for a “messianic solution” from outside, Sonnenfeld said, floating former Google CEO Eric Schmidt as one idea.
Nvidia’s role at the center of a massive and complex circular financing web is what makes this particular predicament so tricky and, undoubtedly, terrifying for a wide number of constituents. Nvidia isn’t just the biggest provider of chips driving the AI boom but also largely the bank behind the buildout. In addition to stakes in hundreds of smaller startups, Nvidia has invested in OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, CoreWeave, and Nebius. In August, it also signed preliminary agreements with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR aimed at mobilizing more than $500 billion over time, and Huang has said Nvidia could backstop up to a quarter of it. The move was widely interpreted as a way to spread risk. Now, a leadership crisis at the center is how a stumble becomes a collapse.
So what’s Nvidia’s board likely doing at this moment? Sonnenfeld noted that Huang’s constant, public advocacy for selling advanced chips to China had already made people anxious. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, whose company Nvidia has backed, had a lot to say about selling chips to China at Davos back in January, likening it to “selling nuclear weapons to North Korea.”
Now the board’s independent members — meaning everyone but Huang — will have to establish what technology reached China if any, and by what routes, including by better understanding Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed. The Singapore cloud company, which grew out of a Chinese gaming business and became Nvidia’s largest buyer in Southeast Asia, bought roughly $2 billion of its chips, The New York Times reported in October 2025, raising broader questions about whether it was helping China circumvent U.S. export restrictions by re-exporting the chips to China or renting them to Chinese customers remotely. (An Nvidia spokesperson told The Hill after the Times report that the allegations were “thoroughly investigated and debunked last year.”)
In the meantime, Huang will keep running the company, Nvidia said Sunday. That’ll be a tall order, even for a CEO who already spends much of his time traveling the world to promote Nvidia. For starters, three House chairmen want a closed-door briefing from Huang on November 18. Nvidia is also reporting its newest earnings on November 17. Sonnenfeld expects that even if Huang keeps the title, he’ll have to hand off some of the day-to-day decision-making.
Only one thing is certain right now. Huang doesn’t own the kind of super-voting stock that would cement his power at Nvidia. Sonnenfeld often argues for dual-class structures that empower founders, and he says Huang’s success without one has been the best counterargument to that case. But if Huang had one, Sonnenfeld continued, removing him would be harder.
This episode may be remembered as a pivotal moment for how the tech industry guards its secrets. Sonnenfeld argues tech has been “way too lax” compared with defense contractors that face clearance regimes. The arrest last month of an OpenAI engineer points to the same problem. He was accused of hiding a recording device behind a TV in an executive conference room, and while OpenAI has said it has no indication that model weights, source code, or customer data were accessed, the case highlights how exposed tech companies are to people who get close.
Huang may well survive the investigation (Sonnenfeld hopes the board clears him of knowingly aiding anyone). The bigger test comes when Nvidia’s employees, customers, and partners, and, indirectly, the millions of Americans with Nvidia in their 401(k) plans, have to decide whether an AI economy built largely on the judgment of Huang still makes sense.

Show HN: Flide: Make Jev-like decision models up to 9.5x faster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
04:43:12 UTC
13:43:12 KST

News · Quick start · Models · Options
Flide is fast inference infrastructure for Jev-style decision models. With exact state forking it is up to 9.5 times faster than vLLM and SGLang, and every answer is the one the model gives the question alone. It serves the Jev /v1/systemone API.
- 🔥 2026-11-09 We added Ainvest-Decision, Darwin-27B-RSI-Decision and KnowLine-31B-Gen1.5 in Flide 0.1.10, and the KnowLine family now reads images.
- 🔥 2026-11-09 We added pplx-decider-v1.1-27b and JEV-35B in Flide 0.1.9, and /v1/systemone now takes several requests in one body.
- 🔥 2026-11-08 We added two decision model families in Flide 0.1.8, including AutoTrust and Clef, and also drex-max-v1.
Earlier news
- 🔥 2026-11-02 We released our paper Flide: Accelerating Decision Inference with Exact State Forking on arXiv.
- 🔥 2026-10-29 We added three decision model families in Flide 0.1.7, including SynACK Decide, Wald and Xor, and Gemma 4 mixture-of-experts models such as KnowLine-26B-A4B.
- 🔥 2026-10-29 We added two decision model families in Flide 0.1.6, including Drex and KnowLine, and flide verify checks exact forking on your own model and requests.
- 🔥 2026-10-28 We added six decision model families in Flide 0.1.5, including Jeffan, JevAny, Kev, Lychee, pplx-decider and StartLux, and images for Lumma and mammoth.
- 🔥 2026-10-26 We added five decision model families in Flide 0.1.4, including cerno, JADE, Linne, mammoth and Sieve, and also Quyet-1.0-Large.
- 🔥 2026-10-26 We added eight decision model families in Flide 0.1.3, including AJev, Bespoke-Nimble, Darwin, jiwo, Lumma, mogan, Quyet and Senova, and LoRA adapters now serve as they are.
- 🔥 2026-10-25 We added two decision model families in Flide 0.1.2, including Intern-Decision and torchcast, and a question now takes up to 256 options.
- 🔥 2026-10-24 We released Flide 0.1.0 on PyPI, serving Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4 chat models and the OneJev and Open-Jev decision models. Welcome to have a try.
See the docs for every model, images, the API and all options.
uv venv -p 3.12 && source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install flide torchvision
flide serve --model OmniJev/OneJev1.6-0.8B
Any model in the model table starts the same way, for example Perplexity's decision model.
flide serve --model perplexity-ai/pplx-decider-flash-v1.2
Every one of them answers this request.
curl http://localhost:8000/v1/systemone -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "state": "Order #1182 arrived with a cracked screen. The customer asks for a refund and attached two photos.",
  "questions": {
    "action": {"type": "choice", "instructions": "What should support do next?",
               "criteria": {"refund": "refund the order", "replace": "send a replacement", "escalate": "ask a human"}},
    "urgent": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Does this need a reply within the hour?"}
  }
}'
The last three columns say how much faster Flide answers one request than the engine its release ships, as the median latency over the requests of each workload on one H200, where DI is the Decision Index. The chat models run against the faster of vLLM and SGLang, and OneJev against qev, the engine it used before Flide. KnowLine 35B runs with --quantize fp8, as its release serves it in FP8. A value marked ~ is the average over the sizes tested.
Apache-2.0. flide/kernels/gdn.py holds a kernel derived from two kernels of
flash-linear-attention (MIT); THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES lists it with
the other code Flide builds on.
If you use Flide in your research, please cite our paper.
@article{li2026flide,
  title   = {Flide: Accelerating Decision Inference with Exact State Forking},
  author  = {Li, Bobo and Song, Jiajia and Fei, Hao and Hsu, Wynne and Lee, Mong Li},
  journal = {arXiv preprint arXiv:2610.42148},
  year    = {2026}

A Critique of GPUI
Germany
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
04:51:10 CET
12:51:10 KST

All posts
A Critique of GPUI
- ui
- rust
- gpui
- signals
- benchmarks
Recently, there has been a trend of more desktop GUI apps being built using native rust GUI frameworks. And there are now even well known electron apps getting official rewrites: Discord announced their app is being rewritten using GPUI.1 Meanwhile, a lot of the LLM-clones being published seem to choose egui. In this post, I want to explain why I am not sure those frameworks are a good foundation to build on.
To put it plainly: I believe both GPUI’s and egui’s state models are dead ends for complex desktop applications. Both are impressive projects, and they have their place. Zed genuinely feels fast and nice to use, and I use egui myself for debug interfaces in bevy games. But I don’t think those frameworks should be the default choice for native desktop apps.
I want to make two arguments:
- Every UI architecture ends up needing to know what changed and who depends on it, or performance characteristics will not scale. A framework whose state model cannot say so makes the application say it by hand, at the cost of whatever made that framework’s API semantics attractive in the first place.
- Once you admit you want that precision, components that run once, with signals and reactive holes, are the simplest API for it.
Disclosure: I ported GPUI’s current Linux renderer to wgpu2, I built the benchmark harness used below, and I work on zgui, a signal-based Rust framework that appears in the charts.
The only question that matters
Raph Levien quotes Ron Minsky: “hidden inside of every UI framework is some kind of incrementalization framework.”3 A UI is a function of state, and state changes a little at a time. But if that function becomes expensive, you might want to start looking for ways to derive a faster way to update pixels on the screen from an incremental state change. So every framework has to answer one question: when one value changes, what runs?
I understand why people like the first three. No state to synchronize, one
place where state lives, a render function that is plain Rust, no macros or
separate compiler. I’m gonna make the argument that these approaches don’t
scale, and fixing the underlying problem defeats what makes these models
simple and easy to reason about.
GPUI: notify is zone.js
GPUI calls itself “a hybrid immediate and retained mode” framework.4 It
retains state in entities. The UI is defined in render functions, changing
state must trigger a rerun.
It is ordinary Rust. You can use if, for and local variables, and there
aren’t any weird wrappers. State changes require an explicit notification:
self.threads.unread = false;
cx.notify;
notify carries the entity id.5 Since Rust doesn’t have a write barrier on
&mut, GPUI cannot see which field changed (or whether anything changed at
all). The Angular team wrote this about zone.js in 2023: it “is only capable of
notifying us when something might have happened”, and “This approach has not
scaled well.”6 notify is more precise than a zone, since it names an
entity, but ultimately it makes the same kind of statement. Below that id, GPUI
knows nothing, so it re-renders every view that is not behind a valid
.cached() boundary. And in practice, GPUI often rerender every view, because
.cached() is rarely used by application authors, and imposes certain
restrictions on layout semantics.
GPUI has a reputation of being “fast”. And while constants might be relatively low, asymptotically, it is leaving a lot on the table. So I ran a few benchmarks, that specifically test how much a sparse state change in a large UI actually costs.
At 3,000 live rows with a cached view per row, changing one label takes 8.4 ms. A hover, a keystroke and writing a value equal to the old one all cost about the same, because the cost follows the tree and not the change. It grows by about 3 ms per 1,000 live rows. Write the rows as plain elements, as in the code above, and the same label takes 92 ms. A hand-written equality guard takes the equal write from 7.9 ms to 0.9 µs (demonstrating how much is left for each call site to find).
This doesn’t mean that every GPUI app is slow, but it shows the limit of the state model. Especially with more expensive layout, you do hit this wall in practice. Zed might feel fast, but the truth is that Zed is a relatively simple app, UI wise. The app’s chrome contains a few buttons, in a simple layout, a sidebar and a text editor, and the text editor is implemented as a custom element, completely bypassing GPUI’s layout and view semantics. By their own account, a window “has tens of nodes and a few thousand elements”.7
Making GPUI precise defeats GPUI
The obvious fix is to retain more. Zed has experimental branches for this, and Longbridge’s gpui-fast is a fork that keeps every view’s subtree between frames.8 9 It works, within a limit: the smallest thing either one can reuse is a view. So to update one label without rebuilding the sidebar, the label has to be a view:
Its owner then has to create it and keep the handle:
let badge = cx.new;
That is an entity, a Render impl, a subscription, a stored copy of the value,
a hand-written guard and an owner, all to express that one label depends on one
count. In a signal framework it is this:
let unread = new;
derived
The rest of GPUI’s API works against this too. Render takes no props, so
parents push values into child entities during their own render. RenderOnce
components, which is what buttons and rows are, draw inside their parent’s view
and are no boundary at all. List rows are closures, so a row view means
managing a keyed map of entities by hand.
And it only helps where state happens to line up with views. I reran gpui-fast’s own 60-panel benchmark, drew each frame once, and then moved the state:
With state owned by each panel, one change saves 83%. With a shared model, retention makes the same frame 11% slower. The window and the edit are identical. In real Zed, the Zed team measured retention “1–3% slower than off on ordinary workloads”, found that “Most of the real-Zed win” came from other work, and warned that “microbenchmark wins didn’t predict real-Zed results”.8 gpui-fast is real progress and costs little to adopt: it takes the 3,000-row label from 8.4 to 3.4 ms. But that frame renders three views and lays out one element, and still spends 3.4 ms, because the frame is still a walk over the whole tree.
The web has already walked this road. Redux’s style guide says “Prefer having more UI components subscribed to the Redux store and reading data at a more granular level”.10 MobX says to “create lots of small observer components”.11 Both tell you to make a boundary per projection, manually, because the framework can’t infer it.
This is the part I find hardest to get past. People choose GPUI because render
is a plain function of state. A UI where each projection is a separately owned
entity with a subscription and a guard is no longer that. It is a signal graph
built by hand from much heavier parts, where a missed edge is silent. Zed’s own
design note says “Missing notifications are application bugs”.12 Keep the
pleasant API and you get view-sized updates. Take the precision and you lose the
pleasant API. A signals crate on top would not change the trade, because its
smallest sink is still a view. Reaching one node with no render running needs
writes the framework can see and nodes that outlive a frame, and that means a
new state model and a new element contract.
Elm: deceptively simple at small scales
At the size it is usually shown, the Elm architecture is a deceptively simple
UI model: one state value, one update, one view, and every change has a
name. While large applications do use it successully,13 14 I do want to
make the point that this clarity belongs to the small case, and in a complex
application signals and stores are arguably easier to reason about.
Take the same unread count. It has to be right after every message, so either
view recomputes it on every update or update maintains it:
match message The definition of unread is now nowhere in particular. It is spread across
every arm that touches a thread, and each new message has to remember it. The
compiler checks that the match is exhaustive, but it does not check the
arithmetic. The memo above has one definition, and a new writer cannot forget
it.
The same thing happens with location. Where does a hover state or a half-typed
draft live? Single source of truth says in the model, with a message type
routed down and an outcome routed back up. Elm’s guide: “Actively trying to
make components is a recipe for disaster in Elm.”15. Iced recommends
returning an Action to the parent.16 Iced’s maintainer says components in
this architecture always end “with pain”, and also makes the best case for the
discipline: avoiding them “forces you to think hard about your data
model”.17 Okay, I guess that’s a fair argument. But cosmic-files has 136
top-level message variants and 73 more for a tab, plus a Tab::update that
returns commands for the parent to interpret.18 Everything in that is
explicit, and none of it is simple.
The architecture also has the same issue GPUI has. The update implementation
tells you what a message writes, it cannot tell you what read the field.
Anything inside the view might. Elm’s architecture doesn’t answer “what
changed?”, it answers “what happened?”. Session export might be useful in some
scenarios, but it is not useful for scalable performance characteristics.19
This is what I read in the web’s history. Redux is the best-known relative of this design, and its docs read like a field report. Treat a portion of your store “as if it were a database”.20 Selectors “will be re-run after every dispatched action”.21 The core package is “obsolete”, replaced by a toolkit made to remove boilerplate.22 Outside React, the mainstream has moved to tracked reads. Angular, Vue, Svelte and Solid build on signals or something equivalent, Preact offers them, and Svelte’s team put it this way: “we’ve come to the realisation that Knockout was right all along.”23 Inside React, Jotai and MobX bring tracking in as libraries, and Legend-State even offers a “render once” style.24 Most applications are still on React, and React’s team disagrees, which I come back to below. So the convergence is on the state model, outside one large exception.
Performance follows the same line. Since Iced rebuilds all of view after
every batch of messages, one label at 3,000 rows builds 39,023 widgets and
takes 7.3 ms. Lazy on every row only gets that to 5.7 ms, because view
still has to visit each row to hash its key. The official lazy example keys
on a version: u8 that four update arms bump by hand.25 That is a dirty
flag with a nicer name. In fairness, cosmic-files and Halloy use no lazy at
all, and on a virtualized list Iced is one of the fastest frameworks I
measured, at 0.19 ms. A bounded screen rebuilds cheaply. But asymptotic
complexity is clear. And similar to GPUI, the API semantics simply can’t
express the necessary information.
There is actually precedence for this: Vizia shows what happens when you add
precision to this model. It moved from lenses to signals in March 2026 and kept
its Model and event dispatch.26 This is its counter, shortened:27
let count = new;
AppData .build;
new
    .on_press;
new.width.live;
The label reads the signal directly, and the same closure that builds the
button created it. The enum, the dispatch and the handler exist to carry one
call to update. Vizia was never strict Elm, since its views are built once,
and signals were a sensible move: it got per-field writes. But look at what
remains of Elm’s reasons. State is a graph of mutable cells, Model is a bag
of handles, and event is a &mut self side effect. You now have two systems
for saying that something changed. So my objection to adding signals to the Elm
architecture really is the same as with GPUI: they work, and they remove what
you came for.
A quick note on immediate mode
egui’s pitch is the best in the field: “You don’t have to worry about app state and GUI state being out-of-sync”.28 For a tool, this is hard to beat:
for row in rows The price is that a frame costs the size of the UI, independent of what changed. At 3,000 rows every small edit takes about 32 ms, or about 19 ms with accessibility off. egui’s author is candid about the trade: immediate mode is “easier to use, but less powerful”.28
As the application grows, the original attraction goes. The layout paradox is “a
fundamental shortcoming”.28 Long lists need show_rows, which takes one
fixed row height. Rerun, the largest egui application I know of, clamps queries
by “inspecting egui state from the previous frame”.29 Anything expensive goes
behind a cache keyed on your data. A cache that has to agree with your data is
the synchronization problem immediate mode set out to remove, now in application
code, one frame late.
One engine, different wiring
The harness can show this directly, because some frameworks can be wired coarsely and finely on the same engine:
I benchmarked some of the engines in two ways, once in the most fine grained way they can be used, and once in a coarser way. The results show how much there is to gain with fine-grained reactivity.
Two things stand out. Iced’s factor is small because the view function still
runs. And Floem’s coarse case is worth a look: every cell reads one global
revision signal, which is notify in signal clothing. It is the slowest result
on the chart. So signals do not rescue coarse state. The React team found the
same thing from the other side: on a benchmark with “one giant input”, a
signals-style runtime disappointed, and Joe Savona concluded the data model “is
just as important, maybe more so” than the algorithm.30 The state has to be
shaped like the reads. That is why I call this a state model problem. A good
API should make it easy to align the data model with its UI projection.
Why run once
Suppose you accept all of that. You want the framework to track reads, and you want state shaped to match. What is the simplest API?
That is the whole thing. The body runs once. The closures you hand to the
framework run again when something they read changes. A local variable is a
local variable. There are no hook rules, no dependency arrays, no stale
closures and no PartialEq on props. Nothing reconstructs a row’s identity,
because the row is still there.
Compare signals with re-running components, which is Freya’s model. It works well: one keystroke at 3,000 rows costs 1.2 ms. But look at a counter:31
;
use_state exists because that line runs again. You now hold both models: read
tracking decides which scope re-runs, and then re-render semantics apply inside
it, with hooks, prop equality and a diff. Finer updates need smaller components,
which is GPUI’s problem at a much lower price. What the re-running body buys is
ordinary control flow, and that is the serious objection.
Dan Abramov makes a compelling argument.32 Run-once puts your rendering logic in closures, so top-level control flow stops working, and you group code around values and not around logic. “The beauty of React is that making things ‘computed’ is an optimization, not a requirement.” He is right about it. This compiles, but the first line never updates:
new,               // read once; never updates
derived,   // a hole; updates
A reactive if has to become a dyn_container, and a for a dyn_stack.
Solid 2.0 had to add dev warnings for top-level reads.33
But the same comment contains the reason I land the other way. He says Solid’s
regrouping is “Similar to how you have to restructure your code around the
values when you optimize it with useMemo.” Exactly. If your application never
needs that, React’s model may be simpler. If it does, you pay for the
regrouping either way, and the only choice is when: from the start, or later
under a profiler. Ryan Carniato’s reply is the one I agree with: “In Solid you
always write as if the data is derived so you don’t refactor to optimize.”32
Once you know you want this precision, run-once is the API that stops
pretending otherwise. The failure modes also favour it. A forgotten hole goes
stale on the first update, in the place you wrote it. A forgotten notify
depends on what else happened to redraw.
To be perfectly honest, the ecosystem’s wider convergence is on read tracking
in general, and not on run-once specifically. Angular considered per-binding
updates and chose per-view, in writing, and it lands within about 1 ms of Solid
on a partial update.6 34 Apple and Google, who control their languages,
kept re-running bodies with @Observable and Compose.35 36 A hole is
itself a re-run scope, so what differs is how big the default scope is. Two things
I want to note on this though:
- First, those systems pay for their larger scopes with a compiler. Compose has
a compiler plugin, Angular compiles templates, and React’s compiler is the
serious rival to everything here: it keeps React’s API and removes many
needless re-renders, with loads up to 12% better.37 For Rust, I suspect that
most people that prefer immediate mode or elm (or whatever GPUI is) would not
like the idea of an additional compiler. A proc macro only sees tokens, not
types, and render is an arbitrary function, so there is no pass that can
split it into scopes. What Rust can express cheaply is a closure.
- Second, their own guidance keeps describing the same problem: “Defer reads as long as possible” for Compose, and “Unnecessary view body updates can really add up” for SwiftUI.38 39 A framework that runs the body once removes that category at component level.
View-level rerun and fine-grained signals can have the same performance ceiling. But signals encourage fine-grained state projections and memoization from the beginning, for view-level rerun its an explicit choice that often leads to more boilerplate.
Signals do not automatically make your app fast
Fine-grained reactivity does not make an app fast on its own.
Floem’s reactivity does exactly what it promises. Changing a label runs 5 effects and spends 0.01 ms in reactive work, then about 14 ms in layout, because Taffy does not know that one leaf moved. (Floem also has a known bug where that edit never repaints, so treat this as a floor.) Vizia runs 4 bindings, then walks all 120,091 entities, for 46 ms. Slint writes an equal value in 4 µs, and takes 172 ms for a label, in a pass that walks about 30,000 items. Freya produces 5 mutations, then visits 57,050 layout nodes to recompute 14. GPUI beats most of them on this edit.
This is the distinction the argument depends on. All of those linear costs are in the engine respectively. Nothing in the application’s code requires them, so they can be fixed behind the same API without changing an application. zgui shows how far that goes: 0.69 ms for the label at 3,000 rows and about 0.26 ms per 1,000 rows, around 12 times flatter than GPUI. It is still not flat, and it is my framework and was tuned on this harness, so take these numbers with a grain of salt. In Iced and egui the linear cost is in the contract: the API says your code runs. No engine work can remove that, and app code has to change. GPUI probably sits somewhere in between, which is why gpui-fast can improve the situation to some extent.
At this point, I wan’t to share a more detailed benchmark matrix. Read the re-running columns down the first five rows and they barely move, because they do not depend on the edit. The signal columns move a lot, because the underlying implementations differ.
The bottom of that grid is also where the cost signals have becomes visible.
- Creation. Filtering at 3,000 live rows takes 56 ms in Iced, 67 in egui and 123 in GPUI, against 371 in zgui, 835 in Floem and 982 in Freya. On a virtualized list it is 1.0 ms in Iced and 7.2 in zgui. “Setting up the dependency graph is not free.”6
- Memory. Resident memory usage for large scenes is generally higher the more a framework retains.
- Effects. Facebook moved away from two-way binding because “cascading updates” became hard to predict.40 That history is true, and Angular’s docs still say “Effects should be the last API you reach for.”41 Modern graphs are glitch-free. Careless effects are still difficult to reason about and quickly result in feedback loops or similar stuff.
- Rust. Signals rely on arena handles and move closures. Levien thinks
such patterns “adapt poorly to Rust”.3 I think they adapt well enough, and
GPUI’s entities are arena handles too, but, admittedly, it is not a free lunch.
Conclusion
GPUI makes a full frame realitively cheap, and that makes it probably good enough for many use-cases. It is certainly enough for an editor whose expensive surface is handled by hand. For a large application it leaves a choice: keep the API people like and pay per view, or get precision by writing a signal graph out of entities. Elm and immediate mode have the same problem. Each is clearest in the small, and each loses the thing it was chosen for as precision becomes necessary, and, from my personal experience, that happens faster than people expect.
Tracked reads are where most of the field has ended up, whatever it started from. If that is where we are going, I think we should start there, and make the component a function that runs once.
Method
- Numbers are medians of apply and settle from my unpublished harness, on one machine: i9-13900K, RTX 3080 Ti, Vulkan, Linux. Windows, compositor and input are not included. Frameworks’ maintainers have not reviewed the adapters.
- GPUI is at ddc9eda925 and gpui-fast at 86a8228229. zgui is at 082337db.
These were through September and November 2026, as the best of three passes.
- Cells marked † in the grid failed their correctness oracle: Floem’s label and keystroke edits, as noted above, and Slint’s font size. Every other charted cell passed.
- The 60-panel results are gpui-fast’s retained_bench with my additions, in
test mode, so no GPU work is included. Retention off there is still gpui-fast.
- Figures from Zed’s plan are its authors’, from experimental branches.
- Rust examples were type-checked against the vendored frameworks. Vizia’s and Freya’s come from their own sources, shortened.

A Critique of GPUI

All posts
A Critique of GPUI
- ui
- rust
- gpui
- signals
- benchmarks
Recently, there has been a trend of more desktop GUI apps being built using native rust GUI frameworks. And there are now even well known electron apps getting official rewrites: Discord announced their app is being rewritten using GPUI.1 Meanwhile, a lot of the LLM-clones being published seem to choose egui. In this post, I want to explain why I am not sure those frameworks are a good foundation to build on.
To put it plainly: I believe both GPUI’s and egui’s state models are dead ends for complex desktop applications. Both are impressive projects, and they have their place. Zed genuinely feels fast and nice to use, and I use egui myself for debug interfaces in bevy games. But I don’t think those frameworks should be the default choice for native desktop apps.
I want to make two arguments:
- Every UI architecture ends up needing to know what changed and who depends on it, or performance characteristics will not scale. A framework whose state model cannot say so makes the application say it by hand, at the cost of whatever made that framework’s API semantics attractive in the first place.
- Once you admit you want that precision, components that run once, with signals and reactive holes, are the simplest API for it.
Disclosure: I ported GPUI’s current Linux renderer to wgpu2, I built the benchmark harness used below, and I work on zgui, a signal-based Rust framework that appears in the charts.
The only question that matters
Raph Levien quotes Ron Minsky: “hidden inside of every UI framework is some kind of incrementalization framework.”3 A UI is a function of state, and state changes a little at a time. But if that function becomes expensive, you might want to start looking for ways to derive a faster way to update pixels on the screen from an incremental state change. So every framework has to answer one question: when one value changes, what runs?
I understand why people like the first three. No state to synchronize, one
place where state lives, a render function that is plain Rust, no macros or
separate compiler. I’m gonna make the argument that these approaches don’t
scale, and fixing the underlying problem defeats what makes these models
simple and easy to reason about.
GPUI: notify is zone.js
GPUI calls itself “a hybrid immediate and retained mode” framework.4 It
retains state in entities. The UI is defined in render functions, changing
state must trigger a rerun.
It is ordinary Rust. You can use if, for and local variables, and there
aren’t any weird wrappers. State changes require an explicit notification:
self.threads.unread = false;
cx.notify;
notify carries the entity id.5 Since Rust doesn’t have a write barrier on
&mut, GPUI cannot see which field changed (or whether anything changed at
all). The Angular team wrote this about zone.js in 2023: it “is only capable of
notifying us when something might have happened”, and “This approach has not
scaled well.”6 notify is more precise than a zone, since it names an
entity, but ultimately it makes the same kind of statement. Below that id, GPUI
knows nothing, so it re-renders every view that is not behind a valid
.cached() boundary. And in practice, GPUI often rerender every view, because
.cached() is rarely used by application authors, and imposes certain
restrictions on layout semantics.
GPUI has a reputation of being “fast”. And while constants might be relatively low, asymptotically, it is leaving a lot on the table. So I ran a few benchmarks, that specifically test how much a sparse state change in a large UI actually costs.
At 3,000 live rows with a cached view per row, changing one label takes 8.4 ms. A hover, a keystroke and writing a value equal to the old one all cost about the same, because the cost follows the tree and not the change. It grows by about 3 ms per 1,000 live rows. Write the rows as plain elements, as in the code above, and the same label takes 92 ms. A hand-written equality guard takes the equal write from 7.9 ms to 0.9 µs (demonstrating how much is left for each call site to find).
This doesn’t mean that every GPUI app is slow, but it shows the limit of the state model. Especially with more expensive layout, you do hit this wall in practice. Zed might feel fast, but the truth is that Zed is a relatively simple app, UI wise. The app’s chrome contains a few buttons, in a simple layout, a sidebar and a text editor, and the text editor is implemented as a custom element, completely bypassing GPUI’s layout and view semantics. By their own account, a window “has tens of nodes and a few thousand elements”.7
Making GPUI precise defeats GPUI
The obvious fix is to retain more. Zed has experimental branches for this, and Longbridge’s gpui-fast is a fork that keeps every view’s subtree between frames.8 9 It works, within a limit: the smallest thing either one can reuse is a view. So to update one label without rebuilding the sidebar, the label has to be a view:
Its owner then has to create it and keep the handle:
let badge = cx.new;
That is an entity, a Render impl, a subscription, a stored copy of the value,
a hand-written guard and an owner, all to express that one label depends on one
count. In a signal framework it is this:
let unread = new;
derived
The rest of GPUI’s API works against this too. Render takes no props, so
parents push values into child entities during their own render. RenderOnce
components, which is what buttons and rows are, draw inside their parent’s view
and are no boundary at all. List rows are closures, so a row view means
managing a keyed map of entities by hand.
And it only helps where state happens to line up with views. I reran gpui-fast’s own 60-panel benchmark, drew each frame once, and then moved the state:
With state owned by each panel, one change saves 83%. With a shared model, retention makes the same frame 11% slower. The window and the edit are identical. In real Zed, the Zed team measured retention “1–3% slower than off on ordinary workloads”, found that “Most of the real-Zed win” came from other work, and warned that “microbenchmark wins didn’t predict real-Zed results”.8 gpui-fast is real progress and costs little to adopt: it takes the 3,000-row label from 8.4 to 3.4 ms. But that frame renders three views and lays out one element, and still spends 3.4 ms, because the frame is still a walk over the whole tree.
The web has already walked this road. Redux’s style guide says “Prefer having more UI components subscribed to the Redux store and reading data at a more granular level”.10 MobX says to “create lots of small observer components”.11 Both tell you to make a boundary per projection, manually, because the framework can’t infer it.
This is the part I find hardest to get past. People choose GPUI because render
is a plain function of state. A UI where each projection is a separately owned
entity with a subscription and a guard is no longer that. It is a signal graph
built by hand from much heavier parts, where a missed edge is silent. Zed’s own
design note says “Missing notifications are application bugs”.12 Keep the
pleasant API and you get view-sized updates. Take the precision and you lose the
pleasant API. A signals crate on top would not change the trade, because its
smallest sink is still a view. Reaching one node with no render running needs
writes the framework can see and nodes that outlive a frame, and that means a
new state model and a new element contract.
Elm: deceptively simple at small scales
At the size it is usually shown, the Elm architecture is a deceptively simple
UI model: one state value, one update, one view, and every change has a
name. While large applications do use it successully,13 14 I do want to
make the point that this clarity belongs to the small case, and in a complex
application signals and stores are arguably easier to reason about.
Take the same unread count. It has to be right after every message, so either
view recomputes it on every update or update maintains it:
match message The definition of unread is now nowhere in particular. It is spread across
every arm that touches a thread, and each new message has to remember it. The
compiler checks that the match is exhaustive, but it does not check the
arithmetic. The memo above has one definition, and a new writer cannot forget
it.
The same thing happens with location. Where does a hover state or a half-typed
draft live? Single source of truth says in the model, with a message type
routed down and an outcome routed back up. Elm’s guide: “Actively trying to
make components is a recipe for disaster in Elm.”15. Iced recommends
returning an Action to the parent.16 Iced’s maintainer says components in
this architecture always end “with pain”, and also makes the best case for the
discipline: avoiding them “forces you to think hard about your data
model”.17 Okay, I guess that’s a fair argument. But cosmic-files has 136
top-level message variants and 73 more for a tab, plus a Tab::update that
returns commands for the parent to interpret.18 Everything in that is
explicit, and none of it is simple.
The architecture also has the same issue GPUI has. The update implementation
tells you what a message writes, it cannot tell you what read the field.
Anything inside the view might. Elm’s architecture doesn’t answer “what
changed?”, it answers “what happened?”. Session export might be useful in some
scenarios, but it is not useful for scalable performance characteristics.19
This is what I read in the web’s history. Redux is the best-known relative of this design, and its docs read like a field report. Treat a portion of your store “as if it were a database”.20 Selectors “will be re-run after every dispatched action”.21 The core package is “obsolete”, replaced by a toolkit made to remove boilerplate.22 Outside React, the mainstream has moved to tracked reads. Angular, Vue, Svelte and Solid build on signals or something equivalent, Preact offers them, and Svelte’s team put it this way: “we’ve come to the realisation that Knockout was right all along.”23 Inside React, Jotai and MobX bring tracking in as libraries, and Legend-State even offers a “render once” style.24 Most applications are still on React, and React’s team disagrees, which I come back to below. So the convergence is on the state model, outside one large exception.
Performance follows the same line. Since Iced rebuilds all of view after
every batch of messages, one label at 3,000 rows builds 39,023 widgets and
takes 7.3 ms. Lazy on every row only gets that to 5.7 ms, because view
still has to visit each row to hash its key. The official lazy example keys
on a version: u8 that four update arms bump by hand.25 That is a dirty
flag with a nicer name. In fairness, cosmic-files and Halloy use no lazy at
all, and on a virtualized list Iced is one of the fastest frameworks I
measured, at 0.19 ms. A bounded screen rebuilds cheaply. But asymptotic
complexity is clear. And similar to GPUI, the API semantics simply can’t
express the necessary information.
There is actually precedence for this: Vizia shows what happens when you add
precision to this model. It moved from lenses to signals in March 2026 and kept
its Model and event dispatch.26 This is its counter, shortened:27
let count = new;
AppData .build;
new
    .on_press;
new.width.live;
The label reads the signal directly, and the same closure that builds the
button created it. The enum, the dispatch and the handler exist to carry one
call to update. Vizia was never strict Elm, since its views are built once,
and signals were a sensible move: it got per-field writes. But look at what
remains of Elm’s reasons. State is a graph of mutable cells, Model is a bag
of handles, and event is a &mut self side effect. You now have two systems
for saying that something changed. So my objection to adding signals to the Elm
architecture really is the same as with GPUI: they work, and they remove what
you came for.
A quick note on immediate mode
egui’s pitch is the best in the field: “You don’t have to worry about app state and GUI state being out-of-sync”.28 For a tool, this is hard to beat:
for row in rows The price is that a frame costs the size of the UI, independent of what changed. At 3,000 rows every small edit takes about 32 ms, or about 19 ms with accessibility off. egui’s author is candid about the trade: immediate mode is “easier to use, but less powerful”.28
As the application grows, the original attraction goes. The layout paradox is “a
fundamental shortcoming”.28 Long lists need show_rows, which takes one
fixed row height. Rerun, the largest egui application I know of, clamps queries
by “inspecting egui state from the previous frame”.29 Anything expensive goes
behind a cache keyed on your data. A cache that has to agree with your data is
the synchronization problem immediate mode set out to remove, now in application
code, one frame late.
One engine, different wiring
The harness can show this directly, because some frameworks can be wired coarsely and finely on the same engine:
I benchmarked some of the engines in two ways, once in the most fine grained way they can be used, and once in a coarser way. The results show how much there is to gain with fine-grained reactivity.
Two things stand out. Iced’s factor is small because the view function still
runs. And Floem’s coarse case is worth a look: every cell reads one global
revision signal, which is notify in signal clothing. It is the slowest result
on the chart. So signals do not rescue coarse state. The React team found the
same thing from the other side: on a benchmark with “one giant input”, a
signals-style runtime disappointed, and Joe Savona concluded the data model “is
just as important, maybe more so” than the algorithm.30 The state has to be
shaped like the reads. That is why I call this a state model problem. A good
API should make it easy to align the data model with its UI projection.
Why run once
Suppose you accept all of that. You want the framework to track reads, and you want state shaped to match. What is the simplest API?
That is the whole thing. The body runs once. The closures you hand to the
framework run again when something they read changes. A local variable is a
local variable. There are no hook rules, no dependency arrays, no stale
closures and no PartialEq on props. Nothing reconstructs a row’s identity,
because the row is still there.
Compare signals with re-running components, which is Freya’s model. It works well: one keystroke at 3,000 rows costs 1.2 ms. But look at a counter:31
;
use_state exists because that line runs again. You now hold both models: read
tracking decides which scope re-runs, and then re-render semantics apply inside
it, with hooks, prop equality and a diff. Finer updates need smaller components,
which is GPUI’s problem at a much lower price. What the re-running body buys is
ordinary control flow, and that is the serious objection.
Dan Abramov makes a compelling argument.32 Run-once puts your rendering logic in closures, so top-level control flow stops working, and you group code around values and not around logic. “The beauty of React is that making things ‘computed’ is an optimization, not a requirement.” He is right about it. This compiles, but the first line never updates:
new,               // read once; never updates
derived,   // a hole; updates
A reactive if has to become a dyn_container, and a for a dyn_stack.
Solid 2.0 had to add dev warnings for top-level reads.33
But the same comment contains the reason I land the other way. He says Solid’s
regrouping is “Similar to how you have to restructure your code around the
values when you optimize it with useMemo.” Exactly. If your application never
needs that, React’s model may be simpler. If it does, you pay for the
regrouping either way, and the only choice is when: from the start, or later
under a profiler. Ryan Carniato’s reply is the one I agree with: “In Solid you
always write as if the data is derived so you don’t refactor to optimize.”32
Once you know you want this precision, run-once is the API that stops
pretending otherwise. The failure modes also favour it. A forgotten hole goes
stale on the first update, in the place you wrote it. A forgotten notify
depends on what else happened to redraw.
To be perfectly honest, the ecosystem’s wider convergence is on read tracking
in general, and not on run-once specifically. Angular considered per-binding
updates and chose per-view, in writing, and it lands within about 1 ms of Solid
on a partial update.6 34 Apple and Google, who control their languages,
kept re-running bodies with @Observable and Compose.35 36 A hole is
itself a re-run scope, so what differs is how big the default scope is. Two things
I want to note on this though:
- First, those systems pay for their larger scopes with a compiler. Compose has
a compiler plugin, Angular compiles templates, and React’s compiler is the
serious rival to everything here: it keeps React’s API and removes many
needless re-renders, with loads up to 12% better.37 For Rust, I suspect that
most people that prefer immediate mode or elm (or whatever GPUI is) would not
like the idea of an additional compiler. A proc macro only sees tokens, not
types, and render is an arbitrary function, so there is no pass that can
split it into scopes. What Rust can express cheaply is a closure.
- Second, their own guidance keeps describing the same problem: “Defer reads as long as possible” for Compose, and “Unnecessary view body updates can really add up” for SwiftUI.38 39 A framework that runs the body once removes that category at component level.
View-level rerun and fine-grained signals can have the same performance ceiling. But signals encourage fine-grained state projections and memoization from the beginning, for view-level rerun its an explicit choice that often leads to more boilerplate.
Signals do not automatically make your app fast
Fine-grained reactivity does not make an app fast on its own.
Floem’s reactivity does exactly what it promises. Changing a label runs 5 effects and spends 0.01 ms in reactive work, then about 14 ms in layout, because Taffy does not know that one leaf moved. (Floem also has a known bug where that edit never repaints, so treat this as a floor.) Vizia runs 4 bindings, then walks all 120,091 entities, for 46 ms. Slint writes an equal value in 4 µs, and takes 172 ms for a label, in a pass that walks about 30,000 items. Freya produces 5 mutations, then visits 57,050 layout nodes to recompute 14. GPUI beats most of them on this edit.
This is the distinction the argument depends on. All of those linear costs are in the engine respectively. Nothing in the application’s code requires them, so they can be fixed behind the same API without changing an application. zgui shows how far that goes: 0.69 ms for the label at 3,000 rows and about 0.26 ms per 1,000 rows, around 12 times flatter than GPUI. GPUI probably sits somewhere in between, which is why gpui-fast can improve the situation to some extent.
At this point, I wan’t to share a more detailed benchmark matrix. Read the re-running columns down the first five rows and they barely move, because they do not depend on the edit. The signal columns move a lot, because the underlying implementations differ.
The bottom of that grid is also where the cost signals have becomes visible.
- Creation. Filtering at 3,000 live rows takes 56 ms in Iced, 67 in egui and 123 in GPUI, against 371 in zgui, 835 in Floem and 982 in Freya. On a virtualized list it is 1.0 ms in Iced and 7.2 in zgui. “Setting up the dependency graph is not free.”6
- Memory. Resident memory usage for large scenes is generally higher the more a framework retains.
- Effects. Facebook moved away from two-way binding because “cascading updates” became hard to predict.40 That history is true, and Angular’s docs still say “Effects should be the last API you reach for.”41 Modern graphs are glitch-free. Careless effects are still difficult to reason about and quickly result in feedback loops or similar stuff.
- Rust. Signals rely on arena handles and move closures. Levien thinks
such patterns “adapt poorly to Rust”.3 I think they adapt well enough, and
GPUI’s entities are arena handles too, but, admittedly, it is not a free lunch.
Conclusion
GPUI makes a full frame realitively cheap, and that makes it probably good enough for many use-cases. It is certainly enough for an editor whose expensive surface is handled by hand. For a large application it leaves a choice: keep the API people like and pay per view, or get precision by writing a signal graph out of entities. Elm and immediate mode have the same problem. Each is clearest in the small, and each loses the thing it was chosen for as precision becomes necessary, and, from my personal experience, that happens faster than people expect.
Tracked reads are where most of the field has ended up, whatever it started from. If that is where we are going, I think we should start there, and make the component a function that runs once.
Method
- Numbers are medians of apply and settle from my unpublished harness, on one machine: i9-13900K, RTX 3080 Ti, Vulkan, Linux. Windows, compositor and input are not included. Frameworks’ maintainers have not reviewed the adapters.
- GPUI is at ddc9eda925 and gpui-fast at 86a8228229. zgui is at 082337db.
These were through September and November 2026, as the best of three passes.
- Cells marked † in the grid failed their correctness oracle: Floem’s label and keystroke edits, as noted above, and Slint’s font size. Every other charted cell passed.
- The 60-panel results are gpui-fast’s retained_bench with my additions, in
test mode, so no GPU work is included. Retention off there is still gpui-fast.
- Figures from Zed’s plan are its authors’, from experimental branches.
- Rust examples were type-checked against the vendored frameworks. Vizia’s and Freya’s come from their own sources, shortened.

Pomera&#8217;s sleek distraction-free writing machine is just too small
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
03:42:35 UTC
12:42:35 KST

Pomera’s digital typewriters are a cult hit with those craving a distraction-free writing experience. Dedicated word processor devices never caught on in the US the way they did in Japan. And the ones available in the US, like the AlphaSmart Neo, just weren’t as sleek and portable as the tiny foldable devices from Pomera.
Pomera’s sleek distraction-free writing machine is just too small
The first of Pomera’s digital typewriters to reach the US has its charm, but it’s too uncomfortable for long typing sessions.
Until last year, Pomera devices were only available in Japan, leaving people to import them and stumble their way through software created for Japanese users. The $549 Pomera DM250US is the company’s first device created for US writers, with a US English keyboard layout and native English software. For those of us who want someplace to write where the temptation of Bluesky isn’t a click away and there’s no danger of disappearing down a Wikipedia rabbit hole, it was an exciting development.
After months of testing, I can say that I get the appeal, but it’s not for me. The tradeoffs it makes to cram so much into such a portable device make it a literal pain to use for its intended purpose.
Pomera DM250US
The Good
- Extremely portable
- Excellent battery life
- Robust editing tools
The Bad
- Painfully cramped keyboard
- Clunky syncing
- Pricey
The DM250 is undeniably the sleekest distraction-free writing device I’ve come across. It’s a wide clamshell, with a serious-looking matte black finish and a 7-inch LCD screen that seems too small for its chassis. Its extremely compact size —10.3 inches wide, 4.7 inches deep, and 0.7 inches thick — means I can toss it in my tiny Uniqlo crossbody bag with room to spare for my Kobo, my iPod, two sets of headphones (wired and Bluetooth), plus a Field Notes and a pen.
Its closest competitor is probably the Freewrite Traveler, which has a similar laptop-like form factor and price. The Traveler is larger in every direction, at 11.3 inches by 5 inches by 1 inch, and its glossy plastic feels cheap in comparison to the Pomera. The Traveler also opts for a crisp E Ink screen that sips battery life, but is also completely useless in a dimly lit room.
Pomera’s battery life is pretty solid, though. It’s rated for 24 hours of continuous use. At least anecdotally, that seems to check out. I’ve been using Pomera sporadically for a little over three months now and have only had to charge it once. I last charged it in mid-September, and it’s still sitting at about 50 percent battery life.
The software on the Pomera is also relatively complex for a distraction-free writing device. It has tons of options for customizing the interface, a basic calendar, and even spell check. I really like the calendar app. Each date has a text file associated with it that’s displayed in a sidebar. It’s easy to open quickly and add appointments, notes, or journal entries without closing the main document you’re working on. It’s the kind of perfect less-is-more tool that stays out of the way yet is incredibly flexible.
Pomera also does have some welcome options for tweaking the interface. By default, it’s black text on a white screen, but you can invert that, which I found far more comfortable for long stretches of writing. There is a small status bar at the bottom that shows the file name, word count, battery level, and time, which you can hide by switching to full-screen mode. You can have ruled lines or even put a frame around your text to limit it to a particular part of the screen.
Pomera’s editing tools are far more robust than its competitors, which tend to be no-frills plain text. You can place markers in your files and build an outline, insert a timestamp, or find and replace strings of text. You can insert templates, compare two files side by side, or even open the same file twice if you need to check multiple parts of a document at once.
Still, the Pomera just never clicked for me. That’s partly a software issue. The interface for writing on the device is thoughtful and feature-rich, but the two wireless syncing options are painful to use. The first is a finicky system for emailing work to yourself: You have to log in to a Gmail account and connect it to the Pomera to send text, which shows up in the body of the email, not as an attachment. (If you don’t have a Gmail account, you actually have to manually enter your SMTP info.) The other option is the convoluted Pomera Link mobile app. To use the app, you have to go to the menu on the Pomera itself and select QR code. Then you open the app and scan the code, which imports the text to your phone. But you can’t simply save it from there. Instead, you have to copy and paste the text into another app, like Google Docs, if you want to save it. It’s a mess.
Thankfully, if you’ve got a USB-C cable, you can get your text off it by plugging your Pomera into a computer and transferring it like you would with any USB drive. The Pomera has a little over 1GB of built-in storage, which should be more than enough for most people — that will store hundreds of thousands of pages of plain text. But it also has an SD card slot if you’d prefer the convenience of storing your manuscripts there for easily moving between devices.
But in the end, it wasn’t the Pomera’s software that sank it for me. Its keyboard is just too small.
The size difference between the Traveler and the DM250US might seem negligible, but it’s painfully obvious the second you start typing. The Traveler features a full-size scissor-switch keyboard with a simplified design that ditches the function and arrow keys. Meanwhile, working with less space, Pomera squeezes in a full set of function keys and cursor keys.
In small bursts, the keyboard isn’t terrible. I won’t be writing any odes to its keys’ shallow yet satisfying action, but I’ve definitely used worse. The thing is, my hands start to cramp, and my wrists hurt pretty quickly. My hands are not particularly large, but the layout and tiny keys are an absolute nightmare for my carpal tunnel. I wrote this review on the Pomera and had to take breaks every 300 words or so because it was just too uncomfortable to keep going for much longer, and its small size meant I also made a lot more typos than usual. If you’ve got particularly small hands it might not be as much of an issue.
Don’t get fooled by the “Bluetooth keyboard” option in the menu — it doesn’t mean you can connect an external keyboard to the Pomera. Instead, this allows you to use the Pomera as a keyboard with other devices, which I guess could be helpful in a pinch. If you were going to use a Bluetooth keyboard anyway, it might be worth looking into BYOK, which, as the name implies, lets you bring your keyboard. It’s quite a bit cheaper than the Pomera, even if its editing features are less robust.
If portability was my number one priority, and I didn’t want to resort to some clunky folding keyboard, the Pomera would fit the bill. It feels sturdier and more premium than its most obvious competitor, the Traveler, and as much as I like the BYOK, that’s definitely got a bit of an amateurish vibe by comparison.
Ultimately, though, the biggest problem is simply ergonomic. The whole draw of devices like the Pomera DM250US is sitting down for long, serious writing sessions. But inevitably, every time I’d use it, I’d find myself reaching for my wrist braces and doing finger stretches afterward. It doesn’t matter how sleek and portable Pomera’s design is, or how much I appreciated its more advanced editing features or its flexible calendar — discomfort is its own distraction.

Asahi Linux Drops MIT, Goes Full GPL After AI Used to Steal Unreleased Code
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
03:06:55 UTC
12:06:55 KST

Asahi Linux is the reason you can run Linux on an Apple Silicon Mac today. For years, the project put most of its own code under the MIT license so that anyone, including the BSDs, could reuse it as needed.
That is changing because Asahi Linux is tired of code laundering. They have announced that Asahi is moving all of its repositories to the GNU General Public License version 2 or later. Going forward, all Asahi Linux code will be under strong copyleft licenses only.
This is because people were taking in-development code straight out of their personal forks, publishing it without credit, or rewriting it with AI to hide its origin for "replacing the project and aggressively monetising Linux on Apple Silicon."
What is code laundering?
Code laundering (also called license laundering) is the practice of taking someone else's code and passing it through a process that hides where it came from, so you can use it without honoring the original license or crediting the author.
Before AI, this usually meant manually rewriting code line by line, renaming variables and stuff, and shuffling functions around until it no longer looked like the original.
LLMs made it much more easy and cheaper of course.
Learning from history
The move has come after the Asahi team was made aware "some time ago" of multiple attempts to exploit its permissive licensing to hijack its work.
In the most extreme cases, feature code that was still under development was lifted from developers' personal forks before it was even publicly released. The report points out that the MIT license "explicitly allows this, and has no carveouts to protect against bad faith actors."
Asahi didn't name anyone in the report. It also didn't spell out how existing contributions will be relicensed or whether every past contributor agreed to it.
Asahi draws parallels with WINE's situation two decades ago. WINE, the compatibility layer that lets you run Windows apps on Linux, was originally MIT-licensed too. But in the late 90s and early 2000s, companies took the code, built proprietary forks on top of it, and sold them commercially. So, in 2002, the WINE team relicensed to the LGPL to discourage proprietary forks and push companies to contribute upstream.
Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it
Asahi has been upset lately
Asahi didn't name anyone so we are left with guesswork on who they are targeting with this license move.
There have been at least two public forks of Asahi's work in recent months, both tied to AI-assisted development. In case you did not know, Asahi Linux forbids AI generated code contribution.
The first is Aurora Silicon and its Vulkan driver, Borealis. Borealis is a fork of Asahi's HoneyKrisp, the Vulkan driver for Apple GPUs. Aurora Silicon submitted a pull request to register its own Vulkan driver ID with Khronos (VK_DRIVER_ID_AURORA_BOREALIS), says the driver runs on M1 to M5 and the A18 Pro, and keeps it in its own Mesa fork rather than upstream. 
The second is Gravity Linux, a Fedora-based distro for Apple Silicon. It was forked from Asahi over the disagreement about LLM use.
To be fair to Gravity, it is open source, it isn't selling anything, and it credits its AI use openly. It even says it plans to sunset the distro once its driver work lands upstream.
It isn't the kind of bad actor the progress report describes. But it does represent the "permissive fork that embraces AI" approach that Asahi has consistently pushed back against.
Why this license change matters
As far as I can tell, this is the first time a major open source project has moved to copyleft specifically because of AI-assisted code laundering. Projects have relicensed before, but usually to stop cloud providers from reselling their work as a service. This one is specifically about AI.
I wouldn't be surprised if more hardware enablement and reverse-engineering projects follow. Making the first changes takes a lot of time and effort but they are easier to "rewrite" once someone has done the hard part.
Will the GPL actually help?
If the problem is people who already ignore the MIT license, why would they respect the GPL? After all, GPL cannot stop a determined bad actor. Nothing does, actually.
Stripping attribution from MIT code already breaks the MIT license, since keeping the copyright notice is its one real condition.
What the GPL changes is the commercial benefit. Under MIT, someone can take Asahi's code, close it up, and sell a product, and that's perfectly legal as long as the notice stays in.
Under the GPL, anyone who distributes a modified version has to release the source under the same license. You can't legally build a closed, paid Apple Silicon distro on top of GPL code. And if a product's source has to be public, the copying is easier to spot.
Not everyone is happy
The move has drawn criticism, particularly from the BSD side, which was one of the main reasons Asahi chose MIT in the first place. OpenBSD's Apple Silicon support relies on Asahi's m1n1 bootloader.
OpenBSD developer Bryan Steele wrote on X:
"Sad to see Asahi out there burning bridges for no reason.. relicensing m1n1 and drivers under GPL2-or-later, seemingly without the consent of all prior contributors, under the guise of "defending against AI bad actors", seems entirely disingenuous and misguided."
Wrapping up
Asahi is betting that copyleft license provides a better defense in this changed world where anyone can launder code with a prompt.
It may not stop the bad actors from rewriting its code, but at least it reduces the chances of a closed commercial fork.
It would be interesting to see whether the BSD community finds a way to keep working with Asahi under the new terms.
