I'm not convinced the AI bubble exists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-08
23:44:36 UTC
08:44:36 KST

I'm Not Convinced The AI Bubble Exists
Posted on Sun 08 November 2026 in AI
The AI bubble is a speculative concept that the AI industry is extremely over-valued. If true, the value of most companies involved in AI (several of whom are worth well over a trillion dollars) will collapse, devastating the entire economy. If you check any online discussion about the financial situation of the AI industry, it's essentially taken for granted that the bubble exists and is going to pop any day now. I don't think that this is a reasonable assumption, though. Nobody can see the future, but I think that there's a pretty realistic chance that the meteoritic growth of AI companies in the past few years is justified, and that they have even more room for growth.
Expenses Are Sky-High, But Constrained
To say that AI companies are spending an absurd amount of money is an understatement. The debt and spending commitments for AI companies are handled through complex vehicles that make it difficult to tell exactly how much their expenses actually are (a serious problem, and one of the most salient points in favour of AI being a bubble), but they've committed to spending at least 3 trillion dollars so far. It's also been estimated that AI companies have already spent 1.9 trillion, bringing the overall expense of the AI industry to around 5 trillion dollars. This is unprecedented levels of investment, and AI just can't be profitable if this level of spending is maintained. However, there's no reason for why this level of spending has to be maintained in the first place. The reason why AI companies are spending so much money is to rollout data centres to run the AI in the first place. These expenses are one-off purchases, not regular operating expenses. Once all the data centres are built, AI spending is going to plummet.
Outside of these expenses, AI doesn't cost that much to run. We don't have the full numbers for the entire industry here, but Anthropic's S-1 filing says that they make $2.08 for every $1 of compute. In other words, once you ignore the cost of building infrastructure, AI is very profitable. Crucially, the S-1 filing indicates that Anthropic has started to make more than their compute and infrastructure investments combined, which cuts against the idea that the cost of building data centres is inherently unsustainable. In a pinch, AI companies can also cut costs by no longer allowing people to use their products for free and temporarily suspending expensive AI research. This can be implemented instantly, whereas other kinds of expenses like leases and spending commitments are a lot harder to cut.
The only serious long-term expenses to contend with here is the massive amount of debt that's been taken out to pay for these data centres in the first place. Like I said before, it's hard to really figure out these commitments because of the complex way that they're issued, but we can do some back of the envelope math. If the AI industry has to pay off 5 trillion dollars over the course of 20 years, that's 250 billion dollars a year. For context, Alphabet (parent company of Google and Youtube) reported earning almost 162 billion dollars of revenue just in 2019. Adjusted for inflation, that's an even more impressive 213 billion dollars. Because this is very rough math, the total needed revenue might come in to well over 250 billion dollars a year, but the point stands. Even though this is an enormous expense, paying it off isn't unthinkable with the data we have so far. Some of the debt is in convertible notes as well, which can be repaid through shares instead of cash. In the first 6 months of 2026, Anthropic has recorded 72 billion dollars of loss in the form of shares that are due to lenders. The cost is only so high because the valuation has skyrocketed to an estimated 1 trillion dollars, which means that Anthropic has more than enough equity to make lenders whole.
Profits Can Grow, By A Lot
In their S-1 filing, Anthropic records their revenue going from 41 million in 2023, 386 million in 2024, 4.585 billion in 2025, and 16.3 billion in the first 6 months of 2026. That's an insane increase in revenue, and it's safe to assume that other major AI companies like OpenAI are also seeing similar increases as well. At some point, the rate of increase has to level off, but that doesn't have to happen anytime soon. When I look at the current capacity of AI, it really feels like there's so much potential for frontier models to be used that just aren't being applied yet. Most (or maybe even all) programmers and mathematicians are worse at their respective field than an AI swarm equipped with a good harness, and a good deal more expensive as well. AI can't replace lawyers and doctors, but they can automate their paperwork and free up time for them to do other things. Outside of generative AI, self-driving cars are becoming a reality, with some evidence to suggest that they're even better than human drivers. AI adoption takes time, but there's no reason to think that AI usage isn't going to massively skyrocket, even if AI doesn't get any better than it is today (and it certainly will get better). In other words, there's massive unmet demand for AI companies to profit from.
There's a weird contradiction you see from AI skeptics where they're afraid of how AI will change the world, but also seem convinced that AI will only ever produce slop that nobody would ever pay money for. You can't really have it both ways here. It's completely valid to be afraid of AI taking your job, but money is going to change hands when that happens. I don't know exactly what the future will look like or how long it'll take for mass AI adoption to really happen, but when I imagine how AI will change the world, it's hard for me to see AI consumption not being 10x what it is now.
Google Has No Moat, But Neither Does McDonald's
In 2023, a memo from Google called "We Have No Moat, And Neither Does OpenAI" was leaked, which outlined how the open source community was keeping pace with AI labs. More broadly, the memo rejected the idea that any company can really have a durable advantage when it comes to AI development. It would certainly be profitable if they could, but there's already so much information and research out there that nobody can ever hope for their frontier models to stay on the frontier for long. That means that there will never be a point where a company wins the AI wars, just nonstop fighting as each company in the industry tries to one-up the others. You know what other company didn't have a moat and found itself in a war to sell a product that its competitors could easily copy? Popeyes during the chicken sandwich war. I know that sounds goofy, but from a business perspective, it's remarkably similar. None of the restaurants involved in the chicken sandwich war had an enduring competitive advantage over any of the others, and all of them had to deal with potential customers choosing to just cookat home instead, but it was still highly profitable for everybody involved. Simply saying that a company doesn't have a moat isn't enough to say that the company can't make money.
In theory, an AI company has to be worried about their users switching over to a competitor or using an open source model instead. In practice, this isn't a major concern. For starters, the average person isn't going to use a locally hosted model, ever. I know that it's a common hobby in tech circles, but normal users don't want to have to deal with the hassle or expense of setting up something that's going to perform at most the exact same as ChatGPT. That means that in principle, there's only going to be a few models that the vast majority of people will ever use. People can theoretically switch from model to model, but people tend to settle in with a product and develop brand loyalty. For example, I pretty much only use ChatGPT, not because I have any really reason to, but because it was the first LLM that I ever used. This partially offsets the risk of losing customers to a different product. Another way that companies can make money without having a moat is through institutional lock-in. Once a large corporation has integrated a particular AI into their day to day operation, transitioning away isn't costless. They may even have contracts agreeing to buy a certain amount of tokens, which binds them to keep using the AI instead of transitioning.
There's Still Plenty Of Capital To Raise
A potential way for a bubble to pop is for the companies involved to run out of capital to spend while they grow, causing them to fail. With the enormous amount of churn and debt that AI companies have, this is a serious risk to consider. Even so, I think that it's premature to worry about these companies failing to raise capital when most of them haven't even had an IPO yet. When SpaceX (which is partially an AI company, despite the name) went public, they raised more than 80 billion dollars. Besides that, many AI companies haven't issued public debt yet, which is a major way to get loans if private lenders decide that they don't want to put more of their capital into AI. The ones that have issued public debt, like Alphabet and Meta, have excellent bond ratings. If they need more capital, they won't struggle to find people to give them a loan.
Of course, investors aren't the only way to get capital. Once AI companies become profitable (as they already seem to be), they can use those profits to fund growth and pay off debts. The idea that AI companies are forced to constantly look for new investors to keep their doors open is probably a few months antiquated. From how it looks from Anthropic's S-1, the AI world may be past the horizon when it came to taking risky bets and can now focus on reaping the rewards.
The AI Industry Doesn't Look Like Any Bubble We've Seen Before
When a bubble happens, it's usually preceded by the companies involved reaching obviously inflated evaluations, which makes the burst obvious in hindsight. With public AI companies, we don't see that happening. Alphabet, Meta, and NVIDIA are all AI companies that have seen their market capitalization explode over the past few years, but all of them have stable P/E ratios in their 20s. If the increase in their valuations were irrational (or even just in expectation of future growth as opposed to current earnings), you would expect the P/E ratios to go up. Instead, their valuations look exactly what we would expect from a healthy trillion dollar company. When the dot-com bubble happened, it was largely driven by companies that couldn't turn a profit or had P/E ratios in the hundreds. I'm not going to pretend that I'm an expert on financial bubbles, but I've never heard of a bubble where the companies involved had such a modest valuation based on their earnings, even if their earnings (and therefore their evaluations) are enormous.
A potential way that this could be a bubble is if AI proves to be a fad. A lot of this rise in valuations has been because of increased demand for GPUs and data centre utilization, which is downstream of the demand for AI. We might imagine that the AI labs are propped up by an enormous amount of invested capital, and this capital ends up propping up the valuations for companies that make or rent out GPUs. However, this doesn't seem to be happening. Alphabet has a full-stack AI supply chain, where they create ASICs for AI, train their own AI, integrate AI into their products, and rent out compute to customers. Their prospectus helpfully divides their revenue streams into Google Cloud for their rented compute and Google Services, which makes it easy to tell if Alphabet's increased earnings are mostly because of their data centres. The answer is no. Google Cloud revenue is growing more in terms of percentage, but Google Services is growing far more in absolute terms. Specifically, Google Services revenue grew by 37.8 billion dollars for a 12% increase, while Google Cloud revenue grew by 15.5 billion dollars for a 36% increase. Alphabet is definitely benefiting from renting out their data centres, but it's not the main reason why their earnings have skyrocketed. Meta doesn't rent out their data centres at all, but their prospectus also records them having massive increases in their revenue, on the order of an extra 30 billion dollars from 2024 to 2025, and another extra 30 billion from 2023 to 2024. This isn't foolhardy investors throwing money at any company that makes AI, this is real profit from companies that have found ways to monetize AI. Anthropic also seems to be experiencing an exponential growth in their revenue as well, based on their S-1 filing. The only real unknown is OpenAI, which purchases an enormous amount of compute from other companies. It's possible that their finances are terrible, but even if they go under, I'm not convinced that this amounts to a bubble bursting. If anything, it seems more likely that their competitors will just consolidate and fight for more of a market share instead of the collapse triggering a chain reaction that takes the industry down with it.
Conclusion
I didn't write this article as some big takedown of the AI bubble theory. Even with this evidence, there are serious risks to the financial sustainability of the AI industry. Public backlash against data centres are going to make it harder for the infrastructure necessary for the AI revolution to continue, and regulatory barriers may make it harder to develop or deploy new models. Besides that, there's an enormous risk of an autonomous AI hacker causing serious damage, causing public demand for AI to plummet. Also, even after writing out it's possible for AI companies to pay off their debt, I'm still concerned by how much it actually is. It's not good that they're using increasingly complex ways to fund their infrastructure investments, and this gamble can backfire if revenue growth suddenly slows down, which it certainly might. Don't YOLO your life savings on the AI revolution, or at least don't blame me if you lose the shirt off of your back. The reason I wrote this article is because I felt that discussion about AI has become something of an echo chamber, which is never a good way to figure out what's right or wrong. Despite the echo chamber, people's stated beliefs and actual behaviour are wildly divergent. It's one thing to say that AI is a bubble that's going to burst, but where is this investor money coming from if we're all in agreement here? At the end of the day, when people have to put their money where their mouth is, they pull it out of their mouth and use it to buy NVIDIA. They might be wrong to do so, but maybe they're not. Time will tell.
As one final note, I don't think the rhetoric about the AI bubble is really about finances. Conversation about the AI bubble is too widespread for it to be a contrarian position, and too gleeful to be driven by investors' fear. More than anything, I think the supposed AI bubble has become such a large talking point because it represents the hope that things can go back to how they used to be. People are afraid of what's going to happen with AI, and rightfully so. Beyond fear for the future, AI in the present has become uncomfortably common, with AI slop everywhere online and increasingly even IRL. This has all happened so fast, it's easy to forget that ChatGPT came out a little less than 4 years ago. Our world has changed in such a scary and odd way, and while I have a pretty optimistic view of AI overall, I get why people would want it all to go away. So, people wishcast. They tell themselves that this is all a giant bubble, and one day soon, everything will crash down and immediately go back to how it used to be. For better or worse, that's not going to happen. Even if AI turns out to be a bubble, it will be a bubble in the same way that the internet was a bubble, where the underlying technology remains useful. We're only ever going to live in the AI era from this point on, and whatever happens as a result of that, hopefully it will at least be good for the economy.

On Sunday, Nvidia announced it was launching an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, an AI executive and agent of the Chinese government.
Here’s the full text of Jensen Huang’s memo to Nvidia
In the memo, Nvidia’s CEO acknowledges having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
In addition to the Board of Directors announcing the investigation, Huang sent a memo to Nvidia employees acknowledging the affair. You can read the full text below.
To my colleagues at NVIDIA,
I owe my family and all of you an apology.
I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.
Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.
To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.
To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.
Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.
My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy.

Soul Glo’s Diaspora Problems is a hardcore record like no other
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-08
22:37:22 UTC
07:37:22 KST

Soul Glo has a new record called NA I’M GON GRAB ALLAT coming out in January, and I, for one, can not wait. While two singles have dropped, it’s not enough to truly tide me over, so I’ve been revisiting Songs to Yeet at the Sun and my favorite album of 2022 — Diaspora Problems.
Soul Glo’s Diaspora Problems is a hardcore record like no other
Diaspora Problems is one of the 21st century’s best punk albums.
Soul Glo’s Diaspora Problems is a hardcore record like no other
Diaspora Problems is one of the 21st century’s best punk albums.
“Gold Chain Punk (whogonbeatmyass?)” is an opening salvo for the ages. Bong rip, into a catchy-as-hell hardcore riff, with frontman Pierce Jordan ranting. Then comes the half-time stomp as Jordan gets fully unhinged, screaming “Who gon beat my ass? Who the fuck gon beat my ass?” From here on out, as the music shifts through a few different sections, the energy never comes down. Jordan shreds his vocal cords, begging, “Can I live?” Before finally spelling it out for anyone still confused:
Say more, say less, it’s all the same
When it’s time to die we can meet outside
To see who gon feel my pain
The record barely lets up from here on out. “Coming Correct” opens with a cough and a steady 808, giving you literally three seconds to catch your breath before Jordan jumps on the mic shouting, “I try to listen the way, I wanna be listened to.” The song starts stacking elements quickly, reaching full firestorm by 25 seconds in, and then doesn’t let up for the rest of its three-minute runtime.
The front chunk of the record is just perfect unrelenting hardcore song after perfect unrelenting hardcore song. Jordan’s crazed charisma is undeniable as he ricochets between leftist rhetoric, goofy bits about smoking weed, and vulnerable explorations of his struggles with depression. You’d be forgiven for struggling to keep up with his rapid-fire delivery, which owes almost as much to modern rappers as it does to classic hardcore acts like Minor Threat or Bad Brains.
Track six, “Driponomics,” fully embraces those more modern influences with trap snares, wall-rattling 808 kicks, and a guest verse from Mother Maryrose. The sampled guitar calls to mind the sax squeals favored by the Bomb Squad… just heavier.
The album eventually culminates in “Spiritual Level Of Gang Shit,” which features guest verses from McKinley Dixon and Lojii over gently echoed guitar melodies and dub-inspired groove. Then, around the 2:20 mark, things take a turn as the guitars turn punishing and the drums shift to a standard hardcore beat. But the song hasn’t reached its final form yet. That comes almost a minute later when the horn section kicks in.
Next to other modern hardcore standard bearers like Turnstile, Soul Glo might almost seem like traditionalists heavily influenced by the DC scene. But Diaspora Problems shows their ambition and willingness to take risks. Soul Glo plays with genre, is confrontational in its politics, and is generally just uncompromising.
Oh, and they put on a hell of a live show (I’ve seen them at least four times now). Don’t miss their incredible Tiny Desk Concert either, which I’m pretty sure is the first mosh pit to even open up in the NPR offices.
Soul Glo’s Diaspora Problems is available on Bandcamp and most major streaming services, including Qobuz, Deezer, YouTube Music, Apple Music, and Spotify.

Nvidia CEO Admits Affair With Alleged Chinese Spy. Investigation Opened
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-08
21:34:00 UTC
06:34:00 KST

Nvidia CEO Admits Affair With Alleged Chinese Spy. Investigation Opened (cnbc.com) 87
			
		 	
				CNBC reports new details about the relationship of alleged Chinese spy with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang:
Huang told Nvidia staff in a email on Sunday that he had an affair with the woman and that Nvidia's board of directors had opened an independent investigation into the spying allegations.   "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," Huang wrote in the message. "I am deeply sorry." 
Nvidia's board "said an independent committee, assisted by outside counsel, will investigate the matter," reports Axios:
The board said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised and expressed confidence in Huang's leadership... Huang has been a key voice in Washington pushing to loosen restrictions on AI chip sales to China. He argued that keeping American technology in the Chinese market strengthens U.S. competitiveness and prevented China from developing their own potentially more advanced chips.  
The board's statement added that their inquiry "will examine all available information," CNBC reports. But "An Nvidia spokesperson said that Huang was committed to continuing as CEO of Nvidia without interruption." 
"I love our country and our company," Jensen Huang wrote in his letter to Nvidia's staff (as reported by CNBC), "and I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American."
But while U.S. lawmakers have requested Huang appear for closed-door committee briefing, Jensen has not confirmed he'll appear, notes CNBC:
When asked by the New York Times whether Huang would appear before lawmakers to discuss the matter, Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo declined to comment. "Our chief executive has an outstanding security team that accompanies him where needed," Mr. Rizzo said in a statement to the Times...
Rizzo said [Thursday] the Nvidia CEO's interactions with [alleged Chinese spy Alice] Huang were consistent with meetings he has had with any of Nvidia's customers.

Show HN: SafeScript, a safe version of JavaScript for executing untrusted code
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-08
21:26:33 UTC
06:26:33 KST

JSON for code. A safe computational subset of JavaScript.
JSON gave the world a safe way to exchange data. SafeScript does the same for computation. It's a strict subset of JavaScript — no eval, no new, no globals, no prototype access — that compiles to plain JS and PHP. Open a .safe file and you see code that's safe to run. The compiler is ~48 KB minified (~12 KB gzipped). Ship it anywhere, verify locally, no trust needed.
SafeScript starts small, the same way JSON did. Anywhere you need a safe handler for data or events:
- Webserver handlers — route logic, request transforms, validation rules submitted by users or tenants
- onclick and event handlers — user-authored browser event handlers that can't escape their sandbox
- Plugin scripts — extend an app with user-submitted logic without risking the host
- Formulas and expressions — spreadsheet-style computed fields, pricing rules, scoring functions
- Bot and agent tools — callable tools for AI agents that are safe by construction (see Safebots)
- Config with logic — when JSON isn't enough but arbitrary JS is too much
// Node.js
const SafeScript = require('safescript');
const result = await SafeScript.run('return x + y;', { x: 10, y: 20 });
// → 30
// Safe globals are available by default — no injection needed
await SafeScript.run('return Math.floor(3.7);');     // → 3
await SafeScript.run('return JSON.parse("{}");');     // → {} (null-prototype, __proto__ stripped)
await SafeScript.run('return Object.keys({a:1});');   // → ['a']
// Math.random is deterministic by default (mulberry32 PRNG, seed 0)
await SafeScript.run('return Math.random();');  // → same value every time<!-- Browser -->
<script src="safescript.min.js"></script>
<script>
  SafeScript.run('return n * 2;', { n: 21 }).then(function(result) {
    // → 42
  });
</script>
SafeScript files use the .safe extension and application/safescript MIME type. A .safe file is self-contained — it declares what capabilities it needs at the top, and the host provides them.
/**
 * @safescript 0.2
 * @needs request: Request
 * @needs db: Database
 * @uses logger: Logger
 * @env browser, node
 */
var body = request.json();
if (logger) logger.log('received', body);
return db.store(body);
The header is an optional /** */ block comment with five directives:
- @safescript <version> — language version
- @needs <name>: <Type> — required capability; the host must provide it or refuse to run the file
- @uses <name>: <Type> — optional capability; the host provides it if available, the script checks with if (name)
- @type <TypeName> { method1, method2 } — declares a return type and the methods the script intends to call on it
- @env <env1>, <env2> — constrains which environments can run this file (optional, comma-separated)
@type declarations tell the host which methods on return types the script intends to call. They're purely declarative — they don't change runtime enforcement, but they enable pre-flight validation at load() time.
/**
 * @safescript 0.2
 * @needs fetch: function
 * @needs log: function
 * @type Response { json, text, status }
 * @type Stream { get, set, fields }
 */
var resp = fetch('/api/data');
var data = resp.json();
log(data);
When load() processes this header, it checks:
- Every @type name is registered with the host (via SafeScript.lib())
- Every declared method is in the host's allowMethods whitelist
This catches mismatches early — before the script runs — rather than failing at the first method call. If a script declares @type Response { json, text, status } but the host only allows json and text, load() throws immediately.
A .safe file is a unit of trust — one set of declarations, one sandbox boundary. Everything about its security posture is visible in a single file:
- What it needs (@needs) — the injected capabilities
- What it optionally uses (@uses) — degradable capabilities
- What return types it touches (@type) — methods on host-provided objects
- What environment it expects (@env) — runtime constraints
If you want two functions with different access patterns, you put them in two .safe files. Each file gets its own scope, its own type declarations, and its own sandbox. The file IS the security boundary.
This is by design. SafeScript protects the host's environment — it ensures that user-submitted code can only call what the host explicitly allows. User protection (ensuring the host acts in the user's interest) comes from a different layer entirely — attestations about the host, not constraints in SafeScript. See Safebots layers for how these layers compose.
A .safe file declares what it needs. It doesn't import, require, or fetch anything. The host reads the declarations and builds the scope — where the host gets the implementations is its business. A Node host might resolve them from node_modules. A browser host might use an import map or a CDN. A sandboxed environment might draw from a curated whitelist. The .safe file doesn't know or care.
This is a deliberate departure from require() and import. Package managers are an implementation detail of a particular host, not a top-level concept in the language. A .safe file that depends on npm to function is not truly portable. A .safe file that declares @needs fetch: http.Fetch works everywhere a host can provide an HTTP client.
This also avoids inheriting the supply chain attack surface of package managers. SafeScript's security story starts at the file boundary — you read the header, you see what the code can touch, you decide whether to run it.
const SafeScript = require('safescript');
// 1. Parse the header
const caps = SafeScript.capabilities(source);
// → { version: '0.2', env: ['browser', 'node'],
//     needs: [{name: 'request', type: 'Request'}, ...],
//     uses: [{name: 'logger', type: 'Logger'}] }
// 2. Check that you can satisfy the requirements
const check = SafeScript.checkScope(source, myScope);
if (!check.ok) throw new Error('Missing: ' + check.missing.join(', '));
// 3. Run with the scope you built
const result = await SafeScript.run(source, myScope);
Four security barriers, defense in depth:
- Token/grammar allowlist — The parser accepts only a subset of JavaScript. No eval, new, delete, class, import, async, await, template literals, or access to globalThis/window/document. The AST is reconstructed from scratch — the original source text never appears in the output.
- Runtime property guards — Bracket access (obj[key]) is rewritten to __at(obj, key) / __set(obj, key, val), which block prototype-chain properties (constructor, __proto__, prototype, caller, callee) at runtime, even when keys are computed dynamically.
- Global shadowing + safe globals — Every native global is declared as undefined inside the compiled function, then a curated set of safe globals is injected automatically: frozen facade objects for Math, JSON, Object, Array, String, Number, error constructors, and standalone functions like parseInt and encodeURI. These facades expose only safe static methods — never raw constructors or mutable prototypes. Additional capabilities are injected via the scope object. Code always runs in "use strict".
- Execution guards + hooks — Compile-time injected __check() calls enforce timeout and operation limits (hardcoded ceilings: 60s, 100M ops), preventing infinite loops and infinite recursion. Hooks intercept every call to injected scope functions, letting the host throttle resources at the boundary.
With an empty scope, SafeScript is pure computation with safe globals — deterministic math, JSON handling, type checking — but no I/O, no side effects, no access to anything outside the function. Additional capabilities are injected via the scope object using an object-capability model.
A .safe file is a function body. The compiler wraps it in a function, the host calls that function with a scope, and the code uses return to hand a value back. run() always returns a Promise.
// Return a computed value
await SafeScript.run('return price * qty;', { price: 9.99, qty: 3 });  // → 29.97
// Return a function (the function itself is async)
var double = await SafeScript.run('return function(n) { return n * 2; };', {});
await double(21);  // → 42
// Return an object — the "module" pattern
var mod = await SafeScript.run(`
  var count = 0;
  return {
    inc: function() { count = count + 1; return count; },
    get: function() { return count; }
  };
`, {});
await mod.inc(); await mod.inc(); await mod.get(); // → 2
// Side-effect only (write to an injected capability, no return needed)
await SafeScript.run('db.store(record);', { db: myDb, record: data });
There is no export, no module.exports, and no implicit last-expression return. return makes intent explicit and keeps .safe files readable.
SafeScript uses an auto-async execution model. The compiler automatically:
- Emits every function (declarations, expressions, arrows, method shorthands) as async
- Wraps every function call with await
This means async and await are not keywords in SafeScript — they are blocked. The compiler handles them transparently. This has two important consequences:
- Promises resolve automatically. When injected objects return Promises, they're awaited at every call site. No unresolved Promises can leak through.
- Sequential execution is guaranteed. There are no concurrent in-flight operations inside a single SafeScript execution. Throughput comes from running many SafeScript instances in parallel (like PHP-FPM workers), not from concurrency within one.
- Transparent cross-context proxying. Because every external call is awaited, SafeScript code can run in a WebWorker while the scope objects proxy calls to the main thread via postMessage. The SafeScript source doesn't change — it was already written as synchronous-looking code, and the compiler already awaits every call. This means a host like Q.Safebox can move untrusted script execution off the main thread with zero code changes to the .safe files.
// Same SafeScript source works identically whether scope is local or proxied:
var el = createElement("div")    // <- auto-awaited, works if createElement
setText(el, "Hello")             //    returns a value OR a Promise
appendTo(el, container)          //    (e.g. from a MessageChannel proxy)
return getText(el)
SafeScript protects against infinite loops, infinite recursion, and runaway computation with compile-time guard injection.
The compiler injects a __check() call at the top of every function body and the start of every loop iteration (all 5 loop types: for, for-in, for-of, while, do-while). At runtime, __check() verifies that the operation count and wall-clock deadline haven't been exceeded. If either limit is hit, execution throws immediately — no waiting for a Promise to time out.
// Abort after 5 seconds
var result = await SafeScript.run(source, scope, { timeout: 5000 });
// Limit total operations (loop iterations + function entries)
var result = await SafeScript.run(source, scope, { maxOps: 10000 });
// Both
var result = await SafeScript.run(source, scope, { timeout: 5000, maxOps: 50000 });
Hardcoded ceilings. Even if the host omits timeout or passes 0, a ceiling of 60 seconds (MAX_TIMEOUT = 60000) is always enforced. Similarly, maxOps is capped at 100 million (MAX_OPS = 100000000). These ceilings cannot be raised — they protect against misconfigured hosts.
Promise.race remains as a secondary defense for slow async injected methods, but the primary protection is the __check() guards in the compiled code itself.
Hooks let the host intercept every call to injected scope functions. This is how you throttle resource usage — data size limits, call counts, rate limiting, cost caps — at the boundary where SafeScript meets external resources.
var result = await SafeScript.run(source, scope, {
  hooks: {
    beforeCall: function(info) {
      // info = { name, args, callCount, elapsed }
      // name is dotted path: "db.query", "api.users.list"
      // Block specific functions
      if (info.name === 'db.drop') return false;
      // Enforce call count limits
      if (info.callCount > 100) throw new Error('too many calls');
      // Short-circuit with cached/default value
      if (info.name === 'fetch' && rateLimited) return { value: null };
      // Transform arguments
      if (info.name === 'db.query') return { args: [sanitizeSQL(info.args[0])] };
      // Return undefined to proceed normally
    },
    afterCall: function(info) {
      // info = { name, args, result, callCount, elapsed }
      // Check response size
      if (JSON.stringify(info.result).length > 1000000) {
        throw new Error('response too large');
      }
      // Transform result
      return { value: redact(info.result) };
    }
  }
});
beforeCall(info) — called before each scope function invocation. Returns:
- undefined — proceed normally
- false — suppress the call (returns undefined to the script)
- { value: x } — short-circuit, return x without calling (including null for graceful degradation)
- { args: [...] } — transform arguments, then call
- throw — kill execution
afterCall(info) — called after each scope function returns. Same return protocol plus access to info.result.
Hooks wrap functions recursively through nested scope objects. If you inject { db: { query: fn, insert: fn } }, hooks see "db.query" and "db.insert" as the name.
SafeScript files don't import each other. Composition happens at the host level — run one SafeScript to produce utilities, then inject the result into another:
// Build a utility library
var utils = await SafeScript.run(utilsSource, { Math });
// Inject it into a handler
var result = await SafeScript.run(handlerSource, { utils, db, request });
This keeps each .safe file self-contained while allowing the host to compose them freely. The host controls the dependency graph, not the scripts.
SafeScript provides a set of frozen facade objects available in every execution — no injection needed. These are safe subsets of their JavaScript counterparts: only static methods, no constructors, no mutable prototypes.
All facade objects are deeply frozen. Attempts to modify them (e.g. Math.PI = 3) silently fail in strict mode. Object.create is restricted to Object.create(null) — passing any other argument throws.
JSON.parse output is deep-walked to convert all objects to null-prototype objects and strip any __proto__ keys. This prevents prototype pollution attacks through parsed JSON data.
Math.random uses a mulberry32 PRNG seeded per invocation. By default, the seed is 0, so every call to run() produces the same sequence of random numbers. This makes SafeScript executions fully reproducible.
// Deterministic — same result every time
await SafeScript.run('return Math.random();');  // → always 0.2267...
// Custom seed
await SafeScript.run('return Math.random();', {}, { seed: 42 });  // → always 0.0020...
// True randomness (requires host approval)
await SafeScript.run('return Math.random();', {}, {
  seed: null,
  env: { Random: true }
});
The seed option controls behavior:
Setting seed: null without env: { Random: true } throws: SafeScript: seed: null requires env: { Random: true } (nondeterministic RNG needs host approval). This ensures nondeterminism is always an explicit host decision.
Hosts can register named libraries that load() auto-resolves for @needs and @uses declarations. This avoids repeating resolver logic for common capabilities.
// Register libraries once at startup
SafeScript.lib('http', myHttpClient);
SafeScript.lib('db', myDbAdapter);
// Scripts that @needs http or @needs db get them automatically
var bundle = await SafeScript.load(source);  // no resolver needed
await SafeScript.run(bundle);
// Resolver scope takes precedence over registered libs
var bundle = await SafeScript.load(source, function(caps) {
  return { http: customHttpClient };  // overrides registered 'http'
});
// Manage registrations
SafeScript.libs();       // → ['http', 'db']
SafeScript.unlib('db');  // unregister
Unregistered @needs still throw Missing capabilities if no resolver provides them.
When host functions return objects, those objects carry methods. Without registration, SafeScript blocks all method calls on unknown types — a sandbox violation. The type registry lets the host declare exactly which methods are safe to call.
// Register a type with its allowed methods
SafeScript.lib(Counter, { allowMethods: ['value', 'increment', 'toString'] });
// Now SafeScript code can call those methods — and only those
var result = await SafeScript.run('return c.value()', { c: new Counter(42) });
// → 42
// Blocked methods throw
await SafeScript.run('c.reset()', { c: new Counter(0) });
// → Error: SafeScript: method "reset" not allowed on Counter
// Unregistered types block everything
await SafeScript.run('return x.anything()', { x: new SomeClass() });
// → Error: SafeScript: cannot call method on unregistered type
The three-argument form registers both a string name (for @type header validation) and a constructor (for runtime enforcement):
// Three-arg: lib(name, Constructor, config)
SafeScript.lib('Response', ResponseClass, { allowMethods: ['json', 'text', 'status'] });
SafeScript.lib('Stream', StreamClass, { allowMethods: ['get', 'set', 'fields'] });
// Now @type Response { json, text } in a .safe header validates at load() time
var bundle = await SafeScript.load(source);  // checks @type declarations
await SafeScript.run(bundle);
The runtime checks every method call through a dispatch chain:
- Primitives (string, number, boolean) → allow all native methods
- Arrays → allow all native methods
- Functions → allow all (call, apply, bind)
- Plain objects → allow callable properties only
- Error family → allow all (toString, message, etc.)
- Registered types → check allowMethods whitelist
- Unregistered types → throw (sandbox violation)
Subclass inheritance works automatically — a SpecialCounter extends Counter instance uses the Counter registration if SpecialCounter isn't registered independently.
// Unregister
SafeScript.unlib(Counter);
// Clear all type registrations
// (accessible through runtime internals)
SafeScript supports this as a keyword. It compiles to an internal __safeThis identifier via a mutable cell pattern. By default, this is undefined everywhere — top level, regular functions, and arrows.
The host controls what this resolves to through the facades option. Facades let injected callback-accepting functions set this for the callbacks they receive.
var result = await SafeScript.run(`
  Q.Tool.define("my-tool", {
    init: function() {
      // 'this' is the facade object created by createToolFacade
      this.state.count = 0;
    },
    methods: {
      increment: function() {
        this.state.count = this.state.count + 1;
      }
    }
  });
`, { Q: myQObject }, {
  facades: {
    'Q.Tool.define': {
      args: [1],        // callback argument indices
      methods: [3],     // method-object argument indices (values are wrapped)
      create: function(name) { return { state: {}, element: null }; }
    }
  }
});
Facade config fields:
- args — indices of arguments that are callbacks (will have this set to the facade)
- methods — indices of arguments that are objects whose values are callbacks
- create — factory function called with the other arguments to build the facade object
All property access on this goes through the same __at/__set guards as any other object — constructor, __proto__, and prototype are blocked.
Compile and execute. Returns a Promise that resolves to the value from the top-level return statement, or undefined if there is none.
await SafeScript.run('return a + b;', { a: 1, b: 2 }); // → 3
// Or pass a bundle from load()
var bundle = await SafeScript.load(source, resolver);
await SafeScript.run(bundle); // same result
Options:
- timeout: N — execution timeout in milliseconds (capped at 60000). Always enforced even if omitted.
- maxOps: N — maximum operations / guard checks (capped at 100000000). Always enforced even if omitted.
- hooks: { beforeCall, afterCall } — intercept calls to injected scope functions. See Hooks.
- seed: N — PRNG seed. Default 0 (deterministic). Any integer for a custom seed. null for true Math.random (requires env: { Random: true }).
- env: { Random: true } — approve environment capabilities. Currently only Random is defined.
- facades: { ... } — per-method this facades. See this and Facades.
Returns { code, ast, hash }. The code is safe JavaScript. The hash is a SHA-256 of the normalized AST (null in browsers — use hashASTAsync).
Returns { ok: boolean, errors: Array|null }. Check without executing.
Returns { version, env, needs: [{name, type}], uses: [{name, type}], types: [{name, methods}] }. Parse the .safe file header.
Async one-call integration. Parses the header, calls resolver(caps) to build the scope (resolver can be sync or async), validates @needs, and returns a Promise that resolves to a { source, scope } bundle you pass to run().
// Load, then run
var bundle = await SafeScript.load(source, function(caps) {
  return {
    request: reqWrapper,
    db: dbHandle,
    logger: caps.uses.find(u => u.name === 'logger') ? myLogger : undefined
  };
});
var result = await SafeScript.run(bundle);
// Prepare once, run many times
var bundle = await SafeScript.load(templateSource, resolver);
for (var req of requests) {
  bundle.scope.request = req;
  results.push(await SafeScript.run(bundle));
}
If no resolver is provided, resolves with an empty scope (fine for scripts with no @needs). Rejects if the scope doesn't satisfy @needs.
Returns { ok: boolean, missing: string[] }. Check whether a scope object satisfies the file's @needs declarations.
Returns the AST (ESTree-like).
Deep-copies an object to null-prototype objects, blocking prototype-chain escapes.
SafeScript.lib(name, value) / SafeScript.lib(Constructor, config) / SafeScript.lib(name, Constructor, config)
Three forms:
- lib(name, value) — register a named library (auto-resolved by load() for @needs/@uses)
- lib(Constructor, { allowMethods: [...] }) — register a type whitelist for runtime method enforcement
- lib(name, Constructor, { allowMethods: [...] }) — register both a named type (for @type header validation) and a constructor whitelist (for runtime enforcement)
Unregister a named library, a type registration, or a named type mapping.
Returns an array of registered library names.
Clear all type registrations (both constructor whitelists and named type mappings).
SafeScript supports a broad computational subset of ES2020:
- Variables: var, let, const
- Control flow: if/else, for, for-in, for-of, while, do-while, switch/case, break, continue, return, labeled statements
- Functions: declarations, expressions, arrows, default params, rest params, this (via facades)
- Expressions: all arithmetic, comparison, logical, ternary, typeof, void, instanceof, nullish coalescing (??), optional chaining (?.)
- Destructuring: array and object patterns, rest elements, nested
- Spread: arrays and objects
- Error handling: try/catch/finally, throw
- Literals: strings, numbers (decimal, hex, binary, octal, BigInt), regex, arrays, objects
- Identifiers: eval, Function, globalThis, window, document, require, process, Proxy, Reflect, Symbol, fetch, setTimeout, and more
- Keywords: new, delete, class, import, export, with, debugger, yield, async, await
- Properties (bracket access): constructor, __proto__, prototype, caller, callee
- Syntax: template literals, generators (function*)
See Specification.md for the formal language definition — starts from ES8 and lists what's removed, rewritten, and added.
See Examples.md for a kitchen-sink collection: basics, control flow, functions, destructuring, spread, and real-world patterns (request handlers, pricing engines, validators, state machines).
Integration packages for common environments:
node test.js               # v0.1 linter/wrapper
node test-compiler.js      # compiler pipeline
node test-battle.js        # adversarial/escape attempts
node test-header.js        # header parser + load() + run(bundle)
node test-guards-hooks.js  # execution guards + hooks system
node test-type-registry.js # type registry — method whitelisting
node test-type-header.js   # @type header declarations + load() validation

Nvidia says it’s investigating CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with possible Chinese spy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-08
21:00:11 UTC
06:00:11 KST

Nvidia’s board of directors announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation following reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation.
Nvidia also published a message that Huang sent to the company admitting that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed (though he didn’t mention her by name). A memo circulating among U.S. policymakers earlier this year claimed that Alice Huang had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO.
“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Jensen Huang wrote. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
Huang added that he’d “fallen short” of his responsibility to the company.
“To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” he said.
As the AI race between the United States and China heats up, chips, especially Nvidia’s chips, have been a major focus. Huang also seems to have a close relationship with President Donald Trump, who’s been a cheerleader of the AI (or “superintelligence”) industry.
In its announcement, Nvidia’s board said that it has “no reason to believe” that either national security or company secrets were compromised. It also said that Huang “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it,” and that the board has “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”
The investigation will be conducted by independent directors working with outside legal counsel.
In response to earlier reports about the CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang, Nvidia had said that the pair’s interactions were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with customers.
Other companies involved in the AI boom have warned employees to be wary of possible spies, including those offering sex or romance.

====================================================================================================

If Snap’s Specs are still ridiculously expensive, they’re also a lot more comfortable than they used to be
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-08
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

When I tried a prototype of Snap’s Specs at CES in Las Vegas earlier this year, the experience left something to be desired. The company’s AR glasses — which the company calls a “new kind of computer” — were heavy (they weighed around 8 ounces) and fit rather uncomfortably on my face. The device was also hot, and made my face feel tingly — a common side-effect of smart glasses where massive computing is happening under the hood.
Fast forward to late October, when I met back up with the Snap team at a Four Seasons in downtown San Francisco. By this time, the company had debuted Specs publicly during an event with CEO Evan Spiegel, and pre-orders of the company’s long-gestating headset were already underway.
What I can say is this: Specs has improved the form factor significantly since my first brush with the device. The glasses now weigh nearly half of what the previous version did, slimming down to 132 grams, or approximately 4.6 ounces. They were quite comfortable and, during the hour-ish that I demo-ed the device, it did not heat up like the previous version had.
Specs now comes in two sizes — 47mm and 52mm. The purpose here is purely to accommodate different head sizes, ensuring the glasses fit snugly on whoever’s face happens to be wearing them. They also now come equipped with spring hinges, which make the device more flexible and comfortable.
However, if the body of the device has improved greatly, its soul is still a work-in-progress. The glasses can be fun — but they also still seem to lack a dedicated purpose, and one struggles to imagine how, specifically, this expensive head gear ($2,200 a pop) would prove useful in a daily capacity. When I asked Snap staff what the device was really for — fun and games or productivity — the answer was vague. The device attempts to be a bunch of things at once and, in the process, ends up feeling a little rudderless.
I have racked my brain to come up with some daily use-cases for Specs. Some of the things I came up with were:
- Watching TV or movies while you’re on a train or some other form of public transportation. There are places where you just have to hang out for awhile and, not infrequently, one way to pass the time is streaming. Specs provides a much more immersive form of mobile entertainment than simply watching a video on your cell phone. The device’s integrations with HBO Max and YouTube make it an appealing entertainment option for users who are in-transit.
- Reading. Because of the immersive nature of Snap’s headset, I feel like they could be a good option for reading while traveling. When you’re reading with Specs, it feels like you’re locked into whatever text you happen to be looking at. It weirdly helped me focus. An integration for newspapers or Kindle could make the glasses a good way to read while you’re mobile (I’m envisioning the ideal setting being on a plane, train, or the back of a car).
- Taking easily shareable weird videos. Like many of Meta’s smart glasses, Specs allows users to take photographs and videos, which is an odd but fun component of the user experience. The ability to generate GoPro-like videos and easily text them to your friends is something that I could see the casual user doing on a somewhat regular basis.
By contrast, here are some of the areas I’m still not totally sold on as Specs use-cases:
- Specs as a daily workspace and productivity tool. Snap is selling Specs as a way to work. The company claims its headset can “transform almost any location into an immersive, flexible workspace.” However, I have a really hard time imagining Specs being something that the average worker is going to want to incorporate into their workflows. It’s less convenient to strap the glasses to your head than it is to simply sit at your computer typing. What can Specs provide that a cell phone and laptop can’t? The social stigma of wearing weird, large glasses and gesticulating to operate them would also seem to be a deterrent.
- A widely used gaming device. Due to the prohibitive cost of the device (again, nearly $2200), I have a really hard time imagining that there is going to be a huge audience for Specs as a gaming device. Most Xboxes are under half the price of this device. Are the games on Specs fun? Sure, kind of. But are teenagers going to be clamoring for them come Christmas time? That I’m not so sure about.
Specs is impressive for how the Snap team has managed to integrate a variety of user experiences into one unified device. There are a lot of impressive achievements here — specifically the spatial synching tech that allows two users to see the same thing simultaneously — that, with some further development, could be deployed towards some really interesting use cases.
The bottom line is that Snap’s device can continue to grow and transform as the company iterates. It’s an interesting product that — like a lot of its peers — doesn’t necessarily seem to have a clear purpose but, in time, could become many things.
What the device currently offers, however, may not be compelling enough to encourage people to shell out the cash that Snap is asking for.

Epic Games Launcher is coming to SteamOS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-08
20:52:05 UTC
05:52:05 KST

In October, Epic Games said that it was “investigating” making Fortnite compatible with Valve’s Linux-based SteamOS. At the time, Epic Games Launcher was in preview, but SteamOS was not specifically listed as a supported distro. Now, Communications Director Jake Jones has confirmed SteamOS compatibility, along with a handful of other distros, to GamingOnLinux. In response to a question about the AppImage being replaced with Debian / Ubuntu .deb downloads, Jones said:
Epic Games Launcher is coming to SteamOS
Epic Games confirmed that its Linux launcher will officially support SteamOS and Steam Decks.
“The new Epic Games Launcher is still in Preview and we plan to support as many Linux distributions as possible, including Fedora, SteamOS, Cachy, Omarchy, and more. We’re testing and evaluating packaging formats for distribution, and we’ll restore AppImage this month.”
That doesn’t necessarily mean Fortnite will come to SteamOS. Easy Anti-Cheat (EAC) Linux v2 support still remains an open question. When it announced its work to bring Fortnite to Linux, the company said that the Steam Deck “does not support the required features for our EAC v2 solution, but we are actively talking with Valve and hope to support it in the future.”

Parents Sue Google Over AI Safety Risks On School Chromebooks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-08
20:34:00 UTC
05:34:00 KST

Parents Sue Google Over AI Safety Risks On School Chromebooks (sfexaminer.com) 23
			
		 	
				The New York Times reports:
After chatting for months with Google's artificial intelligence on a school-issued Chromebook laptop, a 13-year-old student made plans to end her life, according to a lawsuit filed in California Superior Court on Monday, the latest in a wave of litigation over Big Tech's effects on young people.   The lawsuit, which refers to the girl as Emma, said that her parents first learned she had access to Google's AI in mid-March after their daughter's school sent a message warning them that she was in "imminent danger" of self-harm. Emma's mother logged into the teen's school Google account and found her daughter composing a suicide note on Google Docs, the complaint said. Her parents, named as John and Jane Doe in the lawsuit, immediately took Emma for an emergency psychiatric evaluation, and she now goes to therapy every week. 
Emma, a seventh grader in Charlotte, North Carolina, had grown convinced that she had multiple mental health disorders following interactions with AI Mode, a chatbotlike feature on Google Search, the complaint said. She also searched for "what is a suicide note" and made comments like "I am planning my own funeral" to the AI, the complaint said.  The lawsuit is likely the first to claim that Google "hastily integrated" AI features into company apps used on K-12 Chromebooks, Google-powered laptops provided to millions of children by U.S. school districts, while failing to notify their parents of the potential risks...
The case underscores how public school districts have come to depend on classroom laptops, tablets and apps from companies like Google and Microsoft for teaching and learning. In recent years, some Big Tech companies have used their own infrastructure in schools to promote their AI chatbots for teachers and students.  The new lawsuit argues that Google's "sprawling digital ecosystem" of laptops and apps has enabled the tech giant to spread its Gemini AI chatbot across public schools — as well as turn on some students' access to AI features by default — without parents' awareness or permission. While school administrators can toggle company apps like YouTube and Gemini on or off for students in different grades, school administrators have complained that Google's system has not allowed them to disable AI Mode and AI Overview, features that are embedded in Google Search...
The new lawsuit against Google is part of a wave of litigation this year over Big Tech's effect on young users... Several parents have also sued AI companies over allegations that their children died by suicide following interactions with chatbots.  
In a possibly-related development, Google announced a new policy of disabling its AI tools by default for schools this week.  And schools that re-enable searches will have a new choice, the New York Times points out:  "to enable student access to the AI features that the company has already embedded in search or to a new AI feature intended to assist students with schoolwork."
But Google still isn't offering schools an option to turn off AI altogether in search, a company executive told the New York Times, because "search and AI are deeply integrated."
Thanks to long-time Slashdot reader theodp for sharing the article.

Coordinated disturbances haunt grids worldwide. Here’s how researchers solved the mystery.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-08
20:30:00 UTC
05:30:00 KST

For years, mysterious electrical anomalies have been flummoxing grid managers around the world. Every 60 seconds, the frequency on the grid would drop a tiny bit.
Even weirder: The sags happened at the exact same time on power grids across countries and continents.
It was a mystery that Dirk Witthaut, a researcher at Forschungszentrum Jülich in Germany, couldn’t pass up.
Germany’s largest transmission system operator, Tennet Germany, brought the puzzle to Witthaut, and it took years of investigative and modeling work to determine the cause. From Europe to Australia, the U.S. to Malaysia, the same pattern shows up in the data.
Such frequency drops aren’t unheard of, but they are troubling. And the regularity with which they have been occurring can make the phenomenon feel even more ominous.
Balancing the grid
The grid’s orderly operation relies on the frequency being kept within a certain range. If the oscillations get get too large, or if grid operators don’t know the cause and respond improperly, they can lead to blackouts. Even if the sags don’t cause blackouts, they can damage equipment in power plants if they go unchecked, especially in hydropower turbines.
Hydropower plants have historically been a main driver of so-called ultra-low frequency oscillations (UFLOs). Every turbine vibrates, and if those vibrations occur with a certain regularity, known as the resonant frequency, they can magnify, sometimes to dangerous levels. Think of a wine glass breaking before an opera singer’s mighty pipes — that’s resonance.
So Witthaut and his team started investigating hydropower, the most obvious potential culprit. They used a computer model of a hydropower plant control system on the Scandinavian grid to test the hypothesis.
While they managed to find conditions that could generate a resonance that peaked once per minute, they couldn’t explain why it persisted for so long. Typically, resonances in mechanical systems will come and go, and so will the accompanying signal on the electrical grid. But this frequency drop kept happening minute after minute after minute. Every 60 seconds, without fail.
It then dawned on the team that anything operating with such clockwork required, well, a clock. How else could they explain the uncanny timing?
Searching for clues
To that hypothesis, the researchers started close to home, installing more than 80 smart power quality meters around the Jülich campus. The research site is outfitted with medium- and low-voltage distribution lines, transformers, solar panels, and battery energy storage systems that serve as uninterruptible power supplies (UPS). It also has a high-performance computer system as well as the usual office computers powered by much smaller UPS devices. The power quality meters sampled a range of attributes, including frequency, voltage, current, and power, once every three seconds.
Before long, the research team had its answer. The measurements recorded on the transformer attached to the battery energy storage system peaked every minute, just like on the bigger power grids.
It turns out that many stationary batteries, from data center UPSes to large grid-scale batteries, check their state-of-charge every minute. Since these devices are internet-connected, their clocks are in near perfect synchronicity. Every time one checks its charge, the disturbance is imperceptible on the wide grid. But when they all do it together, that disruption becomes apparent.
To find evidence that UPSes were the main culprit on the grid, Witthaut and his team turned to data provided by grid operators. They found their answer in Ireland.
There, data centers have grown to consume a large fraction of the country’s electricity. By 2022, data centers represented 18% of the load on Ireland’s grid, and each facility is served by a fleet of UPSes. Sure enough, between 2016 and 2021, the minute-by-minute frequency drop on the Irish grid quadrupled from 3 milli-Hertz (mHz) in 2016 to 12 mHz in 2021. More recently, some drops have exceeded 20 mHz.
Ireland’s 50 Hz grid is built to withstand swings of plus or minus 200 mHz, though the grid operator would rather limit the swings to 100 mHz. In that range, 20 mHz isn’t a lot, but data centers aren’t the only loads on the grid. If other loads also cause the frequency to sag, the extra bump from every UPS checking its state-of-charge could push the grid toward blackout conditions.
The solution
The problem is entirely preventable. Rather than check state-of-charge exactly on the minute, Witthaus and team recommend that UPS and grid-scale battery manufacturers add some randomization to the schedule.
While UPSes are driving the problem today, there’s a risk that the phenomenon could persist. The researchers also tested IoT devices. In devices as diverse as a smart oven and Raspberry Pi clusters, they were able to detect periodic power fluctuations. The fix is also a simple software patch, but many IoT devices go unpatched. A recent study found that less than 3% of IoT devices are running the latest firmware.
Regulators may soon have to step in to demand changes, but they can only address their corner of the grid. Given the global nature of the issue, it’ll ultimately require global coordination. The mystery may be solved, but the problem could remain for years to come.

Nvidia is investigating Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-08
20:27:28 UTC
05:27:28 KST

Nvidia has announced that it is opening an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang and his relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who was reportedly recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on the company.
Nvidia is investigating Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy
Following reports that Nvidia’s CEO had a ‘close relationship’ with an AI exec, the company is opening an investigation.
A statement posted by the board of directors reads:
The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation.
The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders. While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information. Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.
The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.
The New York Times reported last month that Huang had developed a “close relationship” with the Megaspeed executive, which he later admitted was romantic in nature in a memo to the company. US officials believe she was feeding information directly back to Beijing.
Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia and is the subject of a Commerce Department investigation into whether it was smuggling AI chips to China. The company’s AI chips are viewed as crucial to the US maintaining technological supremacy. Both the Biden and Trump administrations have restricted their sale to China. President Trump has loosened those restrictions but still bars sales of Nvidia’s most powerful chips to Chinese firms, and the Commerce Department must approve individual firms to handle the chips.
Just as importantly, Jensen Huang has gotten quite cozy with Donald Trump, and there is concern about what insights into the administration’s deliberations around AI he may have been privy to. And whether any of that information may have been shared with Alice Huang, and eventually found its way to Beijing.

The Web Is More Than Enough, by Paul Ford
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-08
19:48:32 UTC
04:48:32 KST

The Web Is More Than Enough
Last week was fun. We launched tinylittleoffice.com—you heard it here first!—and it turned out that lots of folks were in the market for an “office suite that stores data in the URL.”
So many people visited that the server went down (well, I maxxed out the CloudFlare free plan), and ultimately, after I put in my credit card, a couple hundred thousand people came by to check it out. People on Hacker News insisted it was a pointless waste of time, and folks on GitHub started asking for features and fixes, all of which we’re considering, and some of which we’re doing. The Register wrote an article about it, and it also made it, for a little while, to the top ten of Product Hunt.
So all good; we will continue to support and enhance it, bit by bit, while we also do stable software development work for our customers and clients. But I did want to pause for a second and point out something that surprised me about the process. It’s this:
 The web browser is very, very, very powerful software for building applications.
I know that is obvious and is the sort of thing I could have said any time in the last 20 years. But now there’s an addendum to the statement:
 The web browser is very, very, very powerful software for applications, and the cost of accessing that power is going down seemingly every day.
I put maybe twice as much effort into building a web-based office suite as I might normally put into writing a long newsletter post. I’m not telling you this because I am a very special boy. I’m telling you because if you want to, you can learn to do it, too.
Fast, cheap, good, right? But even after I had to put in my credit card, CloudFlare hosting costs…$0. Partly because I optimize for cheapness, but partly because that’s just how it goes these days. Fast? Dear God, computers are fast, and software development is also fast compared to the past. But as I code web apps, I keep finding new corners of the browser I didn’t know well. Things are just…wild in there.
- The Web Crypto API is a first-class security platform in the browser.
- The Web Assembly platform lets you run native-speed code in your browser.
- WebGL provides for high-quality 3D and 2D graphics in your browser.
- The Web Audio API lets you mix sound in your browser.
And on and on. The web is really the greatest distribution platform imaginable right now. It’s inherently multilingual—I released TinyLittleOffice in 21 languages (the most common NYC ones, which is why it has Creole and Yiddish), with lots of infrastructure for accessibility. Plus, of course, JavaScript is a full-featured programming language, and HTML can represent most things a document can do on a computer; if you need something more old-school, PDF.js lets you deal with PDFs in the browser. I think you can even hyphenate text reliably these days, although I refuse to believe it.
I knew these things existed. I’d even programmed with them. But I’d never really looked closely; I just downloaded whatever open-source code would make it easier to build and tried to drag software across the finish line.
My quirky 1990s-vintage office suite might not convince you—it’s weird and small. So take a look at Simon Willison’s new web-based browser 3D game, Battle Drones. He’s hosting it on GitHub. He wrote it himself. He’s not a games builder. It just pops right up in the browser and you play it. It’s multiplayer, and it works offline.
 … but I can now see a path to vibe coded games like this being taken seriously. Battle Drones is fun, it looks good, it has innovative features (the multiplayer-over-audio thing is a first for an RTS as far as I can tell). I’d love to see what someone with better taste than me and a driving passion to produce something truly exceptional could build!
All the various cool browser technologies have been around for years. But they are each extremely vast. If you get good at Web Audio, you probably don’t have time to get good at Web Crypto and Web Assembly and WebGL.
The reason they were so complex is, basically, because they were built for teams like those at Google, not for individuals. In the past, the web was for people to build web pages—and, yes, in the present, you can still do that, but for more than a decade, the web has been designed for giant companies so they can deliver software securely to billions of people who buy things with credit cards. These huge mega-libraries were dropped into the web browser to enable large teams to build big things, and the little guy was a bit of an afterthought. But now you can make a game in 3D with sound, and it can work just fine on a plane.
This is one of the places where “are we in an AI bubble” gets fuzzy for me, because it’s totally clear all these giant AI companies are huffing AGI paint fumes, but at the same time, if we actually unlocked the economic transformation of, say, 100 times as many people making software for each other, that would blow an enormous crater into the current tech economy. Don’t like the way your giant industrial looms make carpet? Hack your own firmware and make each carpet totally personalized! Turn any Instagram post into a huge floor covering! Suddenly all the carpet companies have to hack their own firmware to compete. What’s that going to be like?
This also destabilizes the app store economy. The high tax of building for app stores seems less worth paying when you can just test an idea in the world from a web server for $0 after a couple weeks. Perhaps Mozilla should take another swing at launching a mobile phone! (Forget I mentioned that.) In any case, what used to be a large industrial process is now a personal one, if you so desire. Web browsers enable incredibly rich app development—and that’s radically easier than it used to be.
It’s a mixed blessing. I’ve been a writer for years, and software development feels more and more like writing to me every passing week. The awkward part of the comparison is, in general, people do not want to pay writers any money at all. As a writer, you get used to it. But for software people, being perpetually devalued is pretty novel. Then again, if you need software to do something—like our clients!—say, to fix a process, organize a database, get more value out of a big piece of industrial equipment, it’s a pretty amazing time, because you can do just about anything. I’m pretty confident we’ll all meet in the middle, but it’ll take a while, and it will be different on the other side.

====================================================================================================

How I Fight AI Brain Fry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-08
19:37:42 UTC
04:37:42 KST

How I'm fighting the AI Brain Fry
If you work with Claude Code or Codex from the terminal, you know this one.
You start a task. The AI takes time to reply, so you start another one. Then the first one replies, but the reply needs one clarification, one follow up and one side task — and each of them wants its own tab. Then the second tab's reply comes in. You juggle. And all of a sudden you find yourself hopping between 20 threads, trying to keep all those contexts in your brain RAM.
Until you can't. Your brain gets exhausted, your focus smashes, and you don't know anymore what you were doing, where you started, and where you were supposed to finish.
A lot of people are suggesting taking breaks, thinking before typing, limiting scope. I have my own experiment.
I decided this way of working has two major problems: sequencing and context. So I organised my work a bit like a priority queue.
Here is how it actually works.
The queue lives in git. Every ticket is a markdown file in the repo, right next to the code it talks about, and the state of the board is a committed snapshot. Nothing important lives in a chat window and nothing lives in my head. If a session dies, the queue is still there.
An agent works that board in cycles. It researches new tickets, builds the ones a human has tagged as safe to build, runs the tests and a browser check, and verifies what is already deployed. For anything touching sensitive code it builds on a branch and asks first. It never deploys to production — that part is mine.
What it cannot do is decide. So everything that needs me lands in one place I call my owner inbox. A script reads the whole board and hands me a prioritised list of exactly the items waiting on my judgement — review this change, answer this question, rule on this tradeoff.
The reading surface is a Claude artifact. One page, rebuilt from git on every cycle, mirroring the whole board plus a review page per ticket. So I don't scroll back through a terminal trying to reconstruct what a change does. I open one link, read what was built and why, and give my verdict. The verdict goes back into git, onto the card. The page is only a viewer — git is the record.
Then comes the part that matters most.
I take one item. I load its context. I make a decision or request an action. And I close it, by putting it back into the queue.
That closing is the whole trick. The ticket doesn't keep hanging in my memory as a thing to remember about. The context closes with it. So when I pick the next item from the queue, I can actually focus. One thing at a time.
It is still exhausting. But I don't feel distracted or lost.
The challenge was, and still is, the tooling around it. Getting the context served up in a digestible manner, so loading a ticket takes a minute and not twenty. And keeping tickets from going into endless loops because they are blocked waiting for a ruling only I can give.
It's a living organism and I keep improving it. But it felt like a huge step forward in my productivity with AI tools, so I thought it was worth sharing.

Salon, One of the Web's Pioneering News Outlets, Shuts Down After 31 Years
